title: Propose Edits Without Signing In

summary: How anyone can click the edit button on any element to propose a change without an account, how proposals route to the right repository, and how anti-spam checks protect the system without logins.
content: Propose Edits Without Signing In How anyone can click the edit button on any element to propose a change without an account, how proposals route to the right repository, and how anti-spam checks protect the system without logins. contribute L.4  ClearedStack is an open public sandbox. Anyone can browse the Portal, inspect live worker queues, read sanitized errors, and propose fixes or improvements—without creating an account, remembering a password, or signing in. Clicking the edit button anywhere Across the Portal, elements carry a small pencil edit button. Whether you spot a typo in a guide, a stale description on a tool card, or a configuration value that looks off, you can click that button directly on the page to suggest a change. Opening the editor shows what the element currently holds and lets you submit a proposed update righ

title: Clicking the edit button anywhere
subtitle: Propose Edits Without Signing In
summary: Across the Portal, elements carry a small pencil edit button. Whether you spot a typo in a guide, a stale description on a tool card, or a configuration value t...
content: Clicking the edit button anywhere Propose Edits Without Signing In Across the Portal, elements carry a small pencil edit button. Whether you spot a typo in a guide, a stale description on a tool card, or a configuration value that looks off, you can click that button directly on the page to suggest a change. Opening the editor shows what the element currently holds and lets you submit a proposed update right from your browser. There is no account wall and no redirect to an external sign-in screen.

title: How edits route to the owning repository
subtitle: Propose Edits Without Signing In
summary: Behind the scenes, ClearedStack is split into focused repositories: the Portal itself ( clearedstack.com ) and the ten pipeline workers ( cs-01 through cs-10 )....
content: How edits route to the owning repository Propose Edits Without Signing In Behind the scenes, ClearedStack is split into focused repositories: the Portal itself ( clearedstack.com ) and the ten pipeline workers ( cs-01 through cs-10 ). You do not need to memorize which repository owns which part of the site. Every editable element is mapped in ownership map.json , which tells the Portal two things: - Where the change belongs: Routes the proposal to clearedstack.com or the specific worker repository ( cs-01 .. cs-10 ) that owns that data or rule. - What kind of change it is: Classifies the proposal as DATA (catalog or content text), CONFIG (a rule or setting), or ISSUE (a problem report or sub-tool request). Once submitted, the proposal enters the queue API ( hub-queue-api ) and waits in the /guides/decide/ inbox ( cs-04-decide ).

title: Live status tracking on your edit
subtitle: Propose Edits Without Signing In
summary: After you submit a proposal, the edit button on that element turns into a live status pill so you can watch your contribution move through the system in real ti...
content: Live status tracking on your edit Propose Edits Without Signing In After you submit a proposal, the edit button on that element turns into a live status pill so you can watch your contribution move through the system in real time: | Status | What Is Happening | | --- | --- | | Proposed | Your submission passed anti-spam and schema checks and is waiting in /guides/decide/ . | | Approved | The proposal was approved and routed to the internal Git server ( cs-git ). | | Building | The build runner ( cs-runner ) is running automated tests and packaging the updated app or worker image. | | Live | The app-store reconciler ( cs-store ) deployed the update, and your change is now live on the Portal. | If a proposal is declined, it never alters the repository and the queue records the decision transparently.

title: Stopping spam without logins or CAPTCHAs
subtitle: Propose Edits Without Signing In
summary: Allowing anonymous edits on the open internet invites automated bots and scrapers. Instead of forcing human visitors to create accounts or solve frustrating ima...
content: Stopping spam without logins or CAPTCHAs Propose Edits Without Signing In Allowing anonymous edits on the open internet invites automated bots and scrapers. Instead of forcing human visitors to create accounts or solve frustrating image grids, ClearedStack uses a 5-layer anti-spam shield : | Layer | How It Works | Why It Respects Visitors | | --- | --- | --- | | 1. Browser proof-of-work | When you click submit, your browser quietly solves a small cryptographic puzzle that takes about one second. | Invisible to real people, but expensive for bots trying to flood thousands of requests. | | 2. Honeypot field | A hidden form field that normal browsers never display or fill in. | Automated scrapers that fill every field are silently discarded. | | 3. Daily-salted IP rate limit | Converts your network address into a one-way hash using a secret salt that rotates daily, then caps submissions per hash. | Stops rapid-fire abuse without ever storing raw IP addresses. | | 4. Strict schema check | Verifies the target exists in ownership map.json , enforces a 4 KB size limit, and strips all HTML and scripts. | Prevents malformed payloads or code injection before anything reaches storage. | | 5. Review gate | Every proposal sits in pending approval inside cs-04-decide until explicitly approved. | Zero anonymous edits can ever touch cs-git or the live cluster automatically. | This combination keeps the door wide open for helpful visitors while ensuring that nothing reaches the codebase or running cluster without passing automated safety checks and review.

title: Answer every requirement
subtitle: Guide · Section L.2
summary: Turn a solicitation into a numbered list of requirements, a compliance matrix, an outline and a page budget, so nothing is missed.
content: Answer every requirement Turn a solicitation into a numbered list of requirements, a compliance matrix, an outline and a page budget, so nothing is missed. field L.2  Proposals are rarely lost on brilliance. They are lost because a required form was missing, a volume ran over its page limit or one instruction in a long list went unanswered. The cure is mechanical: write down every requirement, give each one a number and record where your proposal answers it. This guide walks through that process. It assumes you have read Read a solicitation. Three kinds of requirement A solicitation asks for three different things, in three different places. Keep them apart, because each is answered differently. | Kind | Where | What it asks | How you answer | | --- | --- |

title: Three kinds of requirement
subtitle: Answer every requirement
summary: A solicitation asks for three different things, in three different places. Keep them apart, because each is answered differently. | Kind | Where | What it asks ...
content: Three kinds of requirement Answer every requirement A solicitation asks for three different things, in three different places. Keep them apart, because each is answered differently. | Kind | Where | What it asks | How you answer | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Instructions | Section L | How to build and submit the proposal | Follow them exactly | | Evaluation factors | Section M | What the government will score | Make each one easy to find and to score | | Work requirements | Section C and attachments | What the contractor will do after award | Show that you understand and can do it | An instruction is pass or fail. An evaluation factor is where points are won. A work requirement is what you are promising to do.

title: Pull out the requirements
subtitle: Answer every requirement
summary: Go through the document and mark every sentence that binds someone. The verb tells you who. | Wording | Usual meaning | | --- | --- | | “The contractor shall” |...
content: Pull out the requirements Answer every requirement Go through the document and mark every sentence that binds someone. The verb tells you who. | Wording | Usual meaning | | --- | --- | | “The contractor shall” | A duty you take on if you win | | “The offeror shall” or “offerors must” | An instruction for the proposal | | “The Government will” | What the government intends to do | | “should”, “may” | A preference or a permission. Treat a “should” in the instructions as a “shall” | Three rules make the list reliable: 1. One requirement per line. A sentence that says “shall design, test and document” is three requirements. Split it. 2. Copy the words exactly. Do not paraphrase at this stage. Paraphrase is where requirements get lost. 3. Record where each one came from : section, paragraph and page. Do not stop at Sections L, M and C. Requirements also hide in Section H, in the attachments and in the answers to bidders’ questions. Go through every amendment the same way.

title: Number them
subtitle: Answer every requirement
summary: Give every requirement an identifier that will not change when you add or remove rows. A prefix for the source and a running number works well: The examples abo...
content: Number them Answer every requirement Give every requirement an identifier that will not change when you add or remove rows. A prefix for the source and a running number works well: The examples above are made up. The numbering is the part to copy.

title: Build the compliance matrix
subtitle: Answer every requirement
summary: A compliance matrix is a table with one row per requirement. It answers one question for each: where in our proposal is this addressed? | Column | What goes in ...
content: Build the compliance matrix Answer every requirement A compliance matrix is a table with one row per requirement. It answers one question for each: where in our proposal is this addressed? | Column | What goes in it | | --- | --- | | ID | Your identifier | | Source | Section, paragraph and page in the solicitation | | Requirement | The exact text | | Proposal location | Volume, section and page where it is answered | | Owner | Who is writing that part | | Status | Not started, drafted, reviewed, final | | Notes | Open questions, assumptions, risks | Build the matrix before anyone writes a paragraph. It is the plan for the proposal, and later it is the checklist for the final review. Some solicitations ask you to submit a compliance matrix, or supply a template for one. If so, the template is an instruction like any other. Use the government’s columns, not yours.

title: Tie the three together
subtitle: Answer every requirement
summary: The strongest proposals connect each part of the work to the factor it will be scored under and the instruction that says where to write about it. Add the links...
content: Tie the three together Answer every requirement The strongest proposals connect each part of the work to the factor it will be scored under and the instruction that says where to write about it. Add the links to your matrix: - For each evaluation factor in Section M, find the instruction in Section L that says where to address it. - For each of those, list the work requirements in Section C that belong under it. Where the three do not line up, you have found something worth a question to the contracting officer. A factor in Section M with no instruction in Section L, or the reverse, is a common flaw in solicitations, and other bidders will be confused by it too.

title: Let the instructions set the outline
subtitle: Answer every requirement
summary: Evaluators often work with a checklist built from Sections L and M. A proposal that follows the same order, with the same headings, is easy to score. One that r...
content: Let the instructions set the outline Answer every requirement Evaluators often work with a checklist built from Sections L and M. A proposal that follows the same order, with the same headings, is easy to score. One that reorganizes the material makes the evaluator hunt for it. - Use the solicitation’s own headings and numbering for your sections. - Keep the order the instructions give, even if another order reads better. - Use the solicitation’s words for things. If it says “transition-in”, do not write “onboarding”. - State compliance plainly near the top of each section, then show how.

title: Budget the pages
subtitle: Answer every requirement
summary: A page limit is a requirement. Pages over the limit are commonly removed and not read. Divide the limit before writing starts, in proportion to what is being sc...
content: Budget the pages Answer every requirement A page limit is a requirement. Pages over the limit are commonly removed and not read. Divide the limit before writing starts, in proportion to what is being scored. Suppose a technical volume is limited to 30 pages and the solicitation describes three factors. Section M usually gives their relative importance in words, such as “significantly more important than”. Turn that into working weights, set a couple of pages aside for the introduction, and split the rest: | Part | Working weight | Pages | | --- | ---: | ---: | | Introduction and summary | | 2 | | Factor 1, technical approach | 50% | 14 | | Factor 2, management approach | 30% | 8 | | Factor 3, staffing | 20% | 6 | | Total | | 30 | The weights are your own reading of the solicitation’s words, not the government’s numbers. The point is that the most important factor gets the most room, and that every writer knows their limit on day one. Check what counts toward the limit. Covers, tables of contents, resumes, figures and fold-out pages are counted in some solicitations and excluded in others.

title: Check the format rules
subtitle: Answer every requirement
summary: Formatting instructions are easy to meet and embarrassing to miss. List them in the matrix like any other requirement: - page size, margins and orientation - ty...
content: Check the format rules Answer every requirement Formatting instructions are easy to meet and embarrassing to miss. List them in the matrix like any other requirement: - page size, margins and orientation - typeface and minimum size, including in tables and figures - line spacing - headers, footers and page numbering - file type, file naming and maximum file size - which volumes are separate files - whether pricing may appear anywhere outside the price volume. Usually it may not

title: Define the acronyms
subtitle: Answer every requirement
summary: Reviewers read many proposals in a short time. Spell out each acronym the first time it appears in a volume, and include a list if the instructions ask for one ...
content: Define the acronyms Answer every requirement Reviewers read many proposals in a short time. Spell out each acronym the first time it appears in a volume, and include a list if the instructions ask for one or allow one outside the page count. Make the list at the end, from the finished text, so it matches what is actually used. Check for an acronym used with two meanings and for acronyms defined but never used again.

subtitle: Answer every requirement

content: What a tool can and cannot do here Answer every requirement Pulling out sentences with “shall” and “must”, numbering them and laying out a matrix is mechanical work, and a tool can do it in seconds. Deciding what a requirement means, whether your answer satisfies it and what the evaluator is really worried about is judgment. Use a tool for the first, and read every row yourself for the second. A tool can miss a requirement that is phrased unusually, or sitting in a table or an image.

Its design came out of a structured five-seat architecture council—bringing together Kubernetes platform operations, real-time interface design, queue systems, security compliance, and solo-maintainer pragmatism—followed by specialized engineering reviews. Every major choice on the site today traces back to a concrete trade-off settled in those discussions. title: Why the council rejected heavy third-party suites
subtitle: How the Architecture Council Designed v3.1
summary: Bundling Forgejo, Harbor, Argo CD, and CasaOS would have required 8–16 GiB of RAM just to run the control plane, along with dozens of upstream database tables a...
content: Why the council rejected heavy third-party suites How the Architecture Council Designed v3.1 Bundling Forgejo, Harbor, Argo CD, and CasaOS would have required 8–16 GiB of RAM just to run the control plane, along with dozens of upstream database tables and mixed licenses. By writing four small, single-purpose Go services from scratch under the MIT License , ClearedStack keeps the control plane under 640 MiB, removes Docker completely, and avoids copying any upstream code.

title: Why two namespaces beat eleven
subtitle: How the Architecture Council Designed v3.1
summary: An early draft proposed 11 separate namespaces (one for the hub and one per worker). The council simplified that to two namespaces : clearedstack for the 7 cont...
content: Why two namespaces beat eleven How the Architecture Council Designed v3.1 An early draft proposed 11 separate namespaces (one for the hub and one per worker). The council simplified that to two namespaces : clearedstack for the 7 control-plane pods and cs-workers for all 10 deterministic workers ( cs-01-intake through cs-10-notify ). Two namespaces keep NetworkPolicy isolation clean without multiplying boilerplate manifests for solo maintainers adopting the stack.

title: Backups and Monthly Restore Drills
subtitle: Guide · Section L.3
summary: What the three persistent storage volumes hold, how nightly encrypted backups protect them, and how automated monthly restore drills prove recovery works on the live Portal.
content: Backups and Monthly Restore Drills What the three persistent storage volumes hold, how nightly encrypted backups protect them, and how automated monthly restore drills prove recovery works on the live Portal. host L.3  Running a self-hosted platform on a single small server is simple and inexpensive, but it also means everything important lives on one machine unless it is copied elsewhere. ClearedStack separates stateless software (programs that can be restarted or recreated anytime) from persistent volumes (virtual hard drives that keep data even when a program restarts). Only three persistent volumes hold data that cannot be recreated automatically. Protecting those three volumes—and proving every month that they can actually be restored—is how the platform stays recoverable without guesswork. What the thr

title: What the three persistent volumes hold
subtitle: Backups and Monthly Restore Drills
summary: Most of ClearedStack's 17 programs do not store permanent data of their own. If the web Portal, the build runner, or any of the 10 deterministic workers ( cs-01...
content: What the three persistent volumes hold Backups and Monthly Restore Drills Most of ClearedStack's 17 programs do not store permanent data of their own. If the web Portal, the build runner, or any of the 10 deterministic workers ( cs-01 through cs-10 ) crashes, Kubernetes simply starts a fresh copy. All real state lives in three persistent volumes inside the clearedstack control-plane namespace. | Persistent Volume | Owner Service | What It Holds | Why It Cannot Be Recreated Easily | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Postgres | postgres | Work queues, item history, evaluation records, public edit proposals ( core. ), and sanitized public views ( pub. ) | Holds the live operational memory of every item, decision, and approved edit | | cs-git | cs-git | Bare Git source repositories for the platform, all 10 workers, sub-tools, and app.yaml manifests | Serves as the internal source of truth before changes are mirrored to GitHub | | cs-registry | cs-registry | Signed container images built inside the cluster (keeping the last 5 versions per app for instant rollback) | GitHub mirrors only source code—zero container images are stored on GitHub | Because container images are never uploaded to GitHub, losing cs-registry without a backup would mean rebuilding every service from scratch before anything could roll back or restart. Likewise, losing Postgres would erase the queue history and decision trail, and losing cs-git would risk un-mirrored commits or internal configuration manifests.

title: Nightly encrypted backups
subtitle: Backups and Monthly Restore Drills
summary: Every night, an automated backup job captures a clean snapshot of all three persistent volumes and sends the result to off-node storage so a hardware failure or...
content: Nightly encrypted backups Backups and Monthly Restore Drills Every night, an automated backup job captures a clean snapshot of all three persistent volumes and sends the result to off-node storage so a hardware failure or disk corruption on the host machine cannot wipe out both the live system and its backups. For Postgres , a database cannot simply be copied like a regular file while programs are actively writing to it; doing so can produce a half-written, unusable copy. Instead, the nightly job takes a consistent database dump (a complete, self-contained snapshot at one exact moment in time). For cs-git and cs-registry , the job captures the repository files and stored container image layers cleanly. Before any backup leaves the cluster, it is encrypted —scrambled using a secret key so the backup files are unreadable to anyone who does not hold that key. Even if an off-node storage bucket or backup drive were ever exposed, the contents remain locked. The decryption key itself is kept separate from the backup files so one does not compromise the other. | Backup Stage | What Happens | Why It Matters | | --- | --- | --- | | Consistent snapshot | Postgres is dumped cleanly; cs-git and cs-registry volumes are archived | Prevents half-written or corrupted files | | Client-side encryption | Archives are encrypted before leaving the host node | Protects data at rest in off-node storage | | Off-node transfer | Encrypted bundles are pushed away from the primary server | Survives full server loss or disk failure | | Retention pruning | Older nightly copies are rotated out on a fixed schedule | Keeps storage costs predictable |

title: Why an automated monthly restore drill proves backups work
subtitle: Backups and Monthly Restore Drills
summary: An untested backup is not a backup—it is a wish. Backups fail silently all the time: an encryption key rotates and no longer matches, a database schema changes ...
content: Why an automated monthly restore drill proves backups work Backups and Monthly Restore Drills An untested backup is not a backup—it is a wish. Backups fail silently all the time: an encryption key rotates and no longer matches, a database schema changes and breaks an old restore script, or a disk fills up halfway through an archive. You rarely discover those problems until the worst possible day, when the live server is already down. To eliminate that blind spot, ClearedStack runs an automated monthly restore drill . Once a month, the cluster spins up a temporary, isolated scratch area that is completely separate from the live Portal and live databases. Inside that scratch area, the drill downloads the latest nightly encrypted backups, decrypts them, and restores all three volumes—Postgres, cs-git , and cs-registry —from scratch. Once restored, deterministic verification checks confirm that the recovered data is actually usable, then clean up the temporary scratch resources so no extra RAM or disk space stays consumed. | Drill Check | What It Verifies | What a Pass Proves | | --- | --- | --- | | Decryption & unpack | The off-node archive downloads cleanly and unlocks with the current key | The backup is readable and keys have not drifted | | Postgres restore | The database loads without errors and core tables pass integrity checks | Queue history, items, and public views are intact | | cs-git restore | Bare repositories mount and pass Git consistency checks | Source code, sub-tools, and app.yaml manifests are whole | | cs-registry restore | Stored container image manifests and signed digests resolve cleanly | Apps can actually start and roll back without internet access |

title: Live status on the public Portal
subtitle: Backups and Monthly Restore Drills
summary: In keeping with ClearedStack's open-by-default design, the outcome of every monthly restore drill is published directly on the live Portal. Visitors and the sit...
content: Live status on the public Portal Backups and Monthly Restore Drills In keeping with ClearedStack's open-by-default design, the outcome of every monthly restore drill is published directly on the live Portal. Visitors and the site owner can see when the last drill ran, whether it passed or failed, and a high-level summary of the four verification checks—without exposing internal IP addresses, server names, or decryption keys. If a backup or restore step ever breaks, it surfaces right away as a visible status alert rather than hiding in a log file until an outage occurs.

title: Build and verify a tool (cs-06 to cs-08)

content: Build and verify a tool (cs-06 to cs-08) How cs-06-build generates static tools from deterministic stack templates, how cs-07-verify enforces the 5-condition test suite, and how cs-08-catalog publishes to /tools. contribute L.4  Every tool in the ClearedStack catalog is a small, static, 100% deterministic web utility built from public regulations—with zero AI at runtime, zero accounts, and zero network calls after the page loads. In ClearedStack v3.1, three workers turn an approved idea into a live listing on /tools : cs-06-build , cs-07-verify , and cs-08-catalog . Before these three stages run, cs-04-decide records owner approval and cs-05-provenance stamps the provenance note and compiles a clean-room JSON build specification. That specification describes what regulatory job the tool performs without copying any th

title: Step 1: Generate the tool with cs-06-build
subtitle: Build and verify a tool (cs-06 to cs-08)
summary: cs-06-build reads the clean-room JSON specification and its worked-example fixtures, then generates an isolated, MIT-licensed static tool repository inside cs-g...
content: Step 1: Generate the tool with cs-06-build Build and verify a tool (cs-06 to cs-08) cs-06-build reads the clean-room JSON specification and its worked-example fixtures, then generates an isolated, MIT-licensed static tool repository inside cs-git . Rather than writing custom boilerplate from scratch each time, cs-06-build uses four deterministic stack templates under stack-templates/ : | Stack Template | Best For | Typical Inputs & Outputs | | --- | --- | --- | | calculator | Rate build-ups, interest math, thresholds | Numeric rates or dates in; step-by-step math and cited totals out | | checklist | Solicitation reviews, compliance prep | Structured yes/no items with regulatory citations and local browser progress | | validator | Checking codes, tables, or local files | User-supplied text or local files parsed in memory against bundled rules | | decision-tree | Eligibility, clause applicability, routing | Guided branching questions leading to a deterministic, cited outcome | Every template produces static files—HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and bundled JSON reference tables—that run entirely in browser memory. There is no backend server, no external font or CDN link, and no runtime LLM. If a clean-room specification requires an interaction pattern that none of the four templates support, cs-06-build fails closed : it pauses the item in needs subtool so a maintainer can add a deterministic template or sub-tool rather than guessing.

title: Step 2: Run the 5-condition suite with cs-07-verify
subtitle: Build and verify a tool (cs-06 to cs-08)
summary: Once cs-06-build produces a tool repository, cs-runner builds the static bundle without Docker (using rootless BuildKit) and cs-07-verify runs the automated 5-c...
content: Step 2: Run the 5-condition suite with cs-07-verify Build and verify a tool (cs-06 to cs-08) Once cs-06-build produces a tool repository, cs-runner builds the static bundle without Docker (using rootless BuildKit) and cs-07-verify runs the automated 5-condition verification suite . A tool cannot be listed unless every check passes: 1. Offline execution: The tool loads once and continues working with the network completely disconnected. All lookup tables, rates, and regulatory dates ship inside the repository. 2. Strict Content Security Policy ( connect-src 'self' ): Every page enforces a Content Security Policy including connect-src 'self' , default-src 'self' , and form-action 'none' . The browser itself blocks any attempt to fetch remote assets or send data off the user's machine. 3. Zero tracking or accounts: Automated checks confirm there are no sign-in walls, analytics scripts, cookies, visitor counters, or third-party beacons. If a tool remembers work in browser storage, it must disclose that on the page and provide a button to clear it. 4. Worked-example assertions: cs-07-verify executes the tool against hand-calculated worked examples, edge cases (such as zero values, empty files, and date boundaries), and made-up test fixtures. Real CUI, proprietary contractor rates, and non-public solicitation text are strictly forbidden. 5. Citations, scope limits, and MIT license: The suite checks that every calculation cites its public source (regulation, paragraph, and revision date), states what the tool does not cover, includes a plain disclaimer that outputs are not legal or compliance advice, and carries an MIT LICENSE file.

title: Step 3: Publish to /tools with cs-08-catalog
subtitle: Build and verify a tool (cs-06 to cs-08)
summary: After cs-07-verify passes all five conditions, cs-08-catalog publishes the tool to the clearedstack.com catalog at /tools . It manages the full catalog lifecycl...
content: Step 3: Publish to /tools with cs-08-catalog Build and verify a tool (cs-06 to cs-08) After cs-07-verify passes all five conditions, cs-08-catalog publishes the tool to the clearedstack.com catalog at /tools . It manages the full catalog lifecycle—adding newly verified tools, linking approved external tools, merging duplicates, or retiring outdated entries—and cs-git mirrors the public source code to GitHub (with zero container images stored on GitHub). From that point on, cs-09-monitor watches the cited federal sources (such as eCFR, Federal Register, and NIST) for revisions, while anyone visiting /tools can inspect the code, run the tool offline, or propose a data or configuration fix using the anonymous ✎ edit button without signing in.

content: How AI is used to build this project (and zero AI at runtime) AI tools assist only at authoring time under human review; zero AI runs in the 10 pipeline workers, the Portal, or any shipped tool. project L.6  This website, its guides, and its supporting code are drafted with the help of artificial intelligence tools—specifically Claude Code by Anthropic and Antigravity by Google. Every line of code, prose, and regulatory reference is reviewed, verified, and merged by a single human project owner, who decides what gets built and remains solely accountable for everything published here. Just as important is where AI is not used. There is a strict wall between how ClearedStack is written and how ClearedStack runs. Zero AI runs at runtime anywhere in the platform: not in the 10 pipeline workers ( cs-01

Zero LLMs and zero AI calls. | | Shipped tools | Static browser tools (JavaScript / WebAssembly) | Runs offline in your browser with connect-src 'self' , zero tracking, and zero external requests. |

title: Why the 10 workers stay 100% deterministic
subtitle: How AI is used to build this project (and zero AI at runtime)
summary: Many software pipelines reach for an AI model whenever they encounter an unfamiliar web page, an awkward PDF table, or a messy edge case. ClearedStack takes the...
content: Why the 10 workers stay 100% deterministic How AI is used to build this project (and zero AI at runtime) Many software pipelines reach for an AI model whenever they encounter an unfamiliar web page, an awkward PDF table, or a messy edge case. ClearedStack takes the opposite approach. All 10 workers—from cs-01-intake (deduplication) and cs-02-observe (page extraction) through cs-03-evaluate (rubric scoring), cs-06-build (tool generation), and cs-07-verify (automated testing)—execute plain, deterministic Go code and explicit rules. When a worker hits an unknown layout it cannot parse cleanly, it fails closed . Instead of guessing with an AI model, the worker pauses that item in a needs subtool state, and cs-10-notify logs a fingerprinted task in the worker's repository in cs-git . During authoring time, a new deterministic sub-tool (stored under tools// with golden test fixtures) is written, reviewed by the owner, and deployed. Once deployed, the queue automatically replays the paused items. Every solved edge case becomes permanent, repeatable code rather than a probabilistic guess.

title: The human review rule and known AI failure modes
subtitle: How AI is used to build this project (and zero AI at runtime)
summary: Language models are useful for drafting, but they fail in predictable ways—especially in federal contracting, where a wrong clause number or outdated threshold ...
content: The human review rule and known AI failure modes How AI is used to build this project (and zero AI at runtime) Language models are useful for drafting, but they fail in predictable ways—especially in federal contracting, where a wrong clause number or outdated threshold can cause real compliance issues. Every AI-assisted draft is checked against three known failure modes before it can be merged: | AI Failure Mode | What Goes Wrong | Human Verification Gate | |---|---|---| | Invented citations | Models hallucinate plausible-looking FAR or DFARS clause numbers that do not exist. | Every citation is verified directly against primary official sources (eCFR, Acquisition.gov, GovInfo, NIST). | | Outdated rules | Models cite repealed provisions, old dollar thresholds, or superseded NIST revisions. | Current effective dates and active statutory text are confirmed before approval. | | Confident wrong math | Models explain formulas clearly while making rounding or boundary-case errors. | Calculations are checked by hand across normal and edge cases, backed by deterministic test suites. |

subtitle: How AI is used to build this project (and zero AI at runtime)

content: Transparency and reporting mistakes How AI is used to build this project (and zero AI at runtime) To keep version history transparent, commits drafted with AI assistance include an Assisted-by trailer naming the tool alongside the human owner's sign-off, and all source code is mirrored publicly from cs-git to GitHub. If you spot an incorrect citation, a misquoted rule, or a calculation error anywhere on ClearedStack, you can propose an edit directly on the Portal without signing in, open an issue on the ClearedStack GitHub repository, or email contact@clearedstack.com with the page URL and supporting official source.

summary: Why one Postgres database in the clearedstack namespace owns all live state and queues, why workers talk through hub-queue-api without database passwords, and how worker local spools prevent lost work when the hub restarts.
content: Shared Hub Database and Worker Local Spools Why one Postgres database in the clearedstack namespace owns all live state and queues, why workers talk through hub-queue-api without database passwords, and how worker local spools prevent lost work when the hub restarts. host L.3  ClearedStack keeps all live platform state in one place while letting workers run independently. A single Postgres database inside the clearedstack control-plane namespace owns the current state and work queues, hub-queue-api acts as the only read-write gatekeeper in front of it, and each worker pod in cs-workers keeps a local spool volume so finished work survives hub restarts. One Postgres database for state and queues Instead of giving each microservice its own separate database, ClearedStack runs one postgres instance (Postgres 17) backed by a Persistent Volume Claim (a durable slice of cl

title: One Postgres database for state and queues
subtitle: Shared Hub Database and Worker Local Spools
summary: Instead of giving each microservice its own separate database, ClearedStack runs one postgres instance (Postgres 17) backed by a Persistent Volume Claim (a dura...
content: One Postgres database for state and queues Shared Hub Database and Worker Local Spools Instead of giving each microservice its own separate database, ClearedStack runs one postgres instance (Postgres 17) backed by a Persistent Volume Claim (a durable slice of cluster disk that survives pod restarts). Keeping current state and queues in one database avoids sync bugs between services and keeps the entire control plane small enough to run on a single 4 GiB k3s node. Inside Postgres, data is split into two schemas with strict boundaries: | Component | Namespace | Database Access | Responsibility | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | postgres | clearedstack | Stores core. and pub. | Single source of truth for items, queue leases, edit proposals, and sanitized public views | | hub-queue-api | clearedstack | Read/write on core. | Manages worker leases, needs subtool pauses, replay, anonymous edit intake, and live SSE updates | | clearedstack-web | clearedstack | Read-only on pub. ( pub ro role) | Serves the public Portal, App Store UI, and live pipeline status without touching internal tables or secrets | Putting queues and state in the same database means a state change and its next queue step happen together in one transaction. An item never ends up marked complete in one system while still sitting in a queue in another.

title: Why workers talk to hub-queue-api instead of Postgres
subtitle: Shared Hub Database and Worker Local Spools
summary: All 10 deterministic workers ( cs-01-intake through cs-10-notify ) run in the cs-workers namespace. None of them ever connect directly to postgres , and none of...
content: Why workers talk to hub-queue-api instead of Postgres Shared Hub Database and Worker Local Spools All 10 deterministic workers ( cs-01-intake through cs-10-notify ) run in the cs-workers namespace. None of them ever connect directly to postgres , and none of them hold database passwords or connection strings. Instead, workers communicate with hub-queue-api over cluster-private HTTP using their Kubernetes ServiceAccount identity. Network policy rules block cs-workers from reaching postgres on the network at all. | Concern | Direct Database Access (Avoided) | Via hub-queue-api (ClearedStack) | | --- | --- | --- | | Credentials in worker pods | Every worker needs a DB password | Zero DB passwords; workers use Kubernetes ServiceAccount HTTP | | Schema changes | Updating a table forces all 10 workers to update | Only hub-queue-api knows core. table layouts | | Queue coordination | Workers must implement locking and retries themselves | hub-queue-api issues leases, tracks heartbeats, and replays needs subtool items | | Live Portal visibility | Database writes happen silently | hub-queue-api streams progress to clearedstack-web via Server-Sent Events (SSE) | This separation keeps the blast radius small. Even if a worker pod processes untrusted public web pages (such as cs-02-observe fetching an external site), it has no database credentials to leak and no direct path to alter core. tables outside the rules enforced by hub-queue-api .

title: How worker local spools protect finished work
subtitle: Shared Hub Database and Worker Local Spools
summary: Because hub-queue-api and postgres are single control-plane services, a rolling upgrade or brief restart can make the hub unreachable for a few seconds. Without...
content: How worker local spools protect finished work Shared Hub Database and Worker Local Spools Because hub-queue-api and postgres are single control-plane services, a rolling upgrade or brief restart can make the hub unreachable for a few seconds. Without local buffering, a worker that just finished a job during that window would either drop its output or fail the task and force a full re-run. To prevent lost work, each worker pod mounts a local spool volume—a small, dedicated storage directory attached to the worker pod. The handoff follows a simple three-step loop: 1. Stage locally first: As soon as a worker finishes a deterministic step (such as extracting page data or running a verification suite), it writes the completed result to its local spool volume before trying to report back. 2. Acknowledge with the hub: The worker sends the result to hub-queue-api . If the hub accepts and saves it to Postgres, the worker deletes the spooled file. 3. Retry after hub restarts: If hub-queue-api is restarting or temporarily unreachable, the finished output stays safely in the worker's local spool. The worker retries delivery on a short backoff until the hub comes back online and confirms receipt. Because every worker is deterministic, combining central queue leases in postgres with local spools on the workers gives the platform clean recovery on both sides: unfinished work is re-leased if a worker restarts, and finished work is preserved in the local spool if the hub restarts.
