content: Find the source Check a tool’s answer Each listed tool has to say which regulation, standard or guide it is built on. Look for that reference in three places: - in the tool itself, next to the result or under a heading such as “Sources” or “How this is calculated” - in the README of the tool’s repository, which the Source link in the catalog opens - in the code, where formulas and data tables should carry a comment naming where they came from A good reference is specific. “FAR Part 31” tells you which book to open. “FAR 31.205-6(a)” tells you which paragraph to read. If a tool gives a result and no reference at all, treat the result as unverified and report the gap.

title: Open the current text
subtitle: Check a tool’s answer
summary: Read the rule where the government publishes it, not in a summary. These are the places most tools will point to: | What | Where the current text lives | | --- ...
content: Open the current text Check a tool’s answer Read the rule where the government publishes it, not in a summary. These are the places most tools will point to: | What | Where the current text lives | | --- | --- | | Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) and the defense supplement (DFARS) | acquisition.gov | | Any other federal regulation, cited as “CFR” | ecfr.gov | | NIST security publications, such as SP 800-171 | csrc.nist.gov | | CUI categories and marking rules | archives.gov/cui | | Small business size standards | sba.gov | | Prompt Payment interest rates | fiscal.treasury.gov | Where the rules live has the full list, with notes on how each source is organized and how to cite it.

title: Compare the dates
subtitle: Check a tool’s answer
summary: Regulations are revised, and a tool is a snapshot of the day it was written. Before you trust a figure, check that the tool and the current text agree on it. So...
content: Compare the dates Check a tool’s answer Regulations are revised, and a tool is a snapshot of the day it was written. Before you trust a figure, check that the tool and the current text agree on it. Some things change on a schedule: | What changes | How often | | --- | --- | | Prompt Payment Act interest rate | Every six months, on January 1 and July 1 | | Small business size standards | Reviewed on a rolling basis, and adjusted for inflation | | Acquisition dollar thresholds | Adjusted for inflation every five years, and by law in between | | NAICS industry codes | Revised every five years | | STIG content | Reissued several times a year | | NIST publications | Revised at irregular intervals; the revision number is part of the citation | Two habits help. First, read the “effective date” or “last amended” line on the source page. Second, check which revision of a standard your contract names. A contract can require an older revision than the newest one published, and the contract is what you are held to. The text wins. Use the figure from the current regulation, and tell the project so the tool can be fixed.

title: Work one example by hand
subtitle: Check a tool’s answer
summary: Arithmetic tools can be tested the way an auditor would test them. Pick one simple case, work it out with a calculator, and compare. For example, to test a labo...
content: Work one example by hand Check a tool’s answer Arithmetic tools can be tested the way an auditor would test them. Pick one simple case, work it out with a calculator, and compare. For example, to test a labor rate calculator, take an hourly wage of $50.00, a fringe rate of 30 percent, an overhead rate of 20 percent applied to wages plus fringe, a G&A rate of 10 percent and a fee of 8 percent: | Step | Calculation | Result | | --- | --- | ---: | | Wage | | $50.00 | | Add fringe | 50.00 × 1.30 | $65.00 | | Add overhead | 65.00 × 1.20 | $78.00 | | Add G&A | 78.00 × 1.10 | $85.80 | | Add fee | 85.80 × 1.08 | $92.66 | If the tool shows $92.66 for the same inputs, you know how it combines the rates. If it shows something else, you have found either a mistake or a different convention, such as overhead applied to wages alone. Both are worth knowing before you use the tool on real numbers. Labor rates and wrap rates explains the conventions. Round numbers make good tests because a wrong result is obvious.

title: Follow the solicitation
subtitle: Check a tool’s answer
summary: A solicitation can set its own rules for format, page counts, pricing structure, rounding and more. When it says something different from a tool’s default, foll...
content: Follow the solicitation Check a tool’s answer A solicitation can set its own rules for format, page counts, pricing structure, rounding and more. When it says something different from a tool’s default, follow the solicitation and change the tool’s inputs to match. Common places where a solicitation overrides a default: - Rounding. Some require rates rounded to the cent before they are multiplied by hours. Others want the extended price rounded. The totals differ. - Labor categories. The solicitation’s category names and descriptions are the ones to price, even if yours differ. - Page and font limits. These count differently from one solicitation to the next. Tables, covers and resumes may or may not be included. - Templates. If a pricing workbook or a compliance matrix is supplied, the deliverable is that file, filled in. Use a tool to work out the answer, then put it in the government’s format. If the solicitation is unclear, ask. Solicitations name a contracting officer or specialist and a deadline for questions. A written answer from them outranks any tool and any guide.

title: Read the code
subtitle: Check a tool’s answer
summary: Every tool is open source. You do not have to be a programmer to get something from the repository: - The README says what the tool covers, what it leaves out a...
content: Read the code Check a tool’s answer Every tool is open source. You do not have to be a programmer to get something from the repository: - The README says what the tool covers, what it leaves out and which sources it uses. - The issue list shows mistakes other people have reported and whether they were fixed. - The commit history shows when a figure or a formula last changed. If you do read code, look for the data tables and formulas first. They are usually short, and they are where an out-of-date figure would be.

title: Keep a record
subtitle: Check a tool’s answer
summary: When a number from a tool goes into a proposal, write down enough to reproduce it later. A pricing reviewer, an auditor or your own future self may ask where it...
content: Keep a record Check a tool’s answer When a number from a tool goes into a proposal, write down enough to reproduce it later. A pricing reviewer, an auditor or your own future self may ask where it came from. - the tool’s name and its version or the date you used it - every input you entered - the result - the regulation or standard the result rests on, with the paragraph number - the date you checked that text A note in the proposal file is enough. The point is that the number can be rebuilt without the tool.

title: Report a mistake
subtitle: Check a tool’s answer
summary: If a tool gets something wrong, say so. Email contact@clearedstack.com or open an issue in the tool’s repository. A useful report has four parts: 1. what you en...
content: Report a mistake Check a tool’s answer If a tool gets something wrong, say so. Email contact@clearedstack.com or open an issue in the tool’s repository. A useful report has four parts: 1. what you entered, using made-up values if the real ones are sensitive 2. what the tool showed 3. what the correct answer is 4. the section of the regulation that shows it A wrong result is the most useful thing you can report. Do not include real contract data, real rates or controlled information in a report. Issues are public.

title: What the tools are not
subtitle: Check a tool’s answer
summary: They are not legal, accounting or compliance advice, and they do not know your contract. For a decision that carries real risk, such as an indirect rate structu...
content: What the tools are not Check a tool’s answer They are not legal, accounting or compliance advice, and they do not know your contract. For a decision that carries real risk, such as an indirect rate structure, a certification you sign or a compliance score you submit to the government, talk to a qualified professional. A tool can make that conversation shorter. It does not replace it.

title: Run it on a closed network
subtitle: Guide · Section L.3
summary: Run the entire self-contained Kubernetes stack inside a disconnected enclave, or carry a frozen Snapshot Mode bundle for single-file offline use.
content: Run it on a closed network Run the entire self-contained Kubernetes stack inside a disconnected enclave, or carry a frozen Snapshot Mode bundle for single-file offline use. host L.3  ClearedStack is built to operate without an internet connection. Everything the platform needs to host code, build container images, store data, and run deterministic tools lives inside the platform itself, with no Docker anywhere and no runtime calls to outside AI services or third-party trackers. When you move ClearedStack onto a closed or air-gapped network, you choose between two modes: running the full self-contained Kubernetes stack inside a disconnected enclave, or exporting a Snapshot Mode bundle for single-file offline use. Choose your closed-network mode | Mode | What runs inside | B

title: Choose your closed-network mode
subtitle: Run it on a closed network
summary: | Mode | What runs inside | Best for | Updates and edits | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Full Enclave Stack | Complete 17-pod Kubernetes platform ( clearedstack a...
content: Choose your closed-network mode Run it on a closed network | Mode | What runs inside | Best for | Updates and edits | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Full Enclave Stack | Complete 17-pod Kubernetes platform ( clearedstack and cs-workers namespaces) on k3s and containerd | Teams that want the live Portal, internal code hosting, in-cluster builds, and all 10 deterministic workers inside an enclave | Users can propose edits, build with cs-runner , and deploy via cs-store completely offline | | Snapshot Mode | A single frozen, timestamped static bundle (HTML, CSS, JavaScript, fonts, and verified tools) | Analysts or small teams who only need to read guides, search the catalog, and run tools in a browser without a cluster | Read-only and fixed at the export timestamp; refresh by carrying in a newer snapshot |

title: Mode 1: Full self-contained Kubernetes stack
subtitle: Run it on a closed network
summary: Because ClearedStack does not depend on GitHub for container images or external registries at runtime, the entire platform can live inside a disconnected enclav...
content: Mode 1: Full self-contained Kubernetes stack Run it on a closed network Because ClearedStack does not depend on GitHub for container images or external registries at runtime, the entire platform can live inside a disconnected enclave with zero internet access. The stack runs on k3s with containerd —no Docker daemon is installed or used anywhere. Go services are built with ko , and the Next.js Portal is built with rootless BuildKit. Inside the cluster, two namespaces keep responsibilities separate: - The clearedstack namespace (control plane): Runs the seven core services— clearedstack-web (the Portal and App Store interface), hub-queue-api (queues and proposals), Postgres 17 (database storage), cs-git (internal Git repositories), cs-registry (internal OCI container image store), cs-runner (in-cluster builder and test runner), and cs-store (app reconciler and health monitor). - The cs-workers namespace (workers): Runs the 10 deterministic workers ( cs-01-intake through cs-10-notify ). Each worker runs predictable, rule-based Go code with zero AI at runtime. For JavaScript-heavy pages, cs-02-observe spawns on-demand headless browser jobs only when needed. Inside an enclave, cs-git , cs-registry , cs-runner , and cs-store form a closed loop. Teams can review proposals in the Portal, commit changes to cs-git , build and sign new images with cs-runner , push them to cs-registry , and roll them out with cs-store without ever touching the public internet. What changes when disconnected | Component | Connected behavior | Disconnected enclave behavior | | --- | --- | --- | | cs-git | Mirrors main and tags outbound to GitHub | Outbound GitHub mirror is disabled; all code stays in local bare repositories | | cs-09-monitor | Checks public regulatory feeds (such as eCFR and NIST) on a schedule | External fetches are paused or pointed at internal enclave mirrors | | cs-02-observe | Fetches public candidate pages over HTTPS | Only fetches addresses reachable inside your enclave, or processes imported local bundles | | cs-registry | Stores signed OCI images built by cs-runner | Serves all cluster images locally via containerd with zero external pulls |

title: Mode 2: Snapshot Mode for single-file offline users
subtitle: Run it on a closed network
summary: Not every closed-network user needs a Kubernetes cluster, a Postgres database, or background workers. Snapshot Mode exports a frozen, timestamped static bundle ...
content: Mode 2: Snapshot Mode for single-file offline users Run it on a closed network Not every closed-network user needs a Kubernetes cluster, a Postgres database, or background workers. Snapshot Mode exports a frozen, timestamped static bundle containing the site, the guides, the tool catalog, and every verified client-side tool. You can open a Snapshot Mode bundle directly from a local folder or serve it from any plain internal web server. Every font, stylesheet, script, and calculation runs locally in the visitor’s browser, and strict Content Security Policy rules ( connect-src 'self' ) prevent any outside network request. Because Snapshot Mode has no backend cluster, interactive control-plane features—such as submitting new proposals, running the 10-worker pipeline, or viewing live cs-09-monitor checks—are turned off. The bundle carries a visible build timestamp so users always know the exact date of the catalog and regulatory rules they are reading.

title: Moving files across the air gap
subtitle: Run it on a closed network
summary: Both modes follow the same transfer discipline: package on a connected machine, record a SHA-256 fingerprint before the move, carry the bundle through your orga...
content: Moving files across the air gap Run it on a closed network Both modes follow the same transfer discipline: package on a connected machine, record a SHA-256 fingerprint before the move, carry the bundle through your organization’s approved transfer process, and verify the fingerprint on arrival before loading anything. | Transfer item | Used for | What it contains | | --- | --- | --- | | Enclave bundle | Mode 1 (Full Enclave Stack) | Signed OCI image archives exported for containerd and cs-registry , Kubernetes manifests, and cs-git repository bundles | | Snapshot archive | Mode 2 (Snapshot Mode) | One compressed, timestamped static bundle ready to extract or open offline | | SHA-256 checksum file | Both modes | The cryptographic fingerprint used on the inside to prove not a single byte changed in transit | If a checksum does not match on the closed side, discard the transfer and move a fresh copy. Before relying on any regulatory threshold or compliance rule inside a disconnected environment, compare the snapshot or enclave sync date against the effective date of the rule you are checking.

title: Codes, registration and small business status
subtitle: Guide · Section L.2
summary: SAM registration, NAICS and PSC codes, size standards, the set-aside programs and what it means to be a nontraditional defense contractor.
content: Codes, registration and small business status SAM registration, NAICS and PSC codes, size standards, the set-aside programs and what it means to be a nontraditional defense contractor. field L.2  Before the government can pay you, it has to be able to identify you, classify what you sell and decide which competitions you are eligible for. That is done with a registration and a handful of codes. This guide explains each one and how they connect. Dollar thresholds, size standards and program rules in this guide were checked in November 2026. Several small business programs were being revised at the time. Confirm anything you rely on with the Small Business Administration and the current regulation. Register in SAM The System for Award Management, at SAM.gov, is the government’s register

title: Register in SAM
subtitle: Codes, registration and small business status
summary: The System for Award Management, at SAM.gov, is the government’s register of the businesses it can contract with. With few exceptions you must be registered the...
content: Register in SAM Codes, registration and small business status The System for Award Management, at SAM.gov, is the government’s register of the businesses it can contract with. With few exceptions you must be registered there before you can be awarded a contract, and stay registered to be paid. - Registration is free. Companies that offer to register you for a fee are not the government. You can do it yourself. - It takes time. Allow several weeks. Your legal name and address are validated against other records, and a mismatch stalls the process. - It expires. Registration has to be renewed every year. A lapsed registration can stop an award or a payment. Registration gives you two identifiers and holds a set of statements: | Item | What it is | | --- | --- | | Unique Entity ID (UEI) | A 12-character identifier assigned in SAM. It replaced the DUNS number | | CAGE code | A 5-character code identifying your company at a physical address, assigned as part of registration | | Representations and certifications | Statements about your company: its size, ownership and compliance with various laws. You confirm them each year, and each offer you submit relies on them | Those statements are made to the government. Read each one before you confirm it.

title: NAICS codes
subtitle: Codes, registration and small business status
summary: The North American Industry Classification System sorts businesses by what they do. A NAICS code has six digits, and each digit narrows the industry. Codes in t...
content: NAICS codes Codes, registration and small business status The North American Industry Classification System sorts businesses by what they do. A NAICS code has six digits, and each digit narrows the industry. Codes in the 54 group, for example, cover professional, scientific and technical services, and the codes under 5415 cover computer systems design and related services. NAICS codes matter in contracting for one reason above all: each code has a size standard, and the size standard decides whether you count as small. Two different sets of codes are in play: - Yours. In SAM you list the codes that describe your business. You can list many. One is marked as primary. - The solicitation’s. The contracting officer assigns one NAICS code to each solicitation, the one that best describes the main purpose of the purchase. That code’s size standard applies to that competition, whatever your primary code is. The codes are revised every five years. The 2022 edition was in use when this guide was checked.

title: Product and service codes
subtitle: Codes, registration and small business status
summary: A product and service code (PSC) describes what is being bought , where a NAICS code describes the kind of business that sells it . A PSC has four characters. |...
content: Product and service codes Codes, registration and small business status A product and service code (PSC) describes what is being bought , where a NAICS code describes the kind of business that sells it . A PSC has four characters. | Starts with | Covers | | --- | --- | | A digit | Products | | A | Research and development | | Another letter | Services. For example, codes beginning with D cover information technology services, and codes beginning with R cover professional and management support | Buyers record a PSC on every contract action, and many search by it when they look for vendors. So PSCs are how you find what an agency has bought before, and from whom. Knowing the handful of PSCs your work falls under makes searching past awards much more precise than searching by keyword. There is no official one-to-one mapping between the two systems. One NAICS code corresponds to many PSCs and the reverse. A crosswalk is a starting point for a search, built from how the codes have been used together.

title: Size standards
subtitle: Codes, registration and small business status
summary: A size standard is the largest a business can be and still count as small for a given NAICS code. The Small Business Administration sets them, in 13 CFR Part 12...
content: Size standards Codes, registration and small business status A size standard is the largest a business can be and still count as small for a given NAICS code. The Small Business Administration sets them, in 13 CFR Part 121, and publishes them in a table. There are two kinds of measure: | Measure | Used mostly for | How it is counted | | --- | --- | --- | | Average annual receipts | Services | Averaged over your last five completed fiscal years | | Number of employees | Manufacturing, and research and development | Averaged over the last 24 months, counting part-time staff | For example, in the table in effect when this guide was checked, custom computer programming services (NAICS 541511) had a size standard of $34 million in average annual receipts. Three things to know: - Affiliates count. Your size includes companies you control or that control you. Ownership, shared management and some contractual relationships can all create affiliation. - Size is judged per solicitation , under the NAICS code assigned to it, as of the date you submit your offer. - The standards move. They are adjusted for inflation and reviewed industry by industry, and a broader restructuring was under consideration in 2026. Always read the current table. For most set-asides you represent your own size. If a competitor believes you are not small, they can protest, and the Small Business Administration decides.

title: Set-asides
subtitle: Codes, registration and small business status
summary: A set-aside is a competition limited to a group of businesses. The basic rule, often called the rule of two: when a contracting officer reasonably expects offer...
content: Set-asides Codes, registration and small business status A set-aside is a competition limited to a group of businesses. The basic rule, often called the rule of two: when a contracting officer reasonably expects offers from at least two capable small businesses at fair prices, the purchase is set aside for small businesses. Dollar value changes the default. As of October 2025: | Purchase size | What generally happens | | --- | --- | | Up to the micro-purchase threshold, $15,000 | Bought without competition, often by card | | Above that, up to the simplified acquisition threshold, $350,000 | Reserved for small businesses unless two capable ones cannot be expected | | Above $350,000 | Set aside when the rule of two is met | This is why answering a request for information matters. Those answers are how a contracting officer learns that two capable small businesses exist.

title: The programs
subtitle: Codes, registration and small business status
summary: Beyond the general small business set-aside there are programs for particular groups, each with its own eligibility rules. All require the business to be small ...
content: The programs Codes, registration and small business status Beyond the general small business set-aside there are programs for particular groups, each with its own eligibility rules. All require the business to be small under the relevant code. | Program | Who it is for, in outline | How status is established | | --- | --- | --- | | Small business | Any business under the size standard | Self-representation in SAM | | 8(a) Business Development | Small businesses owned and controlled by socially and economically disadvantaged individuals | Certification by the Small Business Administration. The program was under substantial revision in 2025 and 2026 | | HUBZone | Small businesses with a principal office in a Historically Underutilized Business Zone, and a share of employees living in one | Certification by the Small Business Administration | | Service-disabled veteran-owned small business | Small businesses at least 51 percent owned and controlled by service-disabled veterans | Certification by the Small Business Administration. Self-certification is not enough for set-asides | | Women-owned small business, and economically disadvantaged women-owned | Small businesses at least 51 percent owned and controlled by women, for work in designated industries | Certification through the Small Business Administration | Each program’s rules run to many pages, and ownership and control are tested closely. Read the regulation and the Small Business Administration’s own guidance before you apply, and do not claim a status in SAM that you have not confirmed. A wrong status on an offer is a false statement to the government.

title: Doing the work yourself
subtitle: Codes, registration and small business status
summary: Winning a set-aside comes with a limit on how much of the work you can hand to others. For a services contract, a small business prime generally may not pay mor...
content: Doing the work yourself Codes, registration and small business status Winning a set-aside comes with a limit on how much of the work you can hand to others. For a services contract, a small business prime generally may not pay more than half of what the government pays it to subcontractors that are not themselves similar small businesses. The percentages differ for supplies and for construction. Check this before you build a team. A small prime that passes most of the work through to a large partner has not met the terms of the set-aside.

title: Nontraditional defense contractors
subtitle: Codes, registration and small business status
summary: A nontraditional defense contractor is defined in law, at 10 U.S.C. 3014, as a business that is not currently performing, and has not performed in at least the ...
content: Nontraditional defense contractors Codes, registration and small business status A nontraditional defense contractor is defined in law, at 10 U.S.C. 3014, as a business that is not currently performing, and has not performed in at least the year before a solicitation, any Department of Defense contract or subcontract that is subject to full coverage under the Cost Accounting Standards. Full coverage under those standards applies only to large contract awards, and contracts with small businesses are exempt from the standards altogether. As a result, most small businesses, and most commercial companies new to defense work, qualify. The status matters because some ways of doing business with the department are built around it: - Other transaction agreements for prototypes , under 10 U.S.C. 4022, generally require that a nontraditional defense contractor or a nonprofit research institution takes a significant part in the project, or that all significant participants are small businesses or nontraditional contractors, or that part of the cost is shared. - Commercial treatment. The law lets the department treat what a nontraditional contractor supplies as commercial, which brings simpler terms. Nobody issues a certificate for this status. You establish it by comparing your own contract history with the definition, and you may be asked to represent it in an offer. If you have ever held a large cost-type defense contract or subcontract, look closely before you claim it.

title: Put it to use
subtitle: Codes, registration and small business status
summary: A short routine for a new company: 1. Register in SAM, and put the renewal date in a calendar. 2. Choose the NAICS codes that describe what you actually do. Loo...
content: Put it to use Codes, registration and small business status A short routine for a new company: 1. Register in SAM, and put the renewal date in a calendar. 2. Choose the NAICS codes that describe what you actually do. Look up the size standard for each. 3. Work out your size under each: average receipts or employees, including affiliates. 4. Identify the PSCs your work falls under. 5. Search past awards by those PSCs and NAICS codes to see who buys what you sell. 6. Check which programs you may be eligible for, and apply for certification where it is required. 7. Answer requests for information in your area, and say plainly that you are small and capable.

title: STIGs, OSCAL and SBOMs
subtitle: Guide · Section L.2
summary: Three machine-readable formats that security compliance work runs on: what each one is, what is inside the file and how to check one.
content: STIGs, OSCAL and SBOMs Three machine-readable formats that security compliance work runs on: what each one is, what is inside the file and how to check one. field L.2  A good deal of security compliance is now exchanged as structured files instead of documents. Three kinds come up again and again: STIGs, which say how to configure a product securely, OSCAL, which describes controls and how a system meets them, and SBOMs, which list what software is made of. This guide explains each one at the level you need to open the file and understand what you are looking at. How they fit together | Format | Answers the question | Published by | File types | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | STIG | How must this product be configured? | Defense Information Systems Agency (DISA

title: How they fit together
subtitle: STIGs, OSCAL and SBOMs
summary: | Format | Answers the question | Published by | File types | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | STIG | How must this product be configured? | Defense Information Syst...
content: How they fit together STIGs, OSCAL and SBOMs | Format | Answers the question | Published by | File types | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | STIG | How must this product be configured? | Defense Information Systems Agency (DISA) | XML | | OSCAL | Which controls apply, and how does this system meet them? | National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) | XML, JSON, YAML | | SBOM | What components is this software built from? | Whoever builds the software | JSON, XML and others | They work at different levels. An SBOM describes one piece of software. A STIG describes the secure settings for one product. OSCAL describes a whole system and the controls around it, and can point to the other two as evidence.

title: What a STIG is
subtitle: STIGs, OSCAL and SBOMs
summary: A Security Technical Implementation Guide is a list of configuration rules for a specific product and version: an operating system, a database, a web server, a ...
content: What a STIG is STIGs, OSCAL and SBOMs A Security Technical Implementation Guide is a list of configuration rules for a specific product and version: an operating system, a database, a web server, a network device. Each rule says what to check and how to fix it. Systems on Department of Defense networks are expected to be configured to the STIGs that apply to them. Related terms: - A Security Requirements Guide (SRG) is the general version for a class of technology. A STIG applies an SRG to one product. - A benchmark is a STIG in a form that scanning tools can run automatically. - A checklist is a filled-in copy of a STIG for one machine, recording the result of every rule. STIGs are public. They are downloaded from DISA’s cyber site at cyber.mil, and they are reissued several times a year. Always note the version and release you worked from.

title: Inside a STIG rule
subtitle: STIGs, OSCAL and SBOMs
summary: A STIG is an XML file in a format called XCCDF. Each rule carries the same fields: | Field | What it holds | Example of the form | | --- | --- | --- | | Group I...
content: Inside a STIG rule STIGs, OSCAL and SBOMs A STIG is an XML file in a format called XCCDF. Each rule carries the same fields: | Field | What it holds | Example of the form | | --- | --- | --- | | Group ID | The identifier for the vulnerability | V- followed by digits | | Rule ID | The identifier for this version of the rule | SV- followed by digits and a revision | | STIG ID | The product-specific identifier | A product code and a number | | Severity | How serious a failure is | Category I, II or III | | Title | One line stating the requirement | | | Discussion | Why it matters | | | Check text | How to tell whether the system complies | | | Fix text | What to change if it does not | | | CCI | A link to the underlying security control | CCI- followed by digits | Severity has three categories: | Category | Label in the file | Meaning | | --- | --- | --- | | I | high | A failure that can directly lead to loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity | | II | medium | A failure that could lead to such a loss | | III | low | A failure that weakens the protections against one | When a rule is reviewed on a real system, its status is one of four: open (the system fails it), not a finding (it passes), not applicable , or not reviewed .

title: Working with STIGs
subtitle: STIGs, OSCAL and SBOMs
summary: - Find the right ones. A single server usually needs several: the operating system, each major application on it, sometimes the container platform underneath. -...
content: Working with STIGs STIGs, OSCAL and SBOMs - Find the right ones. A single server usually needs several: the operating system, each major application on it, sometimes the container platform underneath. - Search by any identifier. People cite rules by Group ID, Rule ID or STIG ID interchangeably. A lookup needs to handle all three. - Read the check text before the fix text. Many rules are already satisfied by default settings. - Record a reason for every exception. “Not applicable” and accepted “open” findings need a written justification that someone else can read later. - Recheck after each release. Rule IDs gain a new revision when the text changes, so a rule you closed can come back altered.

title: What OSCAL is
subtitle: STIGs, OSCAL and SBOMs
summary: The Open Security Controls Assessment Language is a set of formats from NIST for writing security controls, system descriptions and assessment results in a form...
content: What OSCAL is STIGs, OSCAL and SBOMs The Open Security Controls Assessment Language is a set of formats from NIST for writing security controls, system descriptions and assessment results in a form software can process. The aim is to replace the long word-processor documents and spreadsheets that compliance has traditionally run on. The same content can be written as XML, JSON or YAML, and converted between them without loss.

title: The OSCAL models
subtitle: STIGs, OSCAL and SBOMs
summary: OSCAL is several related formats, called models, grouped in three layers. | Layer | Model | What it describes | | --- | --- | --- | | Controls | Catalog | A set...
content: The OSCAL models STIGs, OSCAL and SBOMs OSCAL is several related formats, called models, grouped in three layers. | Layer | Model | What it describes | | --- | --- | --- | | Controls | Catalog | A set of controls, such as a NIST publication’s full list | | Controls | Profile | A selection from one or more catalogs, with adjustments: a baseline | | Implementation | Component definition | How one product or service can satisfy particular controls | | Implementation | System security plan | One system, its boundary and how it implements each control in its baseline | | Assessment | Assessment plan | What will be tested, how and by whom | | Assessment | Assessment results | What was found | | Assessment | Plan of action and milestones | Open findings and the plan to close them | Each file refers to the ones above it. A system security plan points to a profile, and the profile points to a catalog. To read a plan fully you need the files it refers to.

title: Checking an OSCAL file
subtitle: STIGs, OSCAL and SBOMs
summary: There are three levels of “valid”, and they are worth keeping apart. 1. Well-formed. The file is correct JSON, XML or YAML. A missing bracket fails here. 2. Sch...
content: Checking an OSCAL file STIGs, OSCAL and SBOMs There are three levels of “valid”, and they are worth keeping apart. 1. Well-formed. The file is correct JSON, XML or YAML. A missing bracket fails here. 2. Schema-valid. The file has the structure the OSCAL model requires: the right fields, in the right places, with values of the right type. NIST publishes the schemas for each version. 3. Meaningful. The identifiers resolve, the references point to things that exist, and the content says something true about the system. A validator checks the first two, and some of the third. No validator can tell you whether the plan describes your system accurately. A file can pass every check and still be wrong. Note the OSCAL version in the file’s metadata and validate against the schema for that version. An older file checked against a newer schema can fail for reasons that have nothing to do with its content.

title: What an SBOM is
subtitle: STIGs, OSCAL and SBOMs
summary: A software bill of materials is a list of the components a piece of software is built from: the libraries, their versions and how they relate. It is the softwar...
content: What an SBOM is STIGs, OSCAL and SBOMs A software bill of materials is a list of the components a piece of software is built from: the libraries, their versions and how they relate. It is the software equivalent of an ingredients label. It matters for two reasons. When a vulnerability is announced in a library, an SBOM tells you in minutes whether you ship that library. And on a network with no internet connection, it tells the people who approve software exactly what they are being asked to bring in. Two formats dominate: | Format | Maintained by | Common file types | | --- | --- | --- | | SPDX | The Linux Foundation. Also an ISO standard | JSON, tag-value text, others | | CycloneDX | OWASP. Also an Ecma standard | JSON, XML | Both can describe the same things. Tools usually read and write both.

title: What a useful SBOM contains
subtitle: STIGs, OSCAL and SBOMs
summary: Guidance published by the U.S. government in 2021 set out the minimum fields. For each component: - the supplier’s name - the component’s name - its version - o...
content: What a useful SBOM contains STIGs, OSCAL and SBOMs Guidance published by the U.S. government in 2021 set out the minimum fields. For each component: - the supplier’s name - the component’s name - its version - other unique identifiers, such as a package URL - its relationship to the other components, such as “depends on” - who produced the SBOM data - when it was produced When you are handed an SBOM, a few questions tell you how far to trust it: - How deep does it go? Only the direct dependencies, or the dependencies of those as well? - How was it made? From the build itself, from a lockfile, or by scanning the finished product? Each sees slightly different things. - Does it match the artifact? A good SBOM includes a checksum of what it describes. Compare it with the file you actually have. - How old is it? An SBOM describes one build. A new version of the software needs a new one.

title: Before you load a file into a tool
subtitle: STIGs, OSCAL and SBOMs
summary: These files can describe a real system in detail: host names, addresses, open findings, software versions. A filled-in checklist or a system security plan may i...
content: Before you load a file into a tool STIGs, OSCAL and SBOMs These files can describe a real system in detail: host names, addresses, open findings, software versions. A filled-in checklist or a system security plan may itself be controlled information. - Use made-up or public sample files to learn how a tool behaves. - Handle real ones only on a system approved for what they contain. - A tool that runs in the browser does not send the file anywhere, but it also does not change the rules for the computer it runs on. See What happens to what you type. The blank STIGs, the OSCAL schemas and NIST’s published catalogs are public and safe to use anywhere.

title: MIT licensing and the strict clean-room wall
subtitle: How ideas are credited
summary: Every software product separates into functional ideas and copyrightable expression. ClearedStack enforces an absolute technical wall between the two. When cs-0...
content: MIT licensing and the strict clean-room wall How ideas are credited Every software product separates into functional ideas and copyrightable expression. ClearedStack enforces an absolute technical wall between the two. When cs-02-observe inspects public pages, it extracts only structured facts and seals the raw observation snapshot behind the clean-room wall . Downstream build workers ( cs-06-build ) never have access to raw vendor HTML, screenshots, stylesheets, or marketing copy. When reusable open-source libraries under permissive licenses (MIT, BSD, or Apache 2.0) are used inside a repo, all original copyright notices and upstream license files are preserved. Strong copyleft code is never mixed into ClearedStack’s MIT repositories; compliant copyleft tools are linked externally instead.

content: How cs-05-provenance works How ideas are credited Once the owner approves a Build decision in cs-04-decide , the item moves to cs-05-provenance in the cs-workers namespace. Like every worker in the pipeline, cs-05-provenance is a 100% deterministic Go service—no language models, no prompt drift, and identical output on every run. sub-tool, or fail closed into needs subtool.", }, { tag: "Step 4", label: "Compile JSON build spec", detail: "Emit a sanitized JSON spec with inputs, formulas, and public test vectors for cs-06-build.", }, ]} /> If an item requires a tool structure not yet covered by tools/spec-profiles/ , cs-05-provenance fails closed, sets the state to needs subtool , and opens a task via cs-10-notify . Once a new deterministic sub-tool and golden fixture are committed to cs-git , hub-queue-api replays the queued item automatically.

title: Go-template provenance notes
subtitle: How ideas are credited
summary: Every tool inspired by an existing product carries a standardized provenance note stamped by cs-05-provenance using Go’s text/template engine. Because templates...
content: Go-template provenance notes How ideas are credited Every tool inspired by an existing product carries a standardized provenance note stamped by cs-05-provenance using Go’s text/template engine. Because templates are deterministic, attribution phrasing never varies or editorializes. Each rendered provenance note contains three factual lines: Idea seen in ( Tool Name (Vendor Name), observed YYYY-MM from its public pages ), What we took ( the job — one sentence describing the functional task ), and What we did differently ( runs entirely in your browser, free, no account; built from [Official Regulation] ). Provenance notes follow four strict rules: - They record only that a workflow was observed on a public web page on a specific date. - They never rate, criticize, or disparage the observed product. - They never imply partnership, sponsorship, or endorsement by the observed vendor. - Third-party product names are used solely in a nominative sense to identify prior art.

title: Compiling sanitized JSON build specs
subtitle: How ideas are credited
summary: Before cs-06-build can generate an isolated static tool repository, cs-05-provenance compiles a sanitized JSON build spec . This spec is the only artifact allow...
content: Compiling sanitized JSON build specs How ideas are credited Before cs-06-build can generate an isolated static tool repository, cs-05-provenance compiles a sanitized JSON build spec . This spec is the only artifact allowed to cross the clean-room wall into the build stage. | Spec Section | What cs-05-provenance Includes | What Is Stripped | |---|---|---| | provenance | Rendered Go-template note, observation date, opt-out status | Raw HTML snapshots, vendor marketing URLs inside build inputs | | authority | Official FAR, DFARS, NIST, or eCFR citations and effective dates | Vendor interpretations that conflict with government text | | schema | Typed inputs, outputs, units, validation bounds, and formula rules | Vendor field labels, proprietary database schemas, CSS classes | | vectors | Public worked examples and boundary-case assertions | Any scraped vendor test data or non-public inputs | If an observed commercial tool produces an answer that conflicts with an official government publication, cs-05-provenance always encodes the official government publication. The statute is the sole source of truth.

title: 48-hour and 5-day SLAs for corrections and opt-outs
subtitle: How ideas are credited
summary: cs-05-provenance also tracks and enforces response deadlines for vendor corrections and nominative attribution opt-outs. Requests can be submitted by emailing c...
content: 48-hour and 5-day SLAs for corrections and opt-outs How ideas are credited cs-05-provenance also tracks and enforces response deadlines for vendor corrections and nominative attribution opt-outs. Requests can be submitted by emailing contact@clearedstack.com , opening a public GitHub issue, or submitting an anonymous ✎ edit proposal on the Portal (which routes through cs-04-decide for owner verification). - 48-hour verification SLA. Every correction or opt-out request enters a tracked clock in cs-05-provenance so the maintainer’s identity is verified within 48 hours. - 5-day opt-out SLA. When a product owner prefers not to be named, cs-05-provenance updates the provenance metadata to a neutral phrase (such as “a commercial product”), re-runs the Go template deterministically, and pushes the updated entry through cs-08-catalog within 5 days. - Public source integrity. Factual errors in rules or license terms are corrected promptly upon verification, while citations to public-domain statutes and standards are never removed.

title: Why cs-git instead of Forgejo
subtitle: Internal Git Server & GitHub Mirror
summary: Traditional self-hosted Git platforms like Forgejo bundle a full web interface, user accounts, issue trackers, pull request reviews, and background job queues. ...
content: Why cs-git instead of Forgejo Internal Git Server & GitHub Mirror Traditional self-hosted Git platforms like Forgejo bundle a full web interface, user accounts, issue trackers, pull request reviews, and background job queues. ClearedStack does not need any of those features inside its Git server. Public visitors browse status, propose edits, and inspect queues through the clearedstack.com Portal without signing in, and the cluster already separates build jobs ( cs-runner ) and deployment ( cs-store ) into focused microservices. Writing cs-git from scratch in Go under the MIT license removes upstream license baggage and shrinks the Git server down to what the cluster actually uses. It runs inside the clearedstack control-plane namespace with a 64 MiB memory request and stores bare Git repositories on a Persistent Volume Claim (a dedicated slice of durable cluster disk). | Capability | Forgejo (Replaced) | cs-git (ClearedStack) | | --- | --- | --- | | Primary role | Full web forge with UI and accounts | Headless internal Git server and mirror | | Codebase and license | Large upstream project | Clean-room Go under MIT | | Memory footprint | Hundreds of MiB plus database state | 64 MiB RAM requested | | Storage model | App database plus repository files | Bare repositories on a cluster PVC | | Cluster integration | General-purpose webhooks | Push webhooks, lightweight patch API, outbound mirror |

title: How cs-git acts as primary
subtitle: Internal Git Server & GitHub Mirror
summary: Because cs-git sits inside the cluster-private clearedstack namespace behind a ClusterIP service and NetworkPolicy , it is unreachable from the public internet....
content: How cs-git acts as primary Internal Git Server & GitHub Mirror Because cs-git sits inside the cluster-private clearedstack namespace behind a ClusterIP service and NetworkPolicy , it is unreachable from the public internet. Only clearedstack-web exposes a public door. Everything that writes code or configuration inside the platform talks to cs-git first: - Approved public edits: When a visitor proposes a change on clearedstack.com and the owner approves it in cs-04-decide , cs-10-notify commits the patch directly to cs-git . - Missing sub-tool tasks: When a deterministic worker encounters an unfamiliar page or table layout, it pauses in needs subtool , and cs-10-notify opens a fingerprinted task in the owning repository in cs-git . - Image digest updates: After cs-runner builds and tests a new version, it updates the app's app.yaml manifest in cs-git (tagged [skip-ci] so it does not trigger another build loop). Whenever a commit lands on main or a new tag is created, cs-git fires two actions: it sends a push webhook to cs-runner to start a build, and it automatically pushes the updated code commits to the public GitHub mirror.

title: Why container images never touch GitHub
subtitle: Internal Git Server & GitHub Mirror

content: Why container images never touch GitHub Internal Git Server & GitHub Mirror ClearedStack mirrors source code to GitHub so anyone can read, audit, or fork the entire platform, but container images never leave the cluster for GitHub Packages. | Aspect | GitHub (Public Mirror) | cs-registry (Internal OCI Store) | | --- | --- | --- | | What is stored | Source code commits and tags only | Signed OCI v2 container images | | Network path | Outbound push from cs-git on change | Cluster-private inside clearedstack | | Rollback speed | Requires external network pull and auth | Instant local pull from last 5 digests | | Cleanup | External package retention rules | Daily garbage collection on cluster PVC | Keeping images inside cs-registry (a 64 MiB Go service backed by a local PVC) removes external registry credentials from worker pods, keeps cluster-private build artifacts off third-party servers, and guarantees that rollbacks work even if the outside internet is slow or unreachable.

summary: How ClearedStack builds, signs, and stores container images inside the cluster using ko, rootless BuildKit, and cs-registry—with no Docker daemon and no images on GitHub.
content: Internal OCI Registry and No-Docker Builds How ClearedStack builds, signs, and stores container images inside the cluster using ko, rootless BuildKit, and cs-registry—with no Docker daemon and no images on GitHub. host L.3  ClearedStack runs on k3s with containerd as its container runtime and does not use Docker anywhere—not on the host server, not inside build jobs, and not in production. Instead, an internal service called cs-runner builds and signs container images on demand, and an internal registry called cs-registry stores them inside the cluster. Why No Docker Anywhere Traditional setups run a background Docker daemon with root-level privileges to build and manage containers. On a small cluster, that daemon consumes extra memory and creates a wider security surface. Because k3s already uses containerd to s

title: Why No Docker Anywhere
subtitle: Internal OCI Registry and No-Docker Builds
summary: Traditional setups run a background Docker daemon with root-level privileges to build and manage containers. On a small cluster, that daemon consumes extra memo...
content: Why No Docker Anywhere Internal OCI Registry and No-Docker Builds Traditional setups run a background Docker daemon with root-level privileges to build and manage containers. On a small cluster, that daemon consumes extra memory and creates a wider security surface. Because k3s already uses containerd to start and run pods, the cluster only needs standard OCI images (Open Container Initiative—the universal, vendor-neutral format for container images). Removing Docker keeps the entire 17-pod platform—7 control-plane pods in the clearedstack namespace and 10 worker pods in the cs-workers namespace—light enough to run on a single 4 GiB k3s node.

title: How No-Docker Builds Work
subtitle: Internal OCI Registry and No-Docker Builds
summary: When a change lands on main or a new tag is created in cs-git , cs-git sends a webhook to cs-runner (a lightweight Go service requesting 32 MiB of RAM). cs-runn...
content: How No-Docker Builds Work Internal OCI Registry and No-Docker Builds When a change lands on main or a new tag is created in cs-git , cs-git sends a webhook to cs-runner (a lightweight Go service requesting 32 MiB of RAM). cs-runner launches a temporary Kubernetes Job pod to run tests, build the image, and sign it. It picks one of two daemonless builders depending on the repository: | Builder | Used For | How It Works Without Docker | | --- | --- | --- | | ko | All Go services ( cs-git , cs-registry , cs-runner , cs-store , hub-queue-api ) and all 10 workers ( cs-01-intake through cs-10-notify ) | Compiles Go source code directly into a minimal OCI image without a containerfile or container daemon. | | Rootless BuildKit | Web applications such as clearedstack-web (Next.js Portal and App Store UI) | Builds standard container layers inside an unprivileged, rootless pod—no root daemon or privileged flags required. | Before publishing an image, the build job runs the repository's golden tests so broken code never reaches the registry. Once tests pass, the job signs the image's digest (its unique cryptographic fingerprint) with cosign , pushes it to cs-registry , and commits the new digest to app.yaml in cs-git with a [skip-ci] marker so it does not trigger another build loop.

title: What cs-registry Does
subtitle: Internal OCI Registry and No-Docker Builds
summary: cs-registry is a clean-room Go microservice (requesting 64 MiB of RAM) built on standard OCI registry handler primitives. It implements the standard OCI v2 regi...
content: What cs-registry Does Internal OCI Registry and No-Docker Builds cs-registry is a clean-room Go microservice (requesting 64 MiB of RAM) built on standard OCI registry handler primitives. It implements the standard OCI v2 registry API and stores image layers on a PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) inside the clearedstack namespace. | Capability | How It Works in ClearedStack | | --- | --- | | Cluster-private access | cs-registry has no public Ingress. Kubernetes network policy rules restrict access to internal cluster traffic only ( cs-runner pushing, cs-store and containerd pulling). | | Zero images on GitHub | GitHub is a public source-code mirror pushed from cs-git on change. No container images are ever uploaded to or pulled from GitHub. | | Instant 5-version rollback | cs-registry retains the last 5 image digests per app so cs-store can roll back any service or worker in one click without rebuilding. | | Daily garbage collection | A scheduled cleanup pass removes unreferenced layers and manifests older than the retained 5 digests so disk usage stays predictable. |

Ephemeral build Jobs with cs-runner When cs-git receives a commit on main or a tag, it sends a push webhook to cs-runner in the clearedstack namespace. Rather than keeping an always-on CI runner pool or a privileged Docker daemon, cs-runner spawns short-lived Kubernetes Job pods ( ko for Go servic

title: Ephemeral build Jobs with cs-runner
subtitle: No-Docker Builds & the App-Store Reconciler
summary: When cs-git receives a commit on main or a tag, it sends a push webhook to cs-runner in the clearedstack namespace. Rather than keeping an always-on CI runner p...
content: Ephemeral build Jobs with cs-runner No-Docker Builds & the App-Store Reconciler When cs-git receives a commit on main or a tag, it sends a push webhook to cs-runner in the clearedstack namespace. Rather than keeping an always-on CI runner pool or a privileged Docker daemon, cs-runner spawns short-lived Kubernetes Job pods ( ko for Go services and workers; rootless BuildKit for clearedstack-web ), runs the repository's deterministic golden test suite, signs passing images with cosign , pushes them to cs-registry , and writes the new immutable digest back to app.yaml in cs-git with a [skip-ci] marker. (See Internal OCI Registry and No-Docker Builds for the full OCI storage and 5-digest retention breakdown.)

title: Replacing Argo CD and CasaOS with cs-store
subtitle: No-Docker Builds & the App-Store Reconciler
summary: Once an image digest is recorded in app.yaml , cs-store takes over. Traditional GitOps controllers like Argo CD introduce custom resource definitions (CRDs) and...
content: Replacing Argo CD and CasaOS with cs-store No-Docker Builds & the App-Store Reconciler Once an image digest is recorded in app.yaml , cs-store takes over. Traditional GitOps controllers like Argo CD introduce custom resource definitions (CRDs) and complex sync controllers, while home-server dashboards like CasaOS expect Docker Compose. cs-store combines the best parts of both into a single 48 MiB Go binary that speaks native Kubernetes Server-Side Apply—no custom CRDs required. cs-store watches app.yaml files in cs-git alongside image digests in cs-registry , then manages deployments across the platform's two namespaces: clearedstack for the seven control-plane pods and cs-workers for the ten deterministic workers. Through the /guides/apps/ App Store view (and /tools/ apps catalog section) on clearedstack.com , the owner gets four 1-click lifecycle controls backed by cs-store : - Install: Applies the app's manifests into the target namespace for the first time. - Upgrade: Rolls the Deployment forward to the latest signed digest built by cs-runner . - Pause: Scales the workload down cleanly without deleting its configuration or data. - Rollback: Switches app.yaml and the live Deployment back to one of the previous digests retained in cs-registry .

title: Live health and sanitized error reporting
subtitle: No-Docker Builds & the App-Store Reconciler
summary: cs-store continuously watches Kubernetes Pods, Deployments, and Events so /guides/apps/ and /tools/ apps reflect what is actually running. Before sending any st...
content: Live health and sanitized error reporting No-Docker Builds & the App-Store Reconciler cs-store continuously watches Kubernetes Pods, Deployments, and Events so /guides/apps/ and /tools/ apps reflect what is actually running. Before sending any status update to hub-queue-api for display on the public Portal, cs-store strips out internal cluster IP addresses, node names, and pod hostnames. Visitors see clear health states and standardized error codes—such as E TIMEOUT , E PARSE , or E NEEDS SUBTOOL —while the cluster's internal network layout stays completely private.

summary: Why zero AI runs in any worker or shipped tool, how per-case variations live as deterministic sub-tools inside each worker repo, and how unknown layouts fail closed and replay automatically.
content: 100% Deterministic Workers & Sub-Tools Why zero AI runs in any worker or shipped tool, how per-case variations live as deterministic sub-tools inside each worker repo, and how unknown layouts fail closed and replay automatically. project L.6  Every automated worker and every shipped tool in ClearedStack is 100% deterministic . Zero artificial intelligence models run inside any of the ten pipeline workers or any tool published to the catalog. Running an AI model inside a live background worker or a compliance tool is a different stor

title: Why zero AI runs at runtime
subtitle: 100% Deterministic Workers & Sub-Tools
summary: AI assistants are useful when drafting code or prose under human review, because a person reads and verifies the result before it is merged. Running an AI model...
content: Why zero AI runs at runtime 100% Deterministic Workers & Sub-Tools AI assistants are useful when drafting code or prose under human review, because a person reads and verifies the result before it is merged. Running an AI model inside a live background worker or a compliance tool is a different story. | Concern | AI at Runtime | 100% Deterministic Workers | | --- | --- | --- | | Repeatability | Can give different answers to the same input | Identical output every time on any cluster | | Auditability | Hard to trace why a model picked a number or rule | Every decision traces to a specific line of code or rule | | Operating cost | Ongoing API token bills for every page or item | Zero token costs; runs on a single small server | | Failure mode | May guess or invent data when confused | Fails closed and pauses for a deterministic fix | In federal contracting, guessing is worse than stopping. By keeping AI completely out of the runtime pipeline, every calculation, rule check, and page extraction can be inspected, tested, and trusted.

title: How unique cases live as sub-tools
subtitle: 100% Deterministic Workers & Sub-Tools
summary: Real-world websites, government PDFs, and vendor pages do not all look the same. One agency posts a neat table; another buries fees inside a multi-page brochure...
content: How unique cases live as sub-tools 100% Deterministic Workers & Sub-Tools Real-world websites, government PDFs, and vendor pages do not all look the same. One agency posts a neat table; another buries fees inside a multi-page brochure. Instead of asking an AI model to interpret each new layout on the fly, ClearedStack handles variations with deterministic sub-tools . Inside each worker repository, a registry file lists small, self-contained sub-tools organized by case. Each sub-tool has three parts: - Matching rule: Checks whether an incoming page, file, or item fits this specific pattern (such as a particular vendor slug or agency PDF format). - Deterministic logic: Extracts fields, scores criteria, or builds outputs using plain, predictable code. - Golden test fixtures: Saved sample inputs paired with exact expected outputs, so automated tests verify the sub-tool never breaks. Because each sub-tool lives right inside the worker repository that owns that stage of the pipeline, the team and contributors can see every supported variation in one place. | Worker Repo | Deterministic Job | Sub-Tool Variations | | --- | --- | --- | | cs-01-intake | Normalize URLs, deduplicate, and assign tracking IDs | Source adapters ( sam-gov , github-issues , web-sweep , site-form ) | | cs-02-observe | Fetch public pages and extract structured data | Layout extractors ( saas-marketing , gov-portal , agency-pdf , per-vendor slugs) | | cs-03-evaluate | Run knockout gates, 100-point rubric, and tie-breakers | Category rubric profiles | | cs-04-decide | Decision inbox on the Portal | None (human decisions only) | | cs-05-provenance | Stamp provenance notes, enforce SLAs, and compile build specs | Tool-type spec profiles | | cs-06-build | Generate isolated static tool repos from clean-room specs | Stack templates ( calculator , checklist , validator , decision-tree ) | | cs-07-verify | Run the 5-condition offline and zero-tracking test suite | None (universal checks) | | cs-08-catalog | Publish verified, linked, merged, or retired catalog entries | None | | cs-09-monitor | Run scheduled checks on regulations, live tools, and blockers | Source watchers ( federal-register , ecfr , nist-csrc , catalog watches) | | cs-10-notify | Route approved edits, sub-tool tasks, and alerts | Delivery targets ( internal-git , github-mirror , webhook-alert , portal-sse ) |

title: Failing closed into needssubtool
subtitle: 100% Deterministic Workers & Sub-Tools
summary: When a worker encounters a layout or format it does not recognize—for example, a vendor pricing table structured in a brand-new way—it never guesses or improvis...
content: Failing closed into needssubtool 100% Deterministic Workers & Sub-Tools When a worker encounters a layout or format it does not recognize—for example, a vendor pricing table structured in a brand-new way—it never guesses or improvises. Instead, it fails closed : 1. The worker stops processing that specific item and marks its status as needs subtool . 2. The notification worker ( cs-10-notify ) opens a clear task in the owning worker repository describing the unmatched pattern. 3. The paused item becomes visible on the Portal so anyone inspecting the pipeline can see why it stopped and which worker needs a new sub-tool. All other items in the queue continue moving normally. Only the unrecognized pattern waits.

title: Adding a sub-tool and replaying paused items
subtitle: 100% Deterministic Workers & Sub-Tools
summary: Once a contributor or maintainer writes a new deterministic sub-tool and includes a golden test fixture for the layout, the platform handles the rest automatica...
content: Adding a sub-tool and replaying paused items 100% Deterministic Workers & Sub-Tools Once a contributor or maintainer writes a new deterministic sub-tool and includes a golden test fixture for the layout, the platform handles the rest automatically: 1. Test and build: The build runner ( cs-runner ) runs the worker's test suite—including the new golden fixture—and packages an updated container image without Docker. 2. Deploy: The app-store reconciler ( cs-store ) rolls out the updated worker in the cluster. 3. Automatic replay: The queue API ( hub-queue-api ) detects the new capability and automatically replays every item that was paused in needs subtool for that pattern. Each edge case is solved once, tested forever, and turned into permanent deterministic code. Over time, the system grows more capable without ever sacrificing predictability.

title: Working on disconnected networks
subtitle: Guide · Section L.2
summary: The checks you run by hand when nothing can phone home: checksums, transfer manifests, certificates, lockfiles and image digests.
content: Working on disconnected networks The checks you run by hand when nothing can phone home: checksums, transfer manifests, certificates, lockfiles and image digests. field L.2  On a network with no route to the internet, the things a connected machine does quietly in the background stop working. Package managers cannot fetch, certificate checks cannot reach a revocation server, and nothing updates itself. The work moves to people, and it comes down to answering three questions about every file that crosses the boundary: is it the file I meant to bring, is it intact, and what is inside it? This guide covers the basic techniques. It is not a transfer policy. The rules for what may cross, and how, belong to the organization that owns the network. Checksums A checksum, o

title: Checksums
subtitle: Working on disconnected networks
summary: A checksum, or hash, is a short fingerprint computed from the contents of a file. Change one byte and the fingerprint changes completely. Two files with the sam...
content: Checksums Working on disconnected networks A checksum, or hash, is a short fingerprint computed from the contents of a file. Change one byte and the fingerprint changes completely. Two files with the same SHA-256 checksum are, for practical purposes, the same file. Compute one: | System | Command | | --- | --- | | Linux | sha256sum file.tar.gz | | macOS | shasum -a 256 file.tar.gz | | Windows PowerShell | Get-FileHash file.tar.gz -Algorithm SHA256 | Save one alongside the file, and check it later: The second command prints file.tar.gz: OK when the file is unchanged. Use SHA-256 or stronger. MD5 and SHA-1 still appear on old download pages, but both can be deliberately fooled and should not be relied on to detect tampering. A checksum proves a file has not changed since the checksum was made. It does not prove who made the file. If someone can replace the file, they can replace a checksum stored next to it. Send the checksum by a different route than the file, or use a digital signature, which ties the file to a key only the publisher holds.

title: A transfer manifest
subtitle: Working on disconnected networks
summary: When you move a folder instead of one file, make a manifest: a list of every file with its checksum. On the sending side: On the receiving side, with the folder...
content: A transfer manifest Working on disconnected networks When you move a folder instead of one file, make a manifest: a list of every file with its checksum. On the sending side: On the receiving side, with the folder and the manifest both carried across: Every line should end in OK . A line ending in FAILED is a file that changed. A “No such file” message is a file that went missing. The manifest catches changed and missing files. To catch extra files that were not in the original, count them on both sides: The two numbers should match. A useful manifest for a transfer record also notes who prepared it, when, from what source and for what purpose. Keep it with the approval paperwork.

title: Reading a certificate
subtitle: Working on disconnected networks
summary: A certificate binds a name to a public key and is signed by an authority that vouches for it. On a disconnected network you often have to inspect one by hand, b...
content: Reading a certificate Working on disconnected networks A certificate binds a name to a public key and is signed by an authority that vouches for it. On a disconnected network you often have to inspect one by hand, because the browser’s usual machinery cannot reach outside. Print the fields that matter: | Field | What to check | | --- | --- | | Subject | Who the certificate was issued to | | Subject alternative name | The host names it is valid for. This is what a browser matches against the address | | Issuer | The authority that signed it | | Not before, not after | The period it is valid for | Print everything, including key size, permitted uses and the signature algorithm: See the certificates a running server presents:

title: Checking a chain
subtitle: Working on disconnected networks
summary: A server certificate is trusted because of a chain: it is signed by an intermediate authority, which is signed by a root authority your machine already trusts. ...
content: Checking a chain Working on disconnected networks A server certificate is trusted because of a chain: it is signed by an intermediate authority, which is signed by a root authority your machine already trusts. To verify a certificate against a file holding the authorities you trust: It prints server.pem: OK when the chain is complete and every signature checks. The usual failures are: | Message | Meaning | | --- | --- | | unable to get local issuer certificate | An intermediate or the root is missing from the file you supplied | | certificate has expired | Today is past the “not after” date | | certificate is not yet valid | The machine’s clock is behind, or the certificate was issued for a later start | | self-signed certificate | The certificate vouches for itself and is not in your trusted set | Two things are particular to closed networks: - Private authorities. Internal networks, including government ones, run their own certificate authorities. Their root certificates are not built into ordinary browsers and operating systems. They have to be installed, from a source you trust, before anything they signed will verify. - Clocks. A machine with no time source drifts. A wrong clock makes good certificates look expired or not yet valid. Check the date before you blame the certificate.

title: Expiry and revocation
subtitle: Working on disconnected networks
summary: To find certificates about to expire, ask whether one will still be valid a set number of seconds from now. Thirty days is 2,592,000 seconds: The command says w...
content: Expiry and revocation Working on disconnected networks To find certificates about to expire, ask whether one will still be valid a set number of seconds from now. Thirty days is 2,592,000 seconds: The command says whether the certificate will expire in that time, and sets its exit status to match, so it can be used in a script. Revocation is harder. A certificate can be cancelled before it expires, and the normal ways of finding out need a network connection to the issuing authority. On a disconnected network the lists of revoked certificates have to be brought in on a schedule, like any other update. A certificate that verifies against a stale list may have been revoked since.

title: Lockfiles
subtitle: Working on disconnected networks
summary: A lockfile records the exact version of every package a project depends on, usually with a checksum for each. For this site, that file is package-lock.json . An...
content: Lockfiles Working on disconnected networks A lockfile records the exact version of every package a project depends on, usually with a checksum for each. For this site, that file is package-lock.json . An entry looks like this: | Field | What it tells you | | --- | --- | | version | The exact version that will be installed | | resolved | Where it was downloaded from | | integrity | A checksum the installer verifies before using the package | On a closed network a lockfile is three things at once: the list of what to bring in, the means of checking each item, and a record of what a build contained. Install from it with a command that refuses to deviate, such as npm ci , so that the build inside matches the build that was reviewed outside. Read the resolved lines. Every one that points at a public registry is a package that must be mirrored inside before the build can run.

title: Container images (zero Docker)
subtitle: Working on disconnected networks
summary: ClearedStack uses containerd and cs-registry with zero Docker anywhere. A container image is identified two ways: a tag (such as clearedstack-web:1 ), which is ...
content: Container images (zero Docker) Working on disconnected networks ClearedStack uses containerd and cs-registry with zero Docker anywhere. A container image is identified two ways: a tag (such as clearedstack-web:1 ), which is a human label, and a digest (a sha256: string computed from the exact contents), which cannot change silently. When an OCI image archive crosses a boundary as a .tar.gz file, compare its digest on both sides using ctr (containerd's built-in CLI): Check the exported file in transit with an ordinary sha256sum , then import it into containerd and cs-registry on the inside: Inside the network, always pin manifests in cs-git by digest rather than mutable tag:

title: Keep a record
subtitle: Working on disconnected networks
summary: For everything that crosses, write down enough to answer questions a year later: - what it is, and which version - where it came from: the address, the commit o...
content: Keep a record Working on disconnected networks For everything that crosses, write down enough to answer questions a year later: - what it is, and which version - where it came from: the address, the commit or the release - its checksum or digest - who reviewed it and what they checked - the date it was brought in - what it replaced Then set a date to look again. Software on a closed network does not learn about its own vulnerabilities. Someone has to bring that news in.
