Yes. There is no paid tier, no trial, no ads, no sponsorship, and no donation button. The project takes in no revenue. Shipped tools run in your browser, and the entire 17-p

title: About ClearedStack v3.1
subtitle: Common questions
summary: Is it really free? Yes. There is no paid tier, no trial, no ads, no sponsorship, and no donation button. The project takes in no revenue. Shipped tools run in y...
content: About ClearedStack v3.1 Common questions Is it really free? Yes. There is no paid tier, no trial, no ads, no sponsorship, and no donation button. The project takes in no revenue. Shipped tools run in your browser, and the entire 17-pod v3.1 platform (7 control-plane pods plus 10 deterministic workers) fits on a single 4 GiB k3s node. Who runs it? It is an independent personal project, built on personal time with personal equipment. It is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by the Department of Defense or any other government agency. See the About page for the full statement. What are the live Command Portal and App Store? In v3.1, clearedstack.com pairs its contractor-first catalog ( /tools/ ) with live operational factory views under /guides/ . The Command Portal ( /guides/command/ ) uses deterministic priority rules to float P0 errors, P1 stalled queues, and P2 pending decisions or edits to the top while collapsing quiet idle workers to one line. The App Store ( /guides/apps/ and /tools/ apps ) displays CasaOS-style cards for every running app and worker with live version, health, and sanitized errors, plus owner-only 1-click Install / Upgrade / Pause / Rollback controls. See Live Command Portal and Software decides the UI. Why is there no login lock? ClearedStack v3.1 is an open public sandbox. Anyone can browse the Command Portal, inspect running workers, read sanitized error codes, and propose edits using the ✎ button without signing in. To prevent abuse without requiring accounts or CAPTCHAs, public edits pass through a 5-layer shield: a ~1-second browser Proof-of-Work puzzle, a hidden honeypot field, a daily-salted IP hash rate limit, strict ownership map.json schema validation (4 KB max, scripts stripped), and a human approval gate in cs-04-decide . See Open public sandbox and Anonymous edits and anti-spam. What license does ClearedStack use? Every repository in ClearedStack v3.1— clearedstack.com , cs-01 through cs-10 , cs-git , cs-registry , cs-runner , and cs-store —is released under the MIT License . All Go and web code is written clean-room from scratch; while inspired by ideas from Forgejo, Argo CD, and CasaOS, zero upstream code is copied. See MIT clean-room architecture. Does the name mean I am “cleared” for something? No. The name is only a name. ClearedStack does not grant, verify, or imply a security clearance, a facility clearance, an authorization to operate, or a certification such as CMMC or FedRAMP.

title: 10 deterministic workers and zero AI at runtime
subtitle: Common questions
summary: Is AI used when the tools or workers run? No. ClearedStack v3.1 has zero AI at runtime across all 10 pipeline workers ( cs-01-intake through cs-10-notify ) and ...
content: 10 deterministic workers and zero AI at runtime Common questions Is AI used when the tools or workers run? No. ClearedStack v3.1 has zero AI at runtime across all 10 pipeline workers ( cs-01-intake through cs-10-notify ) and all shipped tools. There are no LLMs, no API calls to AI providers, and no token costs at runtime, so the same input produces the exact same output on any cluster. AI may be used as an authoring aid under human review, never inside running workers or tools. See How AI is used to build this project. How do the 10 workers handle unusual cases without AI? Each worker repo supports deterministic sub-tools under tools// listed in tools/registry.yaml . When a worker encounters an unfamiliar page or layout, it fails closed, pauses the item in needs subtool , and cs-10-notify opens a fingerprinted task in the owning repo. Once a deterministic sub-tool and golden test fixture are added and built, hub-queue-api automatically replays all queued items for that pattern. See Deterministic sub-tools. How does cs-02-observe handle JavaScript-heavy sites? cs-02-observe runs as a lightweight Go HTTP pod (~30 MiB RAM) for standard public pages and spawns on-demand headless browser Job pods only when a target site requires JavaScript rendering.

title: Infrastructure, no Docker, and GitHub mirror
subtitle: Common questions
summary: Why is there no Docker? ClearedStack v3.1 uses zero Docker anywhere . cs-runner listens to cs-git push webhooks and spawns ephemeral Kubernetes build Jobs insid...
content: Infrastructure, no Docker, and GitHub mirror Common questions Why is there no Docker? ClearedStack v3.1 uses zero Docker anywhere . cs-runner listens to cs-git push webhooks and spawns ephemeral Kubernetes build Jobs inside k3s + containerd : ko builds Go workers directly into OCI images, and rootless BuildKit builds the Next.js Portal. Images are signed with cosign and stored in the internal cs-registry OCI store, which keeps the last 5 digests per app for instant rollback. See cs-registry and no Docker and cs-runner and cs-store. What is GitHub used for? GitHub is a public code-only mirror . The internal cs-git service is the source of truth for all repositories and automatically pushes commits on main and tags to GitHub when changes are detected. Zero container images are ever pushed to or stored on GitHub. See cs-git and the GitHub mirror. How are cluster internals protected if the Portal is public? The cluster uses a 2-namespace topology : clearedstack holds the 7 control-plane pods ( clearedstack-web , hub-queue-api , postgres , cs-git , cs-registry , cs-runner , cs-store ) and cs-workers holds all 10 workers ( cs-01 through cs-10 ). Only clearedstack-web has a public Ingress. NetworkPolicy rules isolate internal traffic, cs-store strips node names, pod hostnames, and internal IPs before reporting health, and the public Portal reads only from sanitized pub. Postgres views. See Two-namespace topology and Network privacy and public logic.

title: Privacy, CUI, and using the tools
subtitle: Common questions
summary: Does anything I enter into a shipped tool leave my computer? No. Shipped tools run in your browser with zero tracking, zero cookies, zero analytics, and a Conte...
content: Privacy, CUI, and using the tools Common questions Does anything I enter into a shipped tool leave my computer? No. Shipped tools run in your browser with zero tracking, zero cookies, zero analytics, and a Content Security Policy ( connect-src 'self' ) that blocks outside requests. You can verify this in your browser's Network tab or by disconnecting from the internet after loading a tool. See What happens to what you type. Can I enter CUI or classified information? Never enter classified information into any tool or Portal form. For Controlled Unclassified Information (CUI), running in a browser does not change the rules for the machine you are using—handle CUI only on systems your contract and company policy allow, or host a private copy on your own closed network. See Run it on a closed network. Can I trust the numbers, and what if a tool disagrees with a solicitation? Treat tool outputs the way you treat a colleague's spreadsheet: helpful for saving time, not a substitute for verification. If a tool and a solicitation disagree, always follow the solicitation. If a tool disagrees with a published regulation, follow the regulation and propose an ✎ edit or report the citation. See Check a tool's answer.

title: Hosting and offline use
subtitle: Common questions
summary: Can I run my own copy of the v3.1 platform or static tools? Yes. You can deploy the full 17-pod v3.1 platform on a single k3s node with one command, or host the...
content: Hosting and offline use Common questions Can I run my own copy of the v3.1 platform or static tools? Yes. You can deploy the full 17-pod v3.1 platform on a single k3s node with one command, or host the static site and shipped tools on any web server or closed network. See One-command quickstart, Host on Kubernetes, and Host as plain files.

title: When something does not work
subtitle: Common questions
summary: What happens when a worker turns red or an app fails? cs-store watches Pod, Deployment, and Event health and surfaces sanitized error codes (such as E TIMEOUT ,...
content: When something does not work Common questions What happens when a worker turns red or an app fails? cs-store watches Pod, Deployment, and Event health and surfaces sanitized error codes (such as E TIMEOUT , E PARSE , or E NEEDS SUBTOOL ) directly on /guides/command/ , /guides/apps/ , and /tools/ apps . Visitors can inspect the item trail, view [Why?] drawers on /guides/pipeline/ , or propose a fix using ✎ . See When a worker is red. Where else can I report a bug or request a tool? Propose an edit directly on the Portal with ✎ , email contact@clearedstack.com, or open an issue on the GitHub mirror. Never include real contract data or CUI in any report or public proposal.

title: How candidates are found
subtitle: Guide · Section L.4
summary: How cs-01-intake discovers, normalizes, SHA-256 deduplicates, and assigns PA-XXXX records from public sweeps and anonymous no-login submissions.
content: How candidates are found How cs-01-intake discovers, normalizes, SHA-256 deduplicates, and assigns PA-XXXX records from public sweeps and anonymous no-login submissions. contribute L.4  Discovery in ClearedStack v3.1 is handled by cs-01-intake , the first of ten 100% deterministic Go workers running in the cs-workers Kubernetes namespace. Zero AI models run during intake: given the same URL or submission, cs-01-intake produces the exact same output on any cluster, with zero token cost. Its job is to collect public federal-contracting tools, spreadsheets, calculators, and community suggestions, clean their web addresses, check for duplicates, and assign a persistent PA-XXXX tracking identifier before handing the record to cs-02-observe . Deterministic URL normalization Website

title: Deterministic URL normalization
subtitle: How candidates are found
summary: Websites often serve the same tool at slightly different addresses—with tracking tags, uppercase letters, or trailing slashes. Before saving anything, cs-01-int...
content: Deterministic URL normalization How candidates are found Websites often serve the same tool at slightly different addresses—with tracking tags, uppercase letters, or trailing slashes. Before saving anything, cs-01-intake runs every incoming link through fixed, repeatable normalization rules: - Scheme and host casing: Converts the scheme ( https ) and domain name to lowercase. - Tracking and session removal: Strips marketing query parameters ( utm , ref , fbclid , gclid ), session identifiers, and URL fragments. - Path cleanup: Removes redundant trailing slashes and default index filenames where appropriate so equivalent paths resolve to one canonical address. - Public-only boundary check: Rejects non-public schemes, internal network addresses, or links that require credentials or paywall bypass. Because normalization is pure Go code with golden test fixtures, two people submitting the same tool with different referral links always produce the exact same canonical URL.

title: SHA-256 deduplication and PA-XXXX assignment
subtitle: How candidates are found
summary: Once a URL is normalized, cs-01-intake computes its SHA-256 cryptographic hash and checks it against hub-queue-api and Postgres ( core. tables) in the clearedst...
content: SHA-256 deduplication and PA-XXXX assignment How candidates are found Once a URL is normalized, cs-01-intake computes its SHA-256 cryptographic hash and checks it against hub-queue-api and Postgres ( core. tables) in the clearedstack control-plane namespace: 1. Duplicate hash found: If the SHA-256 digest already matches an existing record or known alias, cs-01-intake does not create a duplicate. It logs the sighting against the existing PA-XXXX entry (or links it as a mirror) and stops. 2. New canonical URL: If the hash is new, cs-01-intake mints a persistent PA-XXXX identifier (such as PA-0001 ), records the intake source, and queues the item for cs-02-observe via hub-queue-api . Every state change is immediately visible through read-only pub. Postgres views on the /guides/pipeline/ page of clearedstack.com .

title: Four deterministic sub-tools
subtitle: How candidates are found
summary: Candidate links arrive from very different places—government portals, GitHub issues, scheduled web sweeps, and the Portal submission form. Instead of using an A...
content: Four deterministic sub-tools How candidates are found Candidate links arrive from very different places—government portals, GitHub issues, scheduled web sweeps, and the Portal submission form. Instead of using an AI model to interpret unfamiliar formats, cs-01-intake routes each source through a dedicated sub-tool inside its own repository under tools// (registered in tools/registry.yaml , each with match.yaml , deterministic Go logic, and golden test fixtures). | Sub-tool ( tools// ) | Source | Deterministic job | | --- | --- | --- | | sam-gov | SAM.gov public notices | Extracts public tool links, agency calculators, and attachment URLs from SAM.gov feeds. | | github-issues | GitHub public mirror | Parses structured tool and paperwork suggestions opened on the public GitHub repository. | | web-sweep | Public .gov , .mil , APEX, and vendor sites | Runs scheduled, robots.txt -respecting sweeps across public contracting resources. | | site-form | clearedstack.com Portal | Validates and normalizes direct candidate submissions and ✎ intake proposals from visitors. | If cs-01-intake encounters a new source format that none of its sub-tools recognize, it fails closed : it pauses that item in needs subtool , and cs-10-notify opens a task in the cs-01-intake repository. Once a new sub-tool and golden fixture are committed, cs-runner builds the updated worker with ko (no Docker), cs-store deploys it, and hub-queue-api automatically replays every paused item.

title: Anonymous no-login submissions
subtitle: How candidates are found
summary: ClearedStack has no login lock. Any visitor can submit a candidate tool or propose an intake edit ( ✎ ) on clearedstack.com without creating an account or signi...
content: Anonymous no-login submissions How candidates are found ClearedStack has no login lock. Any visitor can submit a candidate tool or propose an intake edit ( ✎ ) on clearedstack.com without creating an account or signing in. To keep the queue clean without CAPTCHAs or user accounts, site-form and Portal ✎ submissions pass through a five-layer deterministic shield: 1. Browser Proof-of-Work: A roughly one-second SHA-256 puzzle solved in the visitor's browser on submit stops automated bot floods. 2. Honeypot field: A hidden form field silently discards automated scraper submissions. 3. Daily-salted IP hash rate limit: Limits repeated submissions per hashed IP without ever storing raw visitor IP addresses. 4. Strict schema validation: Checks the submission against ownership map.json , caps payload size at 4 KB, and strips all HTML and scripts. 5. Owner gate ( cs-04-decide ): Community proposals sit in core.edit proposal ( pending approval ) and never touch cs-git or the cluster until the owner clicks Approve in /guides/decide/ . Visitors see their submission's progress live on the Portal as a status pill: Proposed -> Approved -> Building -> Live .

title: What intake never does
subtitle: How candidates are found
summary: Discovery and intake remain strictly passive and public. cs-01-intake never creates accounts on third-party sites, requests sales demos, bypasses paywalls or CA...
content: What intake never does How candidates are found Discovery and intake remain strictly passive and public. cs-01-intake never creates accounts on third-party sites, requests sales demos, bypasses paywalls or CAPTCHAs, ignores robots.txt , or accepts Controlled Unclassified Information (CUI) or proprietary bid figures.

title: Invoices and late payment interest
subtitle: Guide · Section L.2
summary: What makes an invoice proper, when the government’s payment is due and how Prompt Payment Act interest is worked out when it is late.
content: Invoices and late payment interest What makes an invoice proper, when the government’s payment is due and how Prompt Payment Act interest is worked out when it is late. field L.2  The government is required by law to pay its bills on time, and to pay interest when it does not. That law is the Prompt Payment Act. It only helps you if your invoice is correct and you know which dates start the clock. This guide covers both, with a worked interest calculation. The rule in one paragraph Under the Prompt Payment Act, an agency generally has to pay within 30 days of receiving a proper invoice or of accepting the work, whichever is later. If it pays after that, it owes interest for every day it is late, at a rate the Treasury sets twice a year. The interest is owed automaticall

title: The rule in one paragraph
subtitle: Invoices and late payment interest
summary: Under the Prompt Payment Act, an agency generally has to pay within 30 days of receiving a proper invoice or of accepting the work, whichever is later. If it pa...
content: The rule in one paragraph Invoices and late payment interest Under the Prompt Payment Act, an agency generally has to pay within 30 days of receiving a proper invoice or of accepting the work, whichever is later. If it pays after that, it owes interest for every day it is late, at a rate the Treasury sets twice a year. The interest is owed automatically. You should not have to ask for it. The details are in the contract. Look for the prompt payment clause, long numbered FAR 52.232-25, and for any payment terms particular to your contract in Sections G and I.

title: What makes an invoice proper
subtitle: Invoices and late payment interest
summary: The clock does not start on an invoice that is missing something. A proper invoice includes: 1. your company’s name and address 2. the invoice date and an invoi...
content: What makes an invoice proper Invoices and late payment interest The clock does not start on an invoice that is missing something. A proper invoice includes: 1. your company’s name and address 2. the invoice date and an invoice number 3. the contract number, and the order number and line item number where they apply 4. a description of what was delivered, with quantity, unit of measure, unit price and extended price 5. shipping and payment terms 6. the name and address where payment is to be sent 7. the name, title and phone number of a person to contact about the invoice 8. your taxpayer identification number and electronic payment details, when the contract requires them on the invoice 9. anything else the contract asks for The contract can add to this list. Read the invoicing instructions before you send the first one, and build a template that matches.

title: If the invoice is rejected
subtitle: Invoices and late payment interest
summary: When an invoice is not proper, the agency is supposed to send it back within 7 days of receiving it and say what is wrong. Fix it and send it again. The 30 days...
content: If the invoice is rejected Invoices and late payment interest When an invoice is not proper, the agency is supposed to send it back within 7 days of receiving it and say what is wrong. Fix it and send it again. The 30 days are counted from the corrected invoice. If the agency takes longer than 7 days to tell you, the extra days are taken off the time it has to pay.

title: Find the due date
subtitle: Invoices and late payment interest
summary: Three dates decide when payment is due. Write each one down as it happens. | Date | What it is | | --- | --- | | Invoice received | The day the billing office n...
content: Find the due date Invoices and late payment interest Three dates decide when payment is due. Write each one down as it happens. | Date | What it is | | --- | --- | | Invoice received | The day the billing office named in the contract receives your proper invoice | | Acceptance | The day the government accepts the goods or services | | Due date | 30 days after the later of the two, unless the contract sets a different period | Two details catch people out: - Acceptance can be deemed. For the purpose of counting interest, acceptance is treated as happening on the 7th day after delivery if the government has not actually accepted or rejected the work by then, unless the contract sets a different period. An agency cannot hold the clock by leaving a delivery unreviewed. - The payment date is the date of the transfer , not the day the money shows in your account. Contracts can set shorter periods, and some categories of goods have their own by law. The contract is where to look.

title: The interest rate
subtitle: Invoices and late payment interest
summary: The Treasury sets the rate for each half of the year, starting January 1 and July 1, and publishes it on its Prompt Payment pages and in the Federal Register. F...
content: The interest rate Invoices and late payment interest The Treasury sets the rate for each half of the year, starting January 1 and July 1, and publishes it on its Prompt Payment pages and in the Federal Register. For July 1 to December 31, 2026 the rate is 4.75 percent a year. The rate that applies to a late payment is the one in effect on the day after the due date. It stays the same for that payment even if a new rate is published while you are waiting. The rate changes every six months. Before you rely on any figure, including the one above or one built into a tool, compare it with the Treasury’s published table for the period your due date falls in.

title: Work out the interest
subtitle: Invoices and late payment interest
summary: For a payment up to 30 days late, interest is simple interest on a 360-day year: Days late run from the day after the due date through the day payment is made. ...
content: Work out the interest Invoices and late payment interest For a payment up to 30 days late, interest is simple interest on a 360-day year: Days late run from the day after the due date through the day payment is made. A made-up example: an invoice for $20,000.00 was due on September 1 and paid on September 21. That is 20 days late, at 4.75 percent. When a payment is more than 30 days late, the interest that has built up is added to the amount owed at the end of each 30-day period, and the next period’s interest is worked out on the larger figure. Take the same invoice paid 45 days late: | Period | Owed at start | Days | Interest | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | First 30 days | $20,000.00 | 30 | $79.17 | | Next 15 days | $20,079.17 | 15 | $39.74 | | Total | | 45 | $118.91 |

title: The limits
subtitle: Invoices and late payment interest
summary: - Under one dollar. An interest amount of less than $1.00 is not paid. - One year. Interest stops building after a year. It also stops if you file a formal clai...
content: The limits Invoices and late payment interest - Under one dollar. An interest amount of less than $1.00 is not paid. - One year. Interest stops building after a year. It also stops if you file a formal claim under the contract’s disputes process, where different interest rules take over. - Disputes. No interest runs while there is a real disagreement about the amount owed or whether the work meets the contract. - Financing payments. Progress payments and other contract financing are not covered. The Act applies to payments for delivered and accepted work. - Your own delay. Interest does not run for time lost to a defective invoice the agency flagged on time.

title: If the interest is not paid
subtitle: Invoices and late payment interest
summary: Interest should arrive with the late payment, without a request. If it does not, there is a further penalty, and this one you do have to ask for. - The agency p...
content: If the interest is not paid Invoices and late payment interest Interest should arrive with the late payment, without a request. If it does not, there is a further penalty, and this one you do have to ask for. - The agency paid late and did not include the interest. - It still has not paid the interest 10 days after the payment. - You send a written demand to the payment office no later than 40 days after the payment was made. The additional penalty is equal to the unpaid interest, with a minimum of $25 and a maximum of $5,000. The 40-day limit is strict, which is one more reason to keep the dates.

title: Sending invoices to the Department of Defense
subtitle: Invoices and late payment interest
summary: Defense contracts normally require invoices to be submitted electronically through Wide Area WorkFlow, which is part of the department’s Procurement Integrated ...
content: Sending invoices to the Department of Defense Invoices and late payment interest Defense contracts normally require invoices to be submitted electronically through Wide Area WorkFlow, which is part of the department’s Procurement Integrated Enterprise Environment at piee.eb.mil. You register your company there, and your contract tells you which document type to submit and the codes that route it to the right offices. A document rejected in that system is the same as a rejected invoice. Check its status, do not assume.

title: What the Act does not cover
subtitle: Invoices and late payment interest
summary: - Payments from a prime contractor to a subcontractor. The Act governs what the government pays its own contractors. What a prime owes you is set by your subcon...
content: What the Act does not cover Invoices and late payment interest - Payments from a prime contractor to a subcontractor. The Act governs what the government pays its own contractors. What a prime owes you is set by your subcontract. Negotiate the payment terms before you sign. - Other transaction agreements and grants. These have their own terms. - Amounts withheld under the contract , such as retainage, until the condition for release is met. Small business primes and subcontractors may benefit from accelerated payment policies, under which agencies try to pay sooner than the law requires. That is a goal agencies work toward. It does not change the date from which interest runs.

title: Keep the record
subtitle: Invoices and late payment interest
summary: For each invoice, keep a line with: - delivery date - acceptance date, or the date acceptance was deemed - date the invoice was received by the billing office -...
content: Keep the record Invoices and late payment interest For each invoice, keep a line with: - delivery date - acceptance date, or the date acceptance was deemed - date the invoice was received by the billing office - due date - payment date and amount - interest owed, and interest received With those six facts you can check any interest figure by hand, and you can show the payment office exactly where a number comes from.

content: Getting started What ClearedStack v3.1 is, how to use the open no-login Portal, Snapshot Mode vs. the live cluster, and how anyone can inspect worker health or propose edits without an account. start L.1  ClearedStack is an open-source, 100% deterministic federal contracting platform and reference library. It combines client-side contracting tools, plain-language regulatory guides, and a transparent 10-worker automation pipeline—all licensed under MIT with no accounts, no paywalls, and no AI at runtime. Everything running and being developed on ClearedStack is open to the public. You do not need to create an account or sign in to read guides, run verified tools, inspect live worker health, or propose edits to the platform. For a deeper look at keyboard shortcuts and reading tracks, see How to n

title: Inspecting worker health without an account
subtitle: Getting started
summary: ClearedStack separates cluster-private internals from public operational transparency . Only the Portal ( clearedstack-web ) faces the internet, and it queries ...
content: Inspecting worker health without an account Getting started ClearedStack separates cluster-private internals from public operational transparency . Only the Portal ( clearedstack-web ) faces the internet, and it queries read-only pub. database views ( pub ro role). When you open /guides/command/ , /guides/apps/ , or /guides/pipeline/ without signing in, you can inspect: - Worker status and versions: Live health for all 10 deterministic workers ( cs-01-intake through cs-10-notify ) and control-plane services. - Queue depths and item trails: Which items are queued, verified, parked, or waiting in needs subtool for a new deterministic sub-tool. - Sanitized error codes: Structured failure codes such as E TIMEOUT , E PARSE , or E NEEDS SUBTOOL so anyone can see why an item paused. At the same time, internal cluster IPs, node names, pod hostnames, .svc.cluster.local DNS names, credentials, and signing keys are stripped by cs-store and never exposed.

title: Proposing edits without an account
subtitle: Getting started
summary: Anyone can suggest a fix, report a broken extractor, or propose a catalog update directly from the Portal—no GitHub account or site login required. To keep the ...
content: Proposing edits without an account Getting started Anyone can suggest a fix, report a broken extractor, or propose a catalog update directly from the Portal—no GitHub account or site login required. To keep the open sandbox safe without CAPTCHAs or logins, every ✎ submission passes through a five-layer deterministic shield: 1. Browser Proof-of-Work: Your browser solves a ~1-second SHA-256 puzzle on submit to stop automated spam. 2. Honeypot field: A hidden form field silently discards automated scraper submissions. 3. Daily-salted IP hash rate limit: Caps submission volume per hashed IP without ever storing raw IP addresses. 4. Strict schema validation: Checks the target element against ownership map.json , enforces the edit class ( DATA , CONFIG , or ISSUE ) and a 4 KB size limit, and strips all HTML or scripts. 5. Human approval gate: Proposals sit in pending approval inside /guides/decide/ and never touch cs-git or the cluster until the owner clicks Approve . Once submitted, your ✎ button turns into a live status pill so you can track your proposal from Proposed to Approved , Building , and Live .

content: What ClearedStack is not Getting started - Not a government agency: ClearedStack is an independent open-source project with no affiliation with the Department of Defense or any federal agency. - Not a security clearance or certification: The name refers to a technical stack for defense technology. It does not grant, verify, or imply security clearances, ATOs, or CMMC certification. - Not professional legal or accounting advice: Tools and guides provide deterministic drafts and educational reference. They do not replace a contracting officer, CPA, or attorney. - Not for classified information: Never enter classified or secret data into any browser on any system. See the About page for the full legal disclaimer.

title: Glossary
subtitle: Guide · Section L.5
summary: The acronyms and terms used across the tools and guides, in plain language, grouped by subject.
content: Glossary The acronyms and terms used across the tools and guides, in plain language, grouped by subject. reference L.5  Government contracting has a large vocabulary, and much of it is acronyms. These are the terms used on this site, grouped by the subject they belong to. Use your browser’s find command to jump to one. Definitions here are short on purpose. Where a term has a legal definition, the regulation is the authority, not this page. Buying and contracts - Acquisition. The government’s word for buying: the whole process from deciding a need to closing out the contract. - Amendment. A written change to a solicitation before award. Each one is part of the solicitation. - Award. The government’s decision to

title: Buying and contracts
subtitle: Glossary
summary: - Acquisition. The government’s word for buying: the whole process from deciding a need to closing out the contract. - Amendment. A written change to a solicita...
content: Buying and contracts Glossary - Acquisition. The government’s word for buying: the whole process from deciding a need to closing out the contract. - Amendment. A written change to a solicitation before award. Each one is part of the solicitation. - Award. The government’s decision to give a contract to an offeror, and the act of signing it. - BPA (blanket purchase agreement). A standing arrangement for repeated small purchases from the same vendor. - CFR (Code of Federal Regulations). The collected regulations of federal agencies, arranged in numbered titles. Title 48 holds the acquisition regulations. - CLIN (contract line item number). A numbered line in a contract for one thing being bought, with its quantity and price. A SLIN is a sub-line under it. - Contracting officer (CO or KO). The government official with authority to sign, change and end a contract. Only a contracting officer can commit the government. - COR (contracting officer’s representative). A government employee who monitors the work day to day. A COR cannot change the contract. - DFARS (Defense Federal Acquisition Regulation Supplement). The Department of Defense’s additions to the FAR. - FAR (Federal Acquisition Regulation). The main rulebook for how federal executive agencies buy goods and services. - GWAC (government-wide acquisition contract). A large ordering contract for technology that any agency can use. - IDIQ (indefinite delivery, indefinite quantity). A contract that sets terms and prices in advance and is then used by placing individual orders. - IFB (invitation for bids). A solicitation for sealed bids, awarded on price. - Modification. A written change to a contract after award. - Offeror. A company that submits a proposal. Also called a bidder, quoter or respondent, depending on the kind of solicitation. - Option. A right the government holds to extend a contract or buy more at prices already agreed. - OT (other transaction). An agreement that is not a FAR contract, used by some agencies for research and prototypes. Also called an OTA. - Period of performance. The dates between which the work is done. - Prime contractor. The company that holds the contract with the government. A subcontractor holds a contract with the prime. - PWS (performance work statement). A description of the work in terms of results required. - RFI (request for information). Market research. Not a solicitation. - RFP (request for proposals). A solicitation for negotiated contracts. - RFQ (request for quotation). A request for prices, usually for simpler purchases. - SBIR and STTR. Small Business Innovation Research and Small Business Technology Transfer: programs that fund research by small businesses in phases. - Section L and Section M. The parts of a solicitation that give proposal instructions (Section L) and evaluation factors for award (Section M). - Section M. The evaluation factors for award in a federal solicitation, used metaphorically on this site for the Prior Art decision engine. - Solicitation. The government’s written request for offers. - SOO (statement of objectives). A short statement of goals. The offeror proposes how to meet them. - Sources sought. A notice asking who is capable of doing a piece of work. Market research, like an RFI. - SOW (statement of work). A description of the work to be done. - Task order. An individual order for services placed under an ordering contract. - UCF (uniform contract format). The traditional layout of a solicitation in lettered Sections A through M.

title: Contract types and evaluation
subtitle: Glossary
summary: - Best value tradeoff. A basis for award in which the government may pay more for a better proposal. - Cost reimbursement. A contract type in which the governme...
content: Contract types and evaluation Glossary - Best value tradeoff. A basis for award in which the government may pay more for a better proposal. - Cost reimbursement. A contract type in which the government pays the contractor’s allowable costs, usually plus a fee. CPFF, cost plus fixed fee, is the common form. - CPARS (Contractor Performance Assessment Reporting System). Where the government records how a contractor performed. Other agencies read it when judging past performance. - FFP (firm fixed price). A contract type with a set price that does not change with the contractor’s costs. - LPTA (lowest price technically acceptable). A basis for award in which the lowest-priced proposal that meets the requirements wins. - Past performance. How well a company did on earlier, similar work. A common evaluation factor. - T&M (time and materials). A contract type that pays fixed hourly rates for labor, plus materials at cost. Labor hour, LH, is the same without materials.

title: Pricing and cost accounting
subtitle: Glossary
summary: - Allocable. Able to be assigned to a contract because it benefits that contract or the business as a whole. - Allocation base. The measure an indirect cost poo...
content: Pricing and cost accounting Glossary - Allocable. Able to be assigned to a contract because it benefits that contract or the business as a whole. - Allocation base. The measure an indirect cost pool is divided by to make a rate, such as direct labor dollars. - Allowable cost. A cost the government will pay on a cost-based contract: reasonable, allocable, consistent with accounting standards and the contract, and not excluded by FAR Part 31. - CAS (Cost Accounting Standards). Accounting rules for large negotiated contracts. Small businesses are exempt. - Certified cost or pricing data. Detailed cost information a contractor must certify as accurate on large negotiated awards without adequate competition. The dollar threshold is set by law and differs between defense and civilian agencies. - Cost pool. A group of indirect costs gathered together to be shared out. - DCAA (Defense Contract Audit Agency). The agency that audits contractors’ costs and accounting systems for the Department of Defense. - DCMA (Defense Contract Management Agency). The agency that administers defense contracts after award. - Direct cost. A cost incurred for one specific contract. - Escalation. A planned yearly increase in a rate or price. - Fee. Profit on a cost-based contract. - Fringe. The cost of employee benefits and payroll taxes, usually expressed as a rate on labor. - Fully burdened rate. An hourly rate that includes the wage, all indirect costs and fee. - G&A (general and administrative). The cost of running the company as a whole. - Incurred cost submission. The yearly report of actual indirect costs that a contractor with cost-reimbursement work sends to the government. - Indirect cost. A cost that supports more than one contract or the business generally. - ODC (other direct cost). A direct cost that is not labor, such as travel or materials. - Overhead. The cost of supporting the people who do contract work. - Proper invoice. An invoice with every element the contract and the prompt payment rules require. - Prompt Payment Act. The law that sets when agencies must pay and requires interest when they pay late. - Provisional billing rate. An indirect rate used for invoicing during the year, settled against actual costs afterward. - Unallowable cost. A cost the government will not pay, such as entertainment or alcohol. - Wage determination. A list of minimum wages and benefits for job classes on certain service and construction contracts. - WAWF (Wide Area WorkFlow). The Department of Defense’s system for submitting invoices and receiving reports. - Wrap rate. The multiplier that turns a wage into a burdened rate.

title: Security and compliance
subtitle: Glossary
summary: - Affirmation. A statement by a senior company official that the company meets, and will keep meeting, its security requirements. - ATO (authorization to operat...
content: Security and compliance Glossary - Affirmation. A statement by a senior company official that the company meets, and will keep meeting, its security requirements. - ATO (authorization to operate). A government official’s formal decision that a system may be used. - Banner marking. The marking at the top of each page of a document containing CUI. - C3PAO. A third-party organization accredited to carry out CMMC assessments. - CMMC (Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification). The Department of Defense program for verifying that contractors protect FCI and CUI. - CDI (covered defense information). The term in the DFARS for CUI handled under a defense contract. - CUI (controlled unclassified information). Unclassified information that a law, regulation or government-wide policy requires to be protected. - CUI Registry. The official list of CUI categories, kept by the National Archives. - Designation indicator. The block on a CUI document that names who controls it. - Export controls. Rules limiting who may receive certain technical data and items. The ITAR covers defense articles and the EAR covers dual-use items. - FCI (federal contract information). Non-public information provided by or created for the government under a contract. - FedRAMP. The government’s program for authorizing cloud services. - NIST. The National Institute of Standards and Technology, which publishes the security standards most contracts refer to. - NIST SP 800-53. The catalog of security and privacy controls for federal systems. - NIST SP 800-171. The requirements for protecting CUI on non-federal systems. - NIST SP 800-172. Enhanced requirements for CUI at higher risk. - POA&M (plan of action and milestones). The list of unmet requirements, with a plan and a date for each. - RMF (Risk Management Framework). The process federal agencies use to authorize their own systems. - SPRS (Supplier Performance Risk System). The Department of Defense system where assessment scores and affirmations are recorded. - SSP (system security plan). The document describing a system and how it meets each security requirement.

title: Technical formats and disconnected work
subtitle: Glossary
summary: - Air gap. A physical separation between a network and all others. - CA (certificate authority). An organization that issues and signs certificates. - Certifica...
content: Technical formats and disconnected work Glossary - Air gap. A physical separation between a network and all others. - CA (certificate authority). An organization that issues and signs certificates. - Certificate chain. The sequence from a server’s certificate through intermediates to a trusted root. - Checksum. A short fingerprint computed from a file’s contents. Also called a hash. - Client-side. Running on the user’s own computer, in the browser, and not on a server. - CSP (content security policy). An instruction from a web page telling the browser what it may load and where it may connect. - Digest. The checksum that identifies a container image by its contents. - Lockfile. A file recording the exact version and checksum of every dependency of a project. - Manifest. A list describing the contents of a package, an image or a transfer. - OSCAL (Open Security Controls Assessment Language). NIST’s formats for security controls, plans and assessment results as structured data. - SBOM (software bill of materials). A list of the components a piece of software is built from. - SHA-256. The checksum algorithm in general use for verifying files. - SRG (Security Requirements Guide). Security requirements for a class of technology. A STIG applies one to a specific product. - STIG (Security Technical Implementation Guide). Configuration rules for a specific product, published by DISA. - X.509. The standard format for certificates. - XCCDF. The XML format STIGs are published in.

title: Registration, codes and small business
subtitle: Glossary
summary: - 8(a). A Small Business Administration business development program for small businesses owned by disadvantaged individuals. - Affiliation. A relationship of c...
content: Registration, codes and small business Glossary - 8(a). A Small Business Administration business development program for small businesses owned by disadvantaged individuals. - Affiliation. A relationship of control between businesses that causes their sizes to be added together. - CAGE code. A five-character code identifying a business location. - HUBZone. Historically Underutilized Business Zone: an area, and the program for small businesses located in one. - Limitations on subcontracting. The rule limiting how much of a set-aside contract a small prime can pass to others. - Micro-purchase threshold. The dollar value under which purchases can be made without competition. - NAICS (North American Industry Classification System). Six-digit codes classifying businesses by industry. Each has a size standard. - NDC (nontraditional defense contractor). A business that has not recently performed defense work subject to full Cost Accounting Standards coverage. - PSC (product and service code). A four-character code describing what is being bought. - Rule of two. The rule that a purchase is set aside when two capable small businesses can be expected to offer at fair prices. - SAM (System for Award Management). The government’s register of the businesses it contracts with, and its site for posting opportunities. - SBA. The Small Business Administration. - SDVOSB. Service-disabled veteran-owned small business. - Set-aside. A competition limited to small businesses, or to one program’s participants. - Simplified acquisition threshold. The dollar value under which simpler buying procedures apply. - Size standard. The largest a business can be, in receipts or employees, and still count as small for a NAICS code. - Sole source. An award made without competition. - UEI (Unique Entity ID). The twelve-character identifier assigned to a business in SAM. - WOSB and EDWOSB. Women-owned small business, and economically disadvantaged women-owned small business.

title: Agencies and names
subtitle: Glossary
summary: - DISA. The Defense Information Systems Agency. It publishes the STIGs. - DoD. The Department of Defense. Since 2025 the department has also used the name Depar...
content: Agencies and names Glossary - DISA. The Defense Information Systems Agency. It publishes the STIGs. - DoD. The Department of Defense. Since 2025 the department has also used the name Department of War on its own sites and correspondence. The regulations and contract clauses cited in these guides still say Department of Defense, and so do the guides. - GSA. The General Services Administration. It runs SAM.gov and many government-wide contracts. - NARA. The National Archives and Records Administration. It oversees the CUI program across the government. - OMB. The Office of Management and Budget. - Treasury. The Department of the Treasury. Its Bureau of the Fiscal Service publishes the Prompt Payment interest rate.

title: Project and authoring
subtitle: Glossary
summary: - Antigravity. An agentic AI coding assistant used during development to draft code, tests, and documentation under human direction. - Claude Code. An agentic A...
content: Project and authoring Glossary - Antigravity. An agentic AI coding assistant used during development to draft code, tests, and documentation under human direction. - Claude Code. An agentic AI coding tool used during development to draft code, tests, and documentation under human direction. - Clean room. Building software from functional specifications and public regulations without examining or copying another tool's proprietary code, text, or design. - Decision log. A public record documenting every evaluation outcome, score rationale, drafting agent, and maintainer decision. - Knockout gate. A non-negotiable pass/fail screening check that an idea must satisfy before being scored or built. - Prior art. Pre-existing tools, spreadsheets, or documents solving a compliance or paperwork task, observed from public pages to identify the job to be done. - Provenance. A record stating where the idea for a tool came from, what was taken (the job), and what was done differently.

title: Host on Kubernetes (No Docker)
subtitle: Guide · Section L.3
summary: Run the full two-namespace ClearedStack platform on k3s and containerd with zero Docker, ~640 MiB control-plane RAM, and four lightweight microservices.
content: Host on Kubernetes (No Docker) Run the full two-namespace ClearedStack platform on k3s and containerd with zero Docker, ~640 MiB control-plane RAM, and four lightweight microservices. host L.3  ClearedStack runs as a complete, self-contained platform on a single lightweight Kubernetes cluster using k3s and containerd . You do not need Docker installed on your server, in your build pipeline, or anywhere on your cluster. The entire 17-pod platform—7 control-plane services and 10 deterministic workers—requests roughly 640 MiB of RAM for the control plane (with a 1.25 GiB limit) and about 300 MiB for all 10 workers combined. That means the whole stack fits comfortably on a single 4 GiB cloud server costing $10 to $20 per month. Why Docker is completely removed Traditional setups rely on

title: Why Docker is completely removed
subtitle: Host on Kubernetes (No Docker)
summary: Traditional setups rely on the Docker daemon to build and run containers, which adds unnecessary memory overhead and security risk inside Kubernetes. ClearedSta...
content: Why Docker is completely removed Host on Kubernetes (No Docker) Traditional setups rely on the Docker daemon to build and run containers, which adds unnecessary memory overhead and security risk inside Kubernetes. ClearedStack removes Docker at every stage: - Direct runtime with containerd: Kubernetes already includes containerd , a minimal container runtime that starts and manages pods directly. Running a separate Docker daemon on the host wastes memory and adds an extra layer to maintain. - No Docker-in-Docker builds: Building images inside a cluster with Docker usually requires mounting the host Docker socket or running privileged containers, both of which give build jobs near-root control over the server. ClearedStack replaces that with ko (which compiles Go services straight into minimal container images) and rootless BuildKit (which builds the Next.js web portal without elevated privileges). - No public image registries: ClearedStack never pushes container images to Docker Hub or GitHub. Source code is mirrored to GitHub for public visibility, while all built container images stay inside your cluster's own private registry.

title: Two-namespace layout
subtitle: Host on Kubernetes (No Docker)
summary: ClearedStack divides the cluster into two namespaces (isolated virtual folders inside Kubernetes) so the control plane and the automated workers stay cleanly se...
content: Two-namespace layout Host on Kubernetes (No Docker) ClearedStack divides the cluster into two namespaces (isolated virtual folders inside Kubernetes) so the control plane and the automated workers stay cleanly separated: | Namespace | What lives here | Purpose | | --- | --- | --- | | clearedstack | 7 control-plane pods | Runs the public web portal, queue API, PostgreSQL database, Git server, image registry, build runner, and app-store reconciler | | cs-workers | 10 deterministic workers ( cs-01 through cs-10 ) | Executes the 10-stage pipeline with zero AI at runtime; cs-02-observe also spawns temporary headless browser jobs only when a page requires JavaScript | Network policies ensure that only the web portal ( clearedstack-web ) accepts traffic from the public internet. Internal IP addresses, database credentials, and cluster hostnames never leave the cluster.

title: The control plane (~640 MiB RAM)
subtitle: Host on Kubernetes (No Docker)
summary: Instead of bundling heavy third-party suites like Forgejo, Harbor, or Argo CD, ClearedStack uses four small, purpose-built Go microservices alongside the web po...
content: The control plane (~640 MiB RAM) Host on Kubernetes (No Docker) Instead of bundling heavy third-party suites like Forgejo, Harbor, or Argo CD, ClearedStack uses four small, purpose-built Go microservices alongside the web portal and database. Each microservice does one job and keeps memory use predictable: | Component | Replaces | What it does | Requested RAM | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | cs-git | Forgejo | Stores bare Git repositories on a persistent volume, triggers build webhooks on push, and mirrors public code commits to GitHub | 64 MiB | | cs-registry | Harbor / GHCR | Stores OCI container images privately inside the cluster, keeps the last five versions per app for instant rollback, and cleans up old layers daily | 64 MiB | | cs-runner | Forgejo Actions | Listens for cs-git push webhooks, launches short-lived ko or rootless BuildKit jobs without Docker, runs tests, signs images, and updates app manifests | 32 MiB | | cs-store | Argo CD + CasaOS | Reads app manifests from cs-git , deploys updates with built-in Kubernetes Server-Side Apply, and reports sanitized pod health back to the portal | 48 MiB | | clearedstack-web , hub-queue-api , postgres | Portal + Hub API + DB | Serves the public ink-on-paper portal, live pipeline views, anonymous edit proposals, and the PostgreSQL 17 database | 432 MiB |

title: How updates flow without Docker
subtitle: Host on Kubernetes (No Docker)
summary: When a change lands in cs-git —either from you or from an approved public edit— cs-git sends a webhook to cs-runner and mirrors the code commit to GitHub. cs-ru...
content: How updates flow without Docker Host on Kubernetes (No Docker) When a change lands in cs-git —either from you or from an approved public edit— cs-git sends a webhook to cs-runner and mirrors the code commit to GitHub. cs-runner spins up a temporary, unprivileged Kubernetes job that builds the new image with ko or rootless BuildKit, signs it, and pushes it to cs-registry . Once the image is stored, cs-runner records the new image digest in the app's manifest inside cs-git . cs-store notices the updated manifest, rolls out the new pods one at a time in the clearedstack or cs-workers namespace, and streams the live status to the portal. If anything looks wrong, cs-store can roll back to any of the last five digests held in cs-registry with a single click.

title: Labor rates and wrap rates
subtitle: Guide · Section L.2
summary: How a wage becomes a billing rate: direct and indirect costs, fringe, overhead, G&A and fee, with a worked example you can check by hand.
content: Labor rates and wrap rates How a wage becomes a billing rate: direct and indirect costs, fringe, overhead, G&A and fee, with a worked example you can check by hand. field L.2  When the government buys labor, the hourly price has to cover far more than the wage. It carries a share of payroll taxes, benefits, rent, software, accounting and every other cost of running the company, plus profit. This guide explains how that price is built, using one made-up company from start to finish. Every number in it is invented. Direct and indirect costs Every cost a company has falls on one side of a line. - A direct cost is spent for one specific contract. The hours an engineer works on that contract, a server bought for it, a trip taken for it. - An indirect cost supports the bu

title: Direct and indirect costs
subtitle: Labor rates and wrap rates
summary: Every cost a company has falls on one side of a line. - A direct cost is spent for one specific contract. The hours an engineer works on that contract, a server...
content: Direct and indirect costs Labor rates and wrap rates Every cost a company has falls on one side of a line. - A direct cost is spent for one specific contract. The hours an engineer works on that contract, a server bought for it, a trip taken for it. - An indirect cost supports the business as a whole or more than one contract. Rent, the accounting system, the time spent writing proposals, health insurance. Direct costs are charged to the contract they belong to. Indirect costs are gathered into groups called pools , and each pool is shared out across contracts in proportion to some measure of activity, called a base . The rule that matters is consistency. The same kind of cost, in the same circumstances, has to be treated the same way every time. A cost cannot be direct on one contract and indirect on another because that is convenient.

title: The three usual pools
subtitle: Labor rates and wrap rates
summary: A small company commonly has three pools. The names are standard. What goes in each, and what each is divided by, is a choice the company makes and then sticks ...
content: The three usual pools Labor rates and wrap rates A small company commonly has three pools. The names are standard. What goes in each, and what each is divided by, is a choice the company makes and then sticks to. | Pool | What is usually in it | A common base | | --- | --- | --- | | Fringe | Payroll taxes, health insurance, retirement contributions, paid leave | Total labor dollars | | Overhead | Costs of supporting the people who do contract work: their supervisors’ time, tools, training, office space | Direct labor dollars, with or without fringe | | General and administrative (G&A) | Costs of running the company as a whole: executives, accounting, legal, insurance, proposal writing | All other costs | Larger companies split these further, for example into separate overhead pools for work done at their own offices and at government sites. A very small company may have only fringe and G&A.

title: Turn pools into rates
subtitle: Labor rates and wrap rates
summary: A rate is a pool divided by its base, over the company’s fiscal year. Take a made-up company with these annual figures: | Item | Amount | | --- | ---: | | Direc...
content: Turn pools into rates Labor rates and wrap rates A rate is a pool divided by its base, over the company’s fiscal year. Take a made-up company with these annual figures: | Item | Amount | | --- | ---: | | Direct labor: wages for hours worked on contracts | $600,000 | | Indirect labor: wages for everything else | $100,000 | | Fringe pool | $210,000 | | Overhead pool | $156,000 | | G&A pool | $112,320 | Fringe rate. The fringe pool is divided by all labor, direct and indirect: Overhead rate. This company applies overhead to direct labor plus the fringe on it: G&A rate. This company applies G&A to everything beneath it: The rates only mean something together with their bases. “Our overhead is 20 percent” is not comparable with another company’s 20 percent unless both are divided by the same thing.

title: Build the rate for one hour
subtitle: Labor rates and wrap rates
summary: Now price one hour of an engineer paid $60.00 an hour. Each layer is applied to the running total beneath it. | Step | Rate | Adds | Running total | | --- | ---...
content: Build the rate for one hour Labor rates and wrap rates Now price one hour of an engineer paid $60.00 an hour. Each layer is applied to the running total beneath it. | Step | Rate | Adds | Running total | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | Hourly wage | | | $60.00 | | Fringe | 30% | $18.00 | $78.00 | | Overhead | 20% | $15.60 | $93.60 | | G&A | 12% | $11.23 | $104.83 | | Fee | 8% | $8.39 | $113.22 | The fully burdened rate is $113.22 an hour.

title: The wrap rate
subtitle: Labor rates and wrap rates
summary: The wrap rate is the single multiplier that takes you from the wage to the burdened rate. It is the layers multiplied together: So every dollar of wage costs th...
content: The wrap rate Labor rates and wrap rates The wrap rate is the single multiplier that takes you from the wage to the burdened rate. It is the layers multiplied together: So every dollar of wage costs this company about $1.75 to deliver, and is priced at about $1.89. Check: $60.00 × 1.8870 = $113.22. People quote wrap rates both with and without fee. When you compare yours with someone else’s, ask which.

title: Conventions that change the answer
subtitle: Labor rates and wrap rates
summary: Two companies with identical costs can show different rates, because they made different structural choices. None of these is wrong. Each has to be applied cons...
content: Conventions that change the answer Labor rates and wrap rates Two companies with identical costs can show different rates, because they made different structural choices. None of these is wrong. Each has to be applied consistently. - What overhead is applied to. Direct labor alone, or direct labor plus fringe. Applying 20 percent to $60.00 gives a different result from applying it to $78.00. - What G&A is applied to. All costs beneath it, known as total cost input, or all costs except subcontracts and materials, known as a value-added base. The second gives a higher rate on a smaller base. - Where paid leave goes. In the fringe pool, or left in the labor base. - Whether fee is applied to everything. Some solicitations limit or forbid fee on travel, materials or subcontracts. Before you trust any calculator, including one listed here, find out which conventions it uses. Check a tool’s answer shows how to test that with one round-number example.

title: From a salary to an hourly wage
subtitle: Labor rates and wrap rates
summary: Rates are applied to an hourly wage, so a salary has to be converted. A full-time year is 2,080 hours: 52 weeks of 40 hours. Nobody works all 2,080 hours on con...
content: From a salary to an hourly wage Labor rates and wrap rates Rates are applied to an hourly wage, so a salary has to be converted. A full-time year is 2,080 hours: 52 weeks of 40 hours. Nobody works all 2,080 hours on contracts. Holidays, leave and sick time come out. How you handle that is tied to the leave convention above: - If paid leave is in the fringe pool , divide the salary by 2,080 and let the fringe rate pay for the time off. - If paid leave is not in fringe , divide the salary by the hours actually worked, often somewhere around 1,880 to 1,920, which gives a higher hourly wage and a lower fringe rate. Doing both at once counts leave twice. Doing neither leaves it out.

title: Costs the government will not pay
subtitle: Labor rates and wrap rates
summary: On contracts priced or reimbursed on the basis of cost, a cost has to be allowable to be included. The cost principles are in FAR Part 31. A cost is allowable w...
content: Costs the government will not pay Labor rates and wrap rates On contracts priced or reimbursed on the basis of cost, a cost has to be allowable to be included. The cost principles are in FAR Part 31. A cost is allowable when it is reasonable, can properly be assigned to the contract, follows accepted accounting practice and the contract’s terms, and is not ruled out by a specific cost principle. Some costs are ruled out whatever the circumstances. They include: | Cost | Cost principle | | --- | --- | | Most advertising and public relations | FAR 31.205-1 | | Bad debts | FAR 31.205-3 | | Contributions and donations | FAR 31.205-8 | | Entertainment | FAR 31.205-14 | | Fines and penalties | FAR 31.205-15 | | Interest on borrowing | FAR 31.205-20 | | Lobbying | FAR 31.205-22 | | Alcoholic beverages | FAR 31.205-51 | Unallowable costs still exist and still have to be paid. They come out of profit instead of going into the rates. Your accounting system needs to keep them in separate accounts so they can be left out of every pool.

title: When these rules apply to you
subtitle: Labor rates and wrap rates
summary: How much of this the government looks at depends on the kind of contract. | Contract type | How the price is set | How closely costs are examined | | --- | --- ...
content: When these rules apply to you Labor rates and wrap rates How much of this the government looks at depends on the kind of contract. | Contract type | How the price is set | How closely costs are examined | | --- | --- | --- | | Fixed price, commercial or competed | You offer a price. The government compares offers | Usually not at all. Your rates are your own business | | Time and materials, labor hour | Fixed hourly rates by labor category, times hours worked | The rates are set at award. The hours are checked | | Cost reimbursement | The government pays your allowable costs plus a fee | Closely. Rates are billed provisionally, then settled each year against actual costs | Even on a fixed-price bid, building your rates properly tells you whether the price you are offering covers your costs. For cost-reimbursement work, a few more things follow. You bill during the year at provisional rates agreed in advance. After the year ends you submit your actual indirect costs, and the difference is settled. Your accounting system has to be able to produce those figures. The Defense Contract Audit Agency publishes a plain-language manual for small contractors on what that takes. The Cost Accounting Standards, a further set of rules for large contracts, do not apply to contracts with small businesses.

title: Lay out the price table
subtitle: Labor rates and wrap rates
summary: Section B of a solicitation lists what is being bought as numbered line items. For labor, a line usually multiplies a rate by a quantity of hours: | Line item |...
content: Lay out the price table Labor rates and wrap rates Section B of a solicitation lists what is being bought as numbered line items. For labor, a line usually multiplies a rate by a quantity of hours: | Line item | Description | Quantity | Unit | Unit price | Amount | | --- | --- | ---: | --- | ---: | ---: | | 0001 | Senior engineer, base year | 1,880 | Hour | $113.22 | $212,853.60 | | 0002 | Travel, not to exceed | 1 | Lot | | $10,000.00 | | 1001 | Senior engineer, option year 1 | 1,880 | Hour | $116.62 | $219,245.60 | Things to settle before you fill one in: - Use the solicitation’s line items, labor categories and hours , not your own. If a pricing workbook is attached, that file is the deliverable. - Rounding. Round the hourly rate to the cent first and then multiply, unless told otherwise. Multiplying an unrounded rate gives a different total. - Option years. Wages rise. The example applies 3 percent to the base-year rate for the option year. State the escalation you used, and apply it the way the solicitation asks. - Wage floors. Some service contracts set minimum wages and benefits for certain job classes through a wage determination attached to the solicitation. Your base wage cannot be lower. - What carries fee. Check whether travel and other direct costs may include fee or G&A.

content: The Live Command Portal & App Store How clearedstack.com pairs a clean contract catalog on /tools/ with live cluster views under /guides/ (Command, Apps, Pipeline, Decide) powered by deterministic priority rules. start L.1  Most documentation sites ask you to read thousands of words of prose before you ever see software do anything. Folks are done reading. ClearedStack v3.1 pairs the contractor-first catalog at /tools/ with a live operational window inside /guides/ —opening directly into the cluster running the software factory. Instead of only reading about how the system is supposed to work, you can open /guides/command/ , /guides/apps/ , /guides/pipeline/ , or /guides/decide/ and inspect live state: which apps are healthy, which workers are busy, what is waiting in a queue, and what paused. From static essays

In v3.1, all operational views live side-by-side with the Section L manual under /guides/ , powered by hub-queue-api and cs-store : - Live status over static claims: Every worker and app reports real health, version, and queue depth straight from the cluster. - Short explanations in context: Instead of forcing you out of context, each live view uses compact [? Every status badge, queue transition, and priority ranking follows fixed, predictable rules.

title: One control plane, one lifecycle
subtitle: The Live Command Portal & App Store
summary: Behind the scenes, the portal connects two halves of the platform without mixing them up: 1. Software delivery ( /guides/apps/ & /tools/ apps ): cs-git stores t...
content: One control plane, one lifecycle The Live Command Portal & App Store Behind the scenes, the portal connects two halves of the platform without mixing them up: 1. Software delivery ( /guides/apps/ & /tools/ apps ): cs-git stores the code, cs-runner builds container images without Docker (using ko for Go and rootless BuildKit for web apps) and pushes them to cs-registry , and cs-store applies those apps to Kubernetes and streams sanitized health back to the App Store. 2. Data and tool production ( /guides/pipeline/ , /guides/decide/ , /tools/ ): The 10 deterministic workers pull tasks from hub-queue-api , process public sources, pause for human judgment at /guides/decide/ , and publish verified browser tools to /tools/ . Every piece you see in the portal is backed by open-source code mirrored to GitHub, so what you see running on clearedstack.com is the exact system you can inspect or host yourself.

title: Clean-Room MIT Architecture
subtitle: Guide · Section L.6
summary: Why ClearedStack builds its own MIT-licensed Go microservices from scratch instead of bundling Forgejo, Argo CD, or CasaOS, and how a clean-room wall separates external observation from tool generation.
content: Clean-Room MIT Architecture Why ClearedStack builds its own MIT-licensed Go microservices from scratch instead of bundling Forgejo, Argo CD, or CasaOS, and how a clean-room wall separates external observation from tool generation. project L.6  Every repository in ClearedStack—the Portal ( clearedstack.com ), all ten pipeline workers ( cs-01 through cs-10 ), and the four platform services ( cs-git , cs-registry , cs-runner , and cs-store )—is published under the MIT license and written from scratch. In software engineering, a clean-room rewrite means studying what a tool needs to accomplish and building a fresh implementation from zero, without copying any source code, templates, or assets from existing projects. ClearedStack applies this clean-room rule in two places: first, in how we build our own lightweight Kubernetes platform se

title: Why we rewrote the platform services in Go
subtitle: Clean-Room MIT Architecture
summary: Self-hosted developer platforms usually stitch together large upstream projects such as Forgejo for Git, Harbor or GitHub Container Registry for images, Argo CD...
content: Why we rewrote the platform services in Go Clean-Room MIT Architecture Self-hosted developer platforms usually stitch together large upstream projects such as Forgejo for Git, Harbor or GitHub Container Registry for images, Argo CD for Kubernetes sync, and CasaOS for app management. Those tools are powerful, but they carry heavy memory footprints, complex databases, and upstream license obligations that ClearedStack does not need. Instead of bundling them, ClearedStack runs four focused, clean-room Go microservices inside the cluster-private clearedstack namespace. They borrow the best ideas from Forgejo, Argo CD, and CasaOS—such as simple app cards and Git-driven deployments—without copying a single line of upstream code. | Upstream Inspiration | Clean-Room Service | What It Does | RAM Requested | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Forgejo | cs-git | Stores bare Git repositories on a cluster disk, handles push webhooks, and mirrors commits to GitHub. | 64 MiB | | GHCR / Harbor | cs-registry | Runs an internal-only OCI v2 container image store, keeps the last 5 image digests for instant rollback, and cleans old layers daily. | 64 MiB | | Forgejo Actions | cs-runner | Listens for cs-git push webhooks, runs Docker-free build jobs ( ko for Go, rootless BuildKit for web), signs images, and updates app.yaml . | 32 MiB | | Argo CD + CasaOS | cs-store | Reads app.yaml from cs-git , provides 1-click Install, Upgrade, Pause, and Rollback via Kubernetes Server-Side Apply, and reports sanitized health to the Portal. | 48 MiB | Because each service does only what ClearedStack needs, all four platform services together request just 208 MiB of memory. Combined with the Portal, Postgres, and all ten deterministic workers, the entire 17-pod platform fits comfortably on a single 4 GiB k3s node.

title: Avoiding license baggage and hidden complexity
subtitle: Clean-Room MIT Architecture
summary: Upstream projects often mix licenses across hundreds of dependencies, or use copyleft licenses that restrict how code can be combined and redistributed. Writing...
content: Avoiding license baggage and hidden complexity Clean-Room MIT Architecture Upstream projects often mix licenses across hundreds of dependencies, or use copyleft licenses that restrict how code can be combined and redistributed. Writing cs-git , cs-registry , cs-runner , and cs-store from scratch in Go under the MIT license keeps the entire stack legally simple and uniform. Anyone can read, fork, or reuse any part of ClearedStack without navigating conflicting license terms. This approach also removes operational surprises. There are no custom Kubernetes Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs) to maintain, no background user-account databases inside the Git server, and no container images pushed to third-party registries. Source code is mirrored publicly to GitHub on every change, while built images stay inside cs-registry .

title: The second clean-room wall: cs-02-observe to cs-06-build
subtitle: Clean-Room MIT Architecture
summary: The same clean-room discipline governs how ClearedStack builds compliance tools inside its ten-worker pipeline. Observing an existing public tool or agency page...
content: The second clean-room wall: cs-02-observe to cs-06-build Clean-Room MIT Architecture The same clean-room discipline governs how ClearedStack builds compliance tools inside its ten-worker pipeline. Observing an existing public tool or agency page is useful for understanding what problem contractors face, but raw page text, HTML layouts, and vendor designs are copyrightable expression. To protect creators and keep every generated tool legally independent, ClearedStack places a strict clean-room wall between cs-02-observe (which reads public surfaces) and cs-06-build (which generates new static tools). | Pipeline Stage | What It Sees | Clean-Room Boundary | | --- | --- | --- | | cs-02-observe | Public web pages, DOM tables, and agency PDFs | Extracts structured facts into strict JSON and seals the raw snapshot behind the clean-room wall. | | cs-03-evaluate & cs-04-decide | Structured evaluation scores and owner determinations | Decides whether to link an existing free tool or approve a clean-room build. | | cs-05-provenance | Official regulatory rules and worked examples | Compiles a clean-room JSON build specification with provenance notes and zero vendor copy. | | cs-06-build | Only the clean-room JSON spec and deterministic stack templates | Generates an isolated, offline-capable static tool without ever seeing raw HTML or competitor code. | By separating observation from generation, cs-06-build can never accidentally echo a third-party layout, phrasing, or script. Together, the MIT-licensed Go platform services and the cs-02-observe -to- cs-06-build pipeline wall ensure that everything ClearedStack runs and ships is small, deterministic, transparent, and built cleanly from the ground up.

content: The contract structure How to navigate this site Federal solicitations under FAR Part 15 follow the Uniform Contract Format (UCF). The UCF organizes complex requirements into standardized lettered sections so that contractors always know where to find line items, statements of work, and submission instructions. ClearedStack borrows this exact structure across its pages. Instead of arbitrary marketing layouts, the site uses UCF conventions to label its data, navigation, and documentation: | UCF Section | Title in Federal Contracting | ClearedStack Location | What you find there | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Section B | Supplies or services and prices/costs | Home and Tools | Contract Line Item Numbers CLIN 0001 – 0006 (browser tools + platform apps), all priced at $0.00. | | Section C | Description/specifications/statement of work | Home and Tools | The statement of work for all 18 single-purpose browser tools and 17 MIT platform/factory apps. | | Section F | Deliveries or performance | Home | The delivery roadmap across three phases: the free arsenal, the community, and the institution. | | Section H | Special contract requirements | Home and About | The four core ground rules: free, open source, client-side & deterministic execution, and independent governance. | | Section L | Instructions, conditions and notices to offerors | Guides | Live factory views ( L.0 ) plus the documentation library numbered L.1 through L.6 . | | Section M | Evaluation factors for award | How we decide | The 10-worker Prior Art evaluation engine: five knockout gates, 100-point rubric, 14-state lifecycle, and provenance rules. | Learning this layout once helps you navigate both ClearedStack and federal requests for proposals (RFPs). When you see a reference like CLIN 0001 or Section L.2.3 , you are reading standard acquisition shorthand.

Instant filtering: As you type, the tool list updates immediately without reloading the page. - Multi-field matching: The search scans across tool names (such as "Wrap Rate Calculator"), summaries (such as "cost pools"), and category titles simultaneously. - Multi-word AND logic: Typing labor rate finds tools containing both "labor" and "rate", filtering out irrelevant items. - Live tally: A counter to the right of the search input displays the exact count of matches ( X of 18 tools ), announced directly to assistive technologies, while apps provides its own namespace tabs and filter for the 17 platform apps. - Clearing your query: Press Escape , click the clear button ( ✕ ) inside the search box, or delete the search text to restore the complete catalog. Reading status labels Every tool card carries a color-coded status badge: - Planned: The tool is defined in the catalog and scheduled for implementation. Work has not yet begun. All 18 tools are currently marked Planned. - In development: The tool is actively being coded and tested in its dedicated repository. - Live: The tool is completed, tested, and operational. Its title links directly to the browser-based application, and a "Source" link points to its public repository. Signaling demand and prioritizing tools ClearedStack builds tools based on what users ask for first. Because the project accepts no revenue or paid sponsorships, backlog prioritization depends entirely on user feedback: 1. Review the planned tools in the Tools catalog. 2. If a planned tool would save you or your team hours of manual spreadsheet work, let the maintainers know. 3. Open a feature request issue on GitHub or send an email to contact@clearedstack.com. 4. Describe your specific use case, governing contract clauses, or input formats. User demand determines the active build sequence. For details on contributing your own tools, see Request a tool or add your own.
