title: Keyboard navigation and accessibility
subtitle: How to navigate this site
summary: ClearedStack is built to comply with federal accessibility standards (Section 508 and WCAG 2.1 Level AA) and supports complete mouse-free operation. Global site...
content: Keyboard navigation and accessibility How to navigate this site ClearedStack is built to comply with federal accessibility standards (Section 508 and WCAG 2.1 Level AA) and supports complete mouse-free operation. Global site search (⌘K or /) Pressing ⌘K (on macOS), Ctrl+K (on Windows and Linux), or / anywhere on the site opens the instant site-wide search dialog. The search engine runs 100% locally in your browser memory: - Zero latency: Queries resolve in 1 to 2 milliseconds using client-side MiniSearch indexing. - Deep heading indexing: Search indexes all 18 planned browser tools, all 17 platform/worker apps, all 49 guides, live factory views under /guides/ , and over 250 individual headings with direct deep links. - Keyboard operation: Use ↓ and ↑ arrow keys to highlight results, Enter to navigate directly to the page or subsection, and Escape to close the dialog. - Strict privacy: No search queries, keystrokes, or IP addresses are transmitted to external servers or search APIs. Skip to main content Pressing Tab upon initial page load reveals a high-contrast "Skip to content" link in the top left corner. Pressing Enter bypasses the header navigation and lands keyboard focus directly on the main container, allowing immediate interaction with page content. High-contrast focus rings and logical tab order All interactive elements—links, search inputs, buttons, and summary disclosures—feature high-contrast focus rings ( focus:border-accent and focus:outline-none ). Tab order follows the visual and logical structure of the document: 1. Skip link (when focused) 2. SiteHeader branding, search trigger, and four main navigation links 3. Guides sub-navigation or catalog section jump links 4. Main article text and internal links 5. Sticky or inline table of contents 6. Footer site map and repository links Screen reader announcements Both the Tool Catalog ( /tools/ ) and Guides Index ( /guides/ ) feature real-time search result counts marked with aria-live="polite" . When you type into a filter input, screen readers announce updated match totals (for example, "4 of 18 tools") without interrupting user keystrokes. Dark mode and system preferences The site automatically detects and honors your operating system color scheme preference ( prefers-color-scheme ). High contrast is maintained in both modes: - Light mode: Warm parchment background ( f5f4ef ) with dense charcoal ink text ( 1a1d1b ) and deep forest accent highlights. - Dark mode: Tactical black/forest background ( 0b0f0d ) with off-white typography and crisp green accents. - Both modes strictly avoid pure 000000 or ffffff extremes to minimize eye fatigue during extended proposal reviews. Deep linking with URL fragments Every second-level heading ( ) automatically generates an anchor ID and an interactive anchor symbol ( ) linking directly to that section. You can right-click or copy any heading link to share or bookmark an exact subsection. Similarly, all CLIN categories ( pricing , proposal , cyber , market , devsecops , apps ) and guide sections ( start , field , host , contribute , reference , project ) support direct fragment URLs.

title: Navigating offline and on closed networks
subtitle: How to navigate this site
summary: ClearedStack is engineered from the ground up to operate reliably in air-gapped facilities, Secure Compartmented Information Facilities (SCIFs), and networks wi...
content: Navigating offline and on closed networks How to navigate this site ClearedStack is engineered from the ground up to operate reliably in air-gapped facilities, Secure Compartmented Information Facilities (SCIFs), and networks with no internet connection. Zero external assets Traditional web platforms load fonts, scripts, stylesheets, and tracking beacons from third-party content delivery networks (CDNs). ClearedStack loads nothing from external servers: - Locally bundled typography: IBM Plex Sans and IBM Plex Mono fonts are packaged directly within the application bundle via @fontsource . - Zero telemetry: No Google Analytics, no tracking scripts, no third-party tags, and no remote telemetry. - Strict Content Security Policy: Production builds enforce default-src 'self' , forbidding your browser from connecting to unauthorized external endpoints. Behavior inside a SCIF or air gap When self-hosting a copy inside a secure enclave (see Run it on a closed network): - The entire interface loads at line speed from your local web server. - The interactive catalog filters and guide search work identically to the public site because all search indexes execute locally in browser memory. - No network requests leave the client machine during tool usage or document searches. External links on closed networks The guides contain references and links to official government publications, including acquisition.gov, SAM.gov, eCFR.gov, and GitHub. When viewing ClearedStack on an air-gapped system, clicking an external link will fail or time out according to your local browser network policy. All essential regulatory summaries, formula explanations, and procedural instructions are written directly into the guides themselves so you can complete your work without external internet access.

title: Network Privacy vs. Public Logic
subtitle: Guide · Section L.3
summary: How ClearedStack keeps internal IPs, hostnames, and cluster layout private while making 100% of its code, deterministic rules, queues, and sanitized error codes public.
content: Network Privacy vs. Public Logic How ClearedStack keeps internal IPs, hostnames, and cluster layout private while making 100% of its code, deterministic rules, queues, and sanitized error codes public. host L.3  ClearedStack is built around a simple split: hide the network, show the logic . Anyone can visit the Portal, inspect what is running, trace how decisions are made, read live queues, see errors, and propose edits without signing in. At the same time, the underlying servers, internal addresses, credentials, and cluster layout remain invisible from the internet. Transparency does not require exposing infrastructure. By separating what the system does from where it runs, ClearedStack stays open to public inspection without giving attackers a map of the cluster. What stays hidden vs. what is public

title: What stays hidden vs. what is public
subtitle: Network Privacy vs. Public Logic
summary: Every piece of data in the platform belongs to one of two sides. Infrastructure details and secrets stay inside the cluster, while behavior, code, and outcomes ...
content: What stays hidden vs. what is public Network Privacy vs. Public Logic Every piece of data in the platform belongs to one of two sides. Infrastructure details and secrets stay inside the cluster, while behavior, code, and outcomes are published openly. | Hidden (Cluster-Private) | 100% Public (Portal and GitHub Mirror) | | --- | --- | | Internal cluster IPs, node names, and pod hostnames | All MIT-licensed source code (mirrored from cs-git to GitHub) | | Internal Kubernetes DNS names | All deterministic pipeline rules, rubric weights, and tie-breakers | | Namespace layout, network policy rules, and Ingress internals | Every deterministic sub-tool and golden test fixture | | Database passwords, ServiceAccount tokens, and signing keys | Live app and worker health, queue depths, and item trails | | GitHub push tokens and the daily salt used to hash visitor IPs | Sanitized error codes such as E TIMEOUT , E PARSE , and E NEEDS SUBTOOL | | Raw visitor IP addresses (never stored in raw form) | Anonymous edit proposals and their live status ( Proposed to Live ) |

title: One public door for the whole cluster
subtitle: Network Privacy vs. Public Logic
summary: The platform runs across two Kubernetes namespaces: clearedstack for the seven control-plane services and cs-workers for the ten deterministic workers ( cs-01 t...
content: One public door for the whole cluster Network Privacy vs. Public Logic The platform runs across two Kubernetes namespaces: clearedstack for the seven control-plane services and cs-workers for the ten deterministic workers ( cs-01 through cs-10 ). Out of all seventeen pods, only clearedstack-web (the Portal and App Store UI) has a public Ingress connected to the internet. Every other service—including hub-queue-api , Postgres, the internal Git server ( cs-git ), the internal container registry ( cs-registry ), the build runner ( cs-runner ), the reconciler ( cs-store ), and all ten workers—is reachable only inside the cluster through private addresses. Network policy rules restrict which pods can talk to each other, so a public visitor can never reach the database, Git server, or worker pods directly.

title: How pub. database views enforce the boundary
subtitle: Network Privacy vs. Public Logic
summary: Inside Postgres, hub-queue-api reads and writes full operational records in internal core. tables. The public Portal never touches those tables. Instead, it con...
content: How pub. database views enforce the boundary Network Privacy vs. Public Logic Inside Postgres, hub-queue-api reads and writes full operational records in internal core. tables. The public Portal never touches those tables. Instead, it connects using a restricted, read-only database role ( pub ro ) that can only query pub. views. A database view acts like a one-way window: it exposes only the specific columns meant for public display—such as queue depths, item states, deterministic evaluation scores, and sanitized error codes—while leaving out internal host references, credentials, and private operational fields. Even if a visitor inspects every page and live stream on the Portal, the database layer itself prevents private fields from leaving Postgres.

title: How cs-store sanitizes health and errors
subtitle: Network Privacy vs. Public Logic
summary: cs-store is the platform's lightweight app-store reconciler. It reads app.yaml manifests from cs-git , deploys or updates workloads in Kubernetes, and watches P...
content: How cs-store sanitizes health and errors Network Privacy vs. Public Logic cs-store is the platform's lightweight app-store reconciler. It reads app.yaml manifests from cs-git , deploys or updates workloads in Kubernetes, and watches Pod, Deployment, and Event health across both namespaces. When a worker fails or stalls, Kubernetes events often include sensitive infrastructure details such as node names, pod hostnames, internal IP addresses, or cluster paths. Before cs-store forwards any status update or error to hub-queue-api for display on the Portal, it strips all node, pod, and IP metadata and maps the failure to a deterministic, sanitized error code—such as E TIMEOUT , E PARSE , or E NEEDS SUBTOOL . Visitors see what broke and which stage stalled, without ever seeing which machine or which internal IP ran it.

title: Open sandbox without exposing the host
subtitle: Network Privacy vs. Public Logic
summary: Because there is no login lock on the Portal, anyone can propose edits or inspect live failures. To keep an open sandbox from becoming a host-safety risk, anony...
content: Open sandbox without exposing the host Network Privacy vs. Public Logic Because there is no login lock on the Portal, anyone can propose edits or inspect live failures. To keep an open sandbox from becoming a host-safety risk, anonymous submissions pass through a deterministic five-layer shield before they ever reach internal systems: | Guardrail Layer | What It Blocks | Privacy Benefit | | --- | --- | --- | | Browser Proof-of-Work | Automated spam bots | Runs a short puzzle in the browser instead of third-party CAPTCHAs | | Honeypot field | Blind form scrapers | Silently discards automated submissions | | Daily-salted IP hash rate limit | Floods from a single source | Caps submissions without ever storing raw visitor IPs | | Strict schema check ( ownership map.json ) | Oversized or malformed payloads | Enforces a 4 KB limit and strips HTML and scripts | | Review gate ( cs-04-decide ) | Unreviewed cluster or code changes | Keeps proposals in pending approval until approved | Together, these layers ensure that public transparency never leaks private infrastructure. The cluster stays quiet and isolated, while every rule, queue, error code, and line of code remains open for anyone to inspect.

title: How cs-02-observe inspects a tool
subtitle: Guide · Section L.4
summary: How tiny 30 MiB Go HTTP pods, on-demand headless browser Jobs, and deterministic sub-tools inspect public tools, seal raw snapshots behind the clean-room wall, and fail closed into needs_subtool.
content: How cs-02-observe inspects a tool How tiny 30 MiB Go HTTP pods, on-demand headless browser Jobs, and deterministic sub-tools inspect public tools, seal raw snapshots behind the clean-room wall, and fail closed into needs_subtool. contribute L.4  In ClearedStack v3.1, observing an existing government-contracting tool is no longer a manual browser checklist—it is the job of cs-02-observe , a 100% deterministic, MIT-licensed Go worker running in the cs-workers Kubernetes namespace. Zero AI models run during observation. Given the same public URL or document, cs-02-observe produces the exact same structured observation record every time. Tiny HTTP pods first, headless browsers only when needed Most public pages, government portals, and agency PDFs do not need a full web browser to inspect. By default, cs-02-observe runs as a tiny Go HTTP

title: Tiny HTTP pods first, headless browsers only when needed
subtitle: How cs-02-observe inspects a tool
summary: Most public pages, government portals, and agency PDFs do not need a full web browser to inspect. By default, cs-02-observe runs as a tiny Go HTTP pod using rou...
content: Tiny HTTP pods first, headless browsers only when needed How cs-02-observe inspects a tool Most public pages, government portals, and agency PDFs do not need a full web browser to inspect. By default, cs-02-observe runs as a tiny Go HTTP pod using roughly 30 MiB of RAM . It claims a time-limited work lease from hub-queue-api , fetches the public target over plain HTTP, and runs deterministic extractors directly against the response. Some vendor tools, however, render their calculators or tables entirely in client-side JavaScript. Only when a target is flagged as JavaScript-heavy does cs-02-observe spawn an on-demand headless browser Job pod (a temporary container that renders the page, records network requests using synthetic test inputs, and exits immediately). Keeping browsers out of the always-on worker pool lets the entire 17-pod ClearedStack platform fit comfortably on a single 4 GiB k3s node. | Execution Mode | Footprint | When cs-02-observe Uses It | | --- | --- | --- | | Default Go HTTP pod | ~30 MiB RAM (always-on) | Static HTML marketing pages, .gov portals, downloadable PDFs, and server-rendered forms | | On-demand browser Job pod | Ephemeral (created and deleted per job) | JavaScript-heavy single-page apps that require DOM rendering or client-side network inspection |

title: Passive public boundaries
subtitle: How cs-02-observe inspects a tool
summary: cs-02-observe is strictly passive and public. It only inspects pages accessible on the open web and never creates accounts, starts free trials, fills out lead-c...
content: Passive public boundaries How cs-02-observe inspects a tool cs-02-observe is strictly passive and public. It only inspects pages accessible on the open web and never creates accounts, starts free trials, fills out lead-capture forms, enters real contracting data, or bypasses paywalls, robots.txt rules, or CAPTCHAs. If a tool sits behind a login or anti-bot challenge, observation stops at the public surface and records vendor claims as Stated rather than Seen .

title: Deterministic sub-tools (tools/<case>/)
subtitle: How cs-02-observe inspects a tool
summary: Real-world websites and agency documents vary widely. Instead of asking an AI model to guess at an unfamiliar page layout, cs-02-observe routes each target thro...
content: Deterministic sub-tools (tools/<case>/) How cs-02-observe inspects a tool Real-world websites and agency documents vary widely. Instead of asking an AI model to guess at an unfamiliar page layout, cs-02-observe routes each target through deterministic sub-tools stored inside its own repository under tools// . Every sub-tool pairs a matching rule ( match.yaml ), predictable Go extraction logic ( extract.go ), and golden test fixtures ( fixtures/ ) so automated tests verify the extractor never breaks. | Sub-Tool | What It Matches and Extracts | | --- | --- | | saas-marketing | Public vendor landing pages and feature tables; extracts stated inputs, outputs, pricing model, and login gates | | gov-portal | Federal .gov and .mil portals and calculators; captures cited FAR, DFARS, or NIST clauses and offline behavior | | agency-pdf | Downloadable procurement PDFs, worksheets, and instructions; extracts form fields, rules, and publication dates | | | Dedicated extractors for specific vendors whose page structure differs from standard layouts | Each sub-tool outputs strict, schema-validated JSON covering the tool's core job, inputs, outputs, login requirement, tracking profile, license or copyright, price model, cited public rule, observation date, and confidence tier ( Seen , Stated , or Unknown ).

title: Sealing raw snapshots behind the clean-room wall
subtitle: How cs-02-observe inspects a tool
summary: While cs-02-observe fetches raw HTML, DOM captures, and PDFs to perform extraction, those raw snapshots are sealed behind the clean-room wall . Downstream build...
content: Sealing raw snapshots behind the clean-room wall How cs-02-observe inspects a tool While cs-02-observe fetches raw HTML, DOM captures, and PDFs to perform extraction, those raw snapshots are sealed behind the clean-room wall . Downstream build workers ( cs-06-build ) and specification compilers ( cs-05-provenance ) never see vendor markup, stylesheets, or client-side scripts. Only the sanitized, structured JSON facts and verified public regulations cross into the build pipeline—ensuring every published ClearedStack tool is an independent, clean-room MIT implementation.

title: Failing closed into needssubtool
subtitle: How cs-02-observe inspects a tool
summary: When cs-02-observe encounters a page layout, table structure, or document format that none of its registered sub-tools recognize, it never guesses . Instead, it...
content: Failing closed into needssubtool How cs-02-observe inspects a tool When cs-02-observe encounters a page layout, table structure, or document format that none of its registered sub-tools recognize, it never guesses . Instead, it fails closed: 1. The worker pauses that item with the sanitized status needs subtool ( E NEEDS SUBTOOL ) and continues processing the rest of the queue normally. 2. cs-10-notify opens a task in the cs-02-observe repository inside cs-git (mirrored publicly to GitHub) describing the unmatched pattern. 3. The paused item appears on the public /guides/pipeline/ view so anyone can see why it stopped. 4. Once a contributor or maintainer adds a new deterministic sub-tool under tools// along with a golden fixture, cs-runner tests and builds the updated worker image with ko (no Docker), cs-store deploys it, and hub-queue-api automatically replays every item paused in needs subtool for that pattern. Every new edge case becomes permanent, tested, deterministic code—and every solved pattern automatically unblocks past items without human re-entry.

content: Adopt and Deploy Your Own ClearedStack Instance How anyone can deploy the entire 17-pod ClearedStack platform on a single 4 GiB k3s node, what the one-time setup job initializes, and how clean-room MIT licensing makes forking easy. host L.3  ClearedStack is designed so anyone can run the entire platform on a single modest server. You do not need a large cloud cluster, a managed Kubernetes service, or a paid container registry. All 17 pods—the public Portal, the internal Git server, the image builder, the private container registry, the app-store reconciler, the database, and all 10 deterministic workers—fit comfortably on a single 4 GiB k3s node costing roughly $10 to $20 per month. One Node, Two Namespaces, Seventeen Pods Traditional self-hosted platforms often bundle heavy third-party suites that demand 8 GiB to 16 GiB of memory

subtitle: Adopt and Deploy Your Own ClearedStack Instance

content: One Node, Two Namespaces, Seventeen Pods Adopt and Deploy Your Own ClearedStack Instance Traditional self-hosted platforms often bundle heavy third-party suites that demand 8 GiB to 16 GiB of memory just to sit idle. ClearedStack replaces those suites with small, single-purpose Go services and runs everything inside two isolated Kubernetes namespaces using k3s and containerd , with no Docker anywhere. | Namespace | Pods | Role | Typical Memory | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | clearedstack | 7 control-plane pods | Public Portal ( clearedstack-web ), queue API ( hub-queue-api ), Postgres 17, internal Git ( cs-git ), internal registry ( cs-registry ), image builder ( cs-runner ), and app-store reconciler ( cs-store ) | ~640 MiB requested (~1.25 GiB limit) | | cs-workers | 10 worker pods | Deterministic pipeline workers ( cs-01-intake through cs-10-notify ) with zero AI at runtime | ~300 MiB total | Because the entire stack requests under 1 GiB of memory at rest, a 4 GiB virtual private server or home mini-PC leaves plenty of headroom for the operating system, Postgres storage, ephemeral build jobs, and occasional on-demand headless browser jobs spawned by cs-02-observe for JavaScript-heavy websites.

title: What the One-Time Setup Job Initializes
subtitle: Adopt and Deploy Your Own ClearedStack Instance
summary: Deploying your own instance requires only a single quickstart manifest apply to a fresh k3s cluster. As soon as the manifest lands, a one-time setup job runs au...
content: What the One-Time Setup Job Initializes Adopt and Deploy Your Own ClearedStack Instance Deploying your own instance requires only a single quickstart manifest apply to a fresh k3s cluster. As soon as the manifest lands, a one-time setup job runs automatically to wire the platform together from scratch so you do not have to configure databases, registries, or secrets by hand. | Setup Step | What Happens Automatically | Why It Matters | | --- | --- | --- | | Cluster-private secrets | Generates database passwords, service-account tokens, cosign image-signing keys, and the daily IP-hashing salt | Credentials never touch Git and stay inside your cluster | | Database bootstrap | Initializes Postgres 17 with internal core tables and read-only pub views | Separates private operational data from what the public Portal displays | | Internal Git seeding | Creates bare repositories in cs-git for the Portal, control-plane services, and all 10 workers with starter app.yaml files | Gives your cluster its own self-contained source of truth | | Local image builds | Triggers cs-runner to compile Go services with ko and the Next.js Portal with rootless BuildKit, then signs and pushes them to cs-registry | Eliminates Docker and avoids pulling prebuilt images from external registries | | Network boundaries | Applies network policy rules so only clearedstack-web accepts public traffic | Keeps internal IPs, the database, Git, registry, and workers unreachable from the internet | Once the setup job finishes, cs-store reconciles the app.yaml manifests and brings up all 17 pods. From there, you can open the Portal, watch the live pipeline, and manage upgrades or rollbacks directly from the built-in App Store view.

title: Clean-Room MIT Licensing and Easy Forking
subtitle: Adopt and Deploy Your Own ClearedStack Instance
summary: Every ClearedStack repository—the Portal, the four control-plane microservices, and all ten workers—is released under the MIT License . Although the architectur...
content: Clean-Room MIT Licensing and Easy Forking Adopt and Deploy Your Own ClearedStack Instance Every ClearedStack repository—the Portal, the four control-plane microservices, and all ten workers—is released under the MIT License . Although the architecture takes inspiration from tools like Forgejo, Argo CD, and CasaOS, every line of Go code is written from scratch in a clean room with zero copied upstream code and zero copyleft obligations. That clean-room MIT foundation makes it straightforward to fork ClearedStack for your own organization, agency, or research project: - Customize without permission or fees: You can rebrand the Portal, change evaluation rubric weights, or run a private instance internally without licensing restrictions. - Add deterministic edge-case handlers: Each worker supports modular sub-tools under its own tools directory. When you add a new parser or rule with a golden test fixture, your cluster's cs-runner automatically tests, builds, signs, and rolls out the updated worker. - Control your public mirror: By default, cs-git mirrors code commits to GitHub on change while keeping container images strictly inside your cluster. When you fork the project, you simply point cs-git at your own repository mirror—or leave mirroring off for a completely self-contained deployment. The result is a small, transparent platform you can stand up in minutes, inspect line by line, and adapt to your own workflow for the price of a basic VPS.

content: No Lock On It: Open Public Sandbox Why ClearedStack runs completely in the open with no login lock, how visitor testing and edits improve the platform, and how isolation and instant rollbacks keep the host safe. start L.1  ClearedStack has no login wall, no waitlist, and no paid tier. Everything running in production and everything being developed is visible to anyone who opens clearedstack.com . You can inspect live worker health, watch queues move, read sanitized error codes, and propose edits without creating an account. This is a deliberate choice: an open public sandbox turns every curious visitor into a potential tester and contributor, while strict technical boundaries keep the underlying host safe. Why there is no lock on the site Most platforms hide their errors, queues, and internal workflows behind lo

title: Why there is no lock on the site
subtitle: No Lock On It: Open Public Sandbox
summary: Most platforms hide their errors, queues, and internal workflows behind login screens or status pages that only say "All systems operational." ClearedStack does...
content: Why there is no lock on the site No Lock On It: Open Public Sandbox Most platforms hide their errors, queues, and internal workflows behind login screens or status pages that only say "All systems operational." ClearedStack does the opposite: - Zero accounts for visitors: You never need to sign in or hand over an email address to browse /guides/apps/ , trace /guides/pipeline/ , use /tools/ , or propose an edit using the ✎ Edit button. - MIT-licensed code: Every repository—from the portal ( clearedstack.com ) to cs-git , cs-registry , cs-runner , cs-store , and all 10 workers ( cs-01 through cs-10 )—is clean-room Go or web code under the MIT license, mirrored publicly on GitHub. - Visible failures: When a worker hits a snag, it does not silently swallow the problem. It logs a sanitized error code (such as E TIMEOUT , E PARSE , or E NEEDS SUBTOOL ) and surfaces it in the portal.

title: How breaking things makes the platform stronger
subtitle: No Lock On It: Open Public Sandbox
summary: When visitors test the sandbox, submit unusual URLs, or spot mistakes on a page, they inevitably find edge cases the system has not seen before. Because Cleared...
content: How breaking things makes the platform stronger No Lock On It: Open Public Sandbox When visitors test the sandbox, submit unusual URLs, or spot mistakes on a page, they inevitably find edge cases the system has not seen before. Because ClearedStack is 100% deterministic—with zero AI guessing at runtime—every failure becomes a permanent improvement: 1. Fail closed, not silent: If cs-02-observe or another worker encounters an unfamiliar page layout, it pauses that item in needs subtool and cs-10-notify opens a fingerprinted task in the owning repository. 2. Build a deterministic sub-tool: A small, targeted sub-tool and golden test fixture are added to handle that exact pattern. 3. Automatic replay: Once cs-runner tests and builds the update and cs-store deploys it, hub-queue-api automatically replays the paused items. Every edge case a visitor triggers turns into permanent, repeatable code.

title: Anonymous edits with a 5-layer safety shield
subtitle: No Lock On It: Open Public Sandbox
summary: Letting anyone propose a change without signing in would normally invite spam bots. ClearedStack stops abuse without forcing humans through logins or third-part...
content: Anonymous edits with a 5-layer safety shield No Lock On It: Open Public Sandbox Letting anyone propose a change without signing in would normally invite spam bots. ClearedStack stops abuse without forcing humans through logins or third-party CAPTCHAs by using five deterministic checks: 1. Browser Proof-of-Work: Submitting an edit runs a quick (~1 second) cryptographic puzzle in your browser, making bulk bot spam expensive. 2. Honeypot field: A hidden form field invisible to humans catches automated scrapers and silently drops their submissions. 3. Daily-salted IP hash rate limit: The server caps submissions per hashed IP using a salt that rotates daily, so raw visitor IP addresses are never stored. 4. Strict schema validation: Every proposal is checked against ownership map.json , limited to 4 KB, restricted to allowed edit classes ( DATA , CONFIG , or ISSUE ), and stripped of HTML or scripts. 5. Human review gate: Proposals sit in a pending queue and never touch cs-git or the cluster until reviewed and approved in /guides/decide/ ( cs-04-decide ). While waiting, your edit button updates live in place so you can watch your contribution move from Proposed to Approved , Building , and Live .

title: How isolation and rollbacks protect the host
subtitle: No Lock On It: Open Public Sandbox
summary: Open visibility does not mean exposing the server's internals or letting bad updates take down the host. Strict separation keeps the cluster healthy even under ...
content: How isolation and rollbacks protect the host No Lock On It: Open Public Sandbox Open visibility does not mean exposing the server's internals or letting bad updates take down the host. Strict separation keeps the cluster healthy even under heavy public use: | 100% Public (Portal & GitHub) | Cluster-Private (Hidden & Isolated) | | --- | --- | | All MIT source code, pipeline rules, rubric weights, and sub-tools | Internal cluster IPs, node names, pod hostnames, and internal DNS | | Live app and worker health, queue depths, and item trails | Network policy rules and Ingress internals | | Sanitized error codes ( E TIMEOUT , E PARSE , E NEEDS SUBTOOL ) | Database passwords, ServiceAccount tokens, signing keys, and daily IP salts | | Read-only pub. database views | Raw captured web snapshots behind the clean-room wall | Four structural guardrails enforce this boundary: - Single public door: Only clearedstack-web has a public Ingress. The control plane and workers cannot be reached directly from the internet. - Two-namespace isolation: The control plane runs in the clearedstack namespace, while all 10 workers run in cs-workers , separated by Kubernetes network policy rules. - Metadata stripping: cs-store strips node names, pod hostnames, and internal IPs before sending any status or error to the portal. - Instant 1-click rollbacks: cs-registry keeps the last five signed image digests for every app. If a new build misbehaves, cs-store restores the previous working version immediately.

summary: The following architectural, licensing, and operational decisions are final for ClearedStack v3.1. 10 deterministic worker repositories Zero AI runs at runtime ...
content: What is decided in v3.1 What is decided and what remains open The following architectural, licensing, and operational decisions are final for ClearedStack v3.1. 10 deterministic worker repositories Zero AI runs at runtime anywhere in the pipeline or in any shipped compliance tool. All pipeline work is executed by 10 deterministic Go worker repositories ( cs-01-intake through cs-10-notify ) that produce identical output on any cluster. | Worker repo | Deterministic responsibility | Edge-case handling | | --- | --- | --- | | cs-01-intake | Normalize URLs, SHA-256 deduplicate, assign PA-XXXX . | Sub-tools in tools// | | cs-02-observe | Fetch public pages and run DOM/PDF extractors into strict JSON behind a clean-room wall. | Tiny ~30 MiB HTTP Go pods; spawns on-demand headless browser Job pods only for JS-heavy sites | | cs-03-evaluate | Run YAML/Go rule engine for 5 knockout gates, 100-point rubric, and 5 tie-breakers. | Category rubric profiles in tools// | | cs-04-decide | Owner-only decision inbox on the Portal for item determinations and edit approvals. | Human gate only | | cs-05-provenance | Stamp provenance notes via Go templates, enforce 48h identity verification and 5d opt-out SLAs, and compile clean-room JSON specs. | Spec profiles in tools// | | cs-06-build | Generate isolated static tool repos from clean-room specs and worked-example fixtures. | Deterministic stack templates | | cs-07-verify | Run 5-condition test suite (offline execution, connect-src 'self' , zero tracking, worked-example parity). | Deterministic pass/fail gate | | cs-08-catalog | Publish verified, linked, merged, or retired entries to the clearedstack.com catalog. | Deterministic catalog sync | | cs-09-monitor | Scheduled ETag, XML, and DOM diff checks on FAR/DFARS/NIST, live tools, and linked tools. | Source watchers in tools// | | cs-10-notify | Route approved Portal edits, needs subtool tasks, and fingerprinted errors into cs-git and owner alerts. | Notification targets in tools// | When a worker encounters an unfamiliar page layout or format, it fails closed into needs subtool , cs-10-notify opens a fingerprinted task in the owning worker repository, and hub-queue-api automatically replays queued items once a new deterministic sub-tool and golden fixture are merged. MIT clean-room Go microservices (no Forgejo, Argo CD, CasaOS, or Docker) Rather than bundling heavy third-party platforms with mixed licenses or upstream operational overhead, ClearedStack v3.1 runs custom clean-room Go microservices licensed under MIT across all repositories ( clearedstack.com , cs-01 through cs-10 , cs-git , cs-registry , cs-runner , and cs-store ). Inspiration is drawn from Forgejo, Argo CD, and CasaOS workflows, with zero copied upstream code. | Replaced component | v3.1 clean-room replacement | Role in platform | | --- | --- | --- | | Forgejo | cs-git | Internal bare .git server on a PVC with Smart HTTP/SSH, webhooks, and outbound push-mirroring to GitHub on change. | | GHCR / Harbor | cs-registry | Internal-only OCI v2 registry on a PVC retaining the last 5 digests per app for instant rollback. | | Forgejo Actions & Docker | cs-runner | Ephemeral Kubernetes build Jobs using ko for Go and rootless BuildKit for Next.js—zero Docker anywhere, running on k3s and containerd . | | Argo CD + CasaOS | cs-store | App-store reconciler reading app.yaml from cs-git for 1-click Install, Upgrade, Pause, and Rollback via Kubernetes Server-Side Apply. | | GitHub as primary host | Public code mirror only | cs-git pushes code changes to GitHub for public visibility; zero container images are ever stored on GitHub. | Two Kubernetes namespaces The entire 17-pod platform fits on a single 4 GiB k3s node and is isolated into 2 namespaces : - clearedstack (control plane): Runs clearedstack-web , hub-queue-api , postgres , cs-git , cs-registry , cs-runner , and cs-store . - cs-workers (pipeline workers): Runs all 10 deterministic worker deployments ( cs-01-intake through cs-10-notify ) and on-demand browser Jobs. Open no-login public sandbox Everything running and being developed is shown publicly and for free with no login lock on clearedstack.com . Any visitor can use the Portal, inspect live worker health and queues, read sanitized error codes ( E TIMEOUT , E PARSE , E NEEDS SUBTOOL ), and propose edits via ✎ buttons without creating an account. Openness is paired with deterministic guardrails so public access never exposes cluster internals or host safety: - Network isolation: Only clearedstack-web has a public Ingress; internal IPs, .svc.cluster.local DNS names, node names, NetworkPolicy rules, and credentials stay cluster-private, and the Portal reads only sanitized pub. Postgres views. - Five-layer edit shield: Anonymous ✎ proposals pass a ~1-second browser Proof-of-Work puzzle, a honeypot field, a daily-salted IP hash rate limit, strict 4 KB schema validation against ownership map.json , and a mandatory human approval gate in cs-04-decide before touching cs-git . - Safe failure and rollback: If a public interaction triggers an unexpected edge case or breaks a view, the sanitized error is logged visibly to help improve the system while cs-store preserves instant rollback across the last 5 signed OCI digests.

content: How the live status pill works Ownership Map & the Edit-to-Repo Loop Because clearedstack.com is an open public sandbox with no login lock , anyone can submit a proposal up to 4 KB. After passing the five-layer anti-spam shield (browser Proof-of-Work, honeypot field, daily-salted IP hash rate limit, schema check against ownership map.json , and owner gate in cs-04-decide ), the exact ✎ Edit button you clicked turns into a live status pill: Proposed → Approved → Building → Live You can watch your change move from cs-04-decide into cs-git , through cs-runner ( ko or rootless BuildKit), and into cs-store without creating an account.

title: The 10-Worker Prior Art Engine
subtitle: Guide · Section L.6
summary: How the old ten-stage essay became ten live, 100% deterministic worker repositories coordinated by hub-queue-api and Postgres, feeding /guides/pipeline/, /guides/decide/, and /tools/.
content: The 10-Worker Prior Art Engine How the old ten-stage essay became ten live, 100% deterministic worker repositories coordinated by hub-queue-api and Postgres, feeding /guides/pipeline/, /guides/decide/, and /tools/. project L.6  Earlier versions of this guide described a ten-stage pipeline as an unbuilt plan. In ClearedStack v3.1, that essay is now running software: ten separate, MIT-licensed Go repositories ( cs-01-intake through cs-10-notify ) that discover existing government-contracting tools, check them against public rules, build clean-room browser alternatives, and keep the live catalog up to date. Every worker in the engine is 100% deterministic —meaning there is zero AI at runtime, no language-model token cost, and no guesswork. Given the same input, each worker produces the exact same output on any cluster.

title: From ten stages on paper to ten live repositories

content: From ten stages on paper to ten live repositories The 10-Worker Prior Art Engine All ten workers run inside the cs-workers Kubernetes namespace. Each repository owns one clear job in the assembly line, and workers that face varied websites or document formats use tools// sub-tools—small, permanent rule modules with golden test fixtures—to handle edge cases without AI. | Worker Repo | What it does (100% deterministic) | Sub-tools ( tools// ) | | --- | --- | --- | | cs-01-intake | Normalizes submitted or discovered URLs, deduplicates via SHA-256, and assigns a PA-XXXX ID. | Yes ( sam-gov , github-issues , web-sweep , site-form ) | | cs-02-observe | Fetches public pages as tiny ~30 MiB Go HTTP pods (spawning on-demand headless browser Job pods only for JS-heavy sites), extracts inputs/outputs into JSON, and seals raw snapshots behind the clean-room wall. | Yes ( saas-marketing , gov-portal , agency-pdf , ) | | cs-03-evaluate | Runs the YAML/Go rule engine for the five knockout gates, the 100-point rubric, and five tie-breakers. | Yes ( rubric-profiles/ ) | | cs-04-decide | Powers the owner-only decision inbox on the Portal (Approve, Link, Merge, Park, Reject, Override, and public edit approvals). | No | | cs-05-provenance | Stamps provenance notes with Go templates, enforces 48-hour identity verification and 5-day opt-out SLAs, and compiles clean-room JSON build specs. | Yes ( spec-profiles/ ) | | cs-06-build | Generates an isolated static tool repository from the clean-room spec and worked-example fixtures. | Yes ( stack-templates/calculator , checklist , validator , decision-tree ) | | cs-07-verify | Runs the five-condition verification suite (offline operation, connect-src 'self' , zero tracking, worked-example assertions). | No | | cs-08-catalog | Publishes verified, linked, merged, or retired entries to the live clearedstack.com catalog. | No | | cs-09-monitor | Runs scheduled ETag, XML, and DOM diff checks on FAR/DFARS/NIST rules, live tools, linked tools, and parked blockers. | Yes ( federal-register , ecfr , nist-csrc , linked-tool-watch , live-catalog ) | | cs-10-notify | Routes approved Portal edits, needs subtool tasks, and fingerprinted errors into cs-git , and sends owner alerts. | Yes ( internal-git , github-mirror , webhook-alert , portal-sse ) | When a worker encounters an unfamiliar page layout or document format, it fails closed : it pauses that item in needs subtool , and cs-10-notify opens a task in the owning repository. Once a new deterministic sub-tool and golden test are added, cs-runner builds the updated worker image with ko (zero Docker anywhere), cs-store rolls it out, and hub-queue-api automatically replays every paused item.

title: How hub-queue-api and Postgres coordinate the line
subtitle: The 10-Worker Prior Art Engine
summary: Workers never talk directly to each other or touch the database themselves. Instead, hub-queue-api and Postgres 17 sit in the clearedstack control-plane namespa...
content: How hub-queue-api and Postgres coordinate the line The 10-Worker Prior Art Engine Workers never talk directly to each other or touch the database themselves. Instead, hub-queue-api and Postgres 17 sit in the clearedstack control-plane namespace and act as the central dispatcher: - Lease-based queues: Each worker polls hub-queue-api over internal ServiceAccount HTTP to claim a time-limited lease on its next item, then writes back the result or a sanitized error code ( E TIMEOUT , E PARSE , E NEEDS SUBTOOL ). - Clean-room separation: Raw HTML or vendor snapshots captured by cs-02-observe stay sealed behind the clean-room boundary; downstream build workers ( cs-06-build ) only read sanitized JSON specs derived from public regulations. - Public mirror without cluster exposure: Code changes live in cs-git and mirror outward to GitHub on change, while internal IPs, tokens, and cluster topology stay private inside the control plane.

title: Protecting government information
subtitle: Guide · Section L.2
summary: FCI and CUI, the security requirements that come with each, how NIST SP 800-171 and CMMC fit together, and how CUI is marked.
content: Protecting government information FCI and CUI, the security requirements that come with each, how NIST SP 800-171 and CMMC fit together, and how CUI is marked. field L.2  A government contract usually comes with information the government expects you to protect, and with security requirements that depend on what kind of information it is. This guide sorts out the vocabulary, shows which rule applies to which information, and describes the work in the order a small company would do it. The rules below were checked in November 2026. The CMMC rollout schedule was altered in 2026, and several contract clauses are being renumbered. Treat the dates and clause numbers here as a starting point, and confirm each one against your contract and the official pages listed un

title: Two kinds of information
subtitle: Protecting government information
summary: Most of the rules hang on one question: what kind of government information will you hold? | | Federal contract information (FCI) | Controlled unclassified info...
content: Two kinds of information Protecting government information Most of the rules hang on one question: what kind of government information will you hold? | | Federal contract information (FCI) | Controlled unclassified information (CUI) | | --- | --- | --- | | What it is | Information provided by or created for the government under a contract, not intended for public release | Information a law, regulation or government-wide policy says must be protected or have its sharing limited | | Examples | Contract documents, schedules, routine correspondence, status reports | Controlled technical drawings, export-controlled data, certain privacy and procurement information | | Who decides | It follows from the contract | The government. Categories are listed in the national CUI Registry | | Baseline protection | 15 basic safeguards | The 110 requirements of NIST SP 800-171 | Neither is classified information. Classified information has entirely separate rules, facilities and clearances, and nothing in this guide applies to it. The government is responsible for telling you what is CUI under your contract and for marking it. If a contract mentions CUI but you cannot tell what you will receive or create, ask the contracting officer in writing before you price the work. The answer changes your costs.

title: Which rule applies
subtitle: Protecting government information
summary: | If your systems hold | The contract will usually include | Which requires | | --- | --- | --- | | FCI only | The basic safeguarding clause, long numbered FAR ...
content: Which rule applies Protecting government information | If your systems hold | The contract will usually include | Which requires | | --- | --- | --- | | FCI only | The basic safeguarding clause, long numbered FAR 52.204-21 | 15 basic security requirements | | CUI on a defense contract | DFARS 252.204-7012 | NIST SP 800-171, reporting cyber incidents within 72 hours, and cloud services that meet a FedRAMP Moderate baseline or its equivalent | | Either, on a defense contract with a CMMC requirement | DFARS 252.204-7021 | A CMMC status at the level named in the solicitation, held at the time of award | Read the clauses in your own contract. They are what bind you. A prime contractor must pass the same requirements down to any subcontractor that will handle the same information, so they reach you as a subcontractor too.

title: The 15 basic safeguards
subtitle: Protecting government information
summary: The basic safeguarding clause lists fifteen practices. In plain terms: 1. Only authorized users, devices and processes can get in. 2. Users can do only what the...
content: The 15 basic safeguards Protecting government information The basic safeguarding clause lists fifteen practices. In plain terms: 1. Only authorized users, devices and processes can get in. 2. Users can do only what they are permitted to do. 3. Connections to outside systems are controlled. 4. Nothing sensitive is posted on public systems. 5. Every user and device is identified. 6. Identities are verified before access is granted. 7. Media holding the information is wiped or destroyed before disposal. 8. Physical access to equipment is limited. 9. Visitors are escorted and physical access is logged. 10. Traffic is monitored and controlled at the network boundary. 11. Public-facing systems sit on a separate network segment. 12. Flaws are found and fixed in good time. 13. Protection against malicious code is in place. 14. That protection is kept up to date. 15. Systems and incoming files are scanned. Most companies with ordinary good practice meet most of these. The work is in confirming each one and writing down how.

title: NIST SP 800-171
subtitle: Protecting government information
summary: NIST Special Publication 800-171 is the standard for protecting CUI on a contractor’s own systems. Revision 2 has 110 requirements in 14 families: | Family | Fa...
content: NIST SP 800-171 Protecting government information NIST Special Publication 800-171 is the standard for protecting CUI on a contractor’s own systems. Revision 2 has 110 requirements in 14 families: | Family | Family | | --- | --- | | Access control | Media protection | | Awareness and training | Personnel security | | Audit and accountability | Physical protection | | Configuration management | Risk assessment | | Identification and authentication | Security assessment | | Incident response | System and communications protection | | Maintenance | System and information integrity | NIST published Revision 3 in 2024, which reorganizes the requirements into 17 families. The Department of Defense has continued to assess contractors against Revision 2. Use the revision your contract and the current DoD guidance name, not simply the newest one. Two documents sit beside the requirements: - A system security plan describes the system that holds CUI, its boundary, and how each requirement is met. - A plan of action and milestones lists each requirement not yet met, what will be done about it and by when.

title: Scoring an assessment
subtitle: Protecting government information
summary: The Department of Defense scores an 800-171 assessment with a published method. You start at 110. For each requirement that is not fully implemented, points com...
content: Scoring an assessment Protecting government information The Department of Defense scores an 800-171 assessment with a published method. You start at 110. For each requirement that is not fully implemented, points come off: 5, 3 or 1, depending on how much the requirement matters. Because the deductions add up to more than 110, a score can be negative. Two practical points follow: - The score measures what is implemented , not what is planned. A requirement on your plan of action still loses its points until it is done. - A few requirements can earn partial credit. Most cannot. Scores from self-assessments are reported to the government in the Supplier Performance Risk System. An affirmation that goes with a score is a statement made to the government by a senior official of your company. Do not sign one you cannot support.

title: CMMC
subtitle: Protecting government information
summary: The Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification program is how the Department of Defense checks that the requirements above have actually been met, before award....
content: CMMC Protecting government information The Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification program is how the Department of Defense checks that the requirements above have actually been met, before award. It has three levels. | Level | Protects | Requirements | How it is assessed | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 1 | FCI | The 15 basic safeguards | Self-assessment every year, with an annual affirmation | | 2 | CUI | The 110 requirements of NIST SP 800-171 Revision 2 | Self-assessment, or assessment by an accredited third-party organization, depending on the contract. Every three years, with an annual affirmation | | 3 | CUI needing more protection | Level 2 plus selected requirements from NIST SP 800-172 | Assessment by the government | The level you need is stated in the solicitation.

title: Where the CMMC rollout stands
subtitle: Protecting government information
summary: The program rule, 32 CFR Part 170, took effect in December 2024. The contract clause followed in November 2025, with requirements to be phased in over three yea...
content: Where the CMMC rollout stands Protecting government information The program rule, 32 CFR Part 170, took effect in December 2024. The contract clause followed in November 2025, with requirements to be phased in over three years. - Phase 1 began on November 10, 2025. Solicitations can require a Level 1 or Level 2 self-assessment as a condition of award. - Later phases , which were to bring in third-party Level 2 certification from November 2026 and Level 3 after that, were put on hold by the department in mid-2026. As checked for this guide, new solicitations could require only self-assessments, and no new date had been announced. This is the part of this guide most likely to be out of date when you read it. Check the Department of Defense Chief Information Officer’s CMMC pages for the current schedule, and read the solicitation for what it actually requires.

title: Where to start
subtitle: Protecting government information
summary: The order matters more than the speed. 1. Find the information. List where FCI and CUI will arrive, where they will be stored and who will touch them. Email, la...
content: Where to start Protecting government information The order matters more than the speed. 1. Find the information. List where FCI and CUI will arrive, where they will be stored and who will touch them. Email, laptops, file shares, cloud services, backups, printers. 2. Shrink the boundary. The requirements apply to the systems that handle the information. Keeping CUI in one separate, well-controlled environment is far cheaper than securing a whole company to that standard. 3. Check your cloud services. A cloud service that stores CUI for a defense contract has to meet the FedRAMP Moderate baseline or its equivalent. Many ordinary commercial plans do not. 4. Assess honestly. Go through the requirements one at a time and record what is implemented, with evidence. 5. Write the system security plan as you go. 6. Put every gap on the plan of action , with an owner and a date. 7. Close the gaps , starting with the ones that carry the most points. 8. Be ready to report. Know how you would detect an incident and how you would report it within 72 hours. Reporting to the Department of Defense needs an account and a certificate that take time to obtain, so set them up before you need them. A checklist tool helps with steps 4 to 6. It does not do steps 1 to 3 for you, and it cannot tell you whether a requirement is truly met.

title: Marking CUI
subtitle: Protecting government information
summary: Marking tells the next person that a document needs protection. The government-wide rules are in 32 CFR Part 2002, and the Department of Defense adds its own in...
content: Marking CUI Protecting government information Marking tells the next person that a document needs protection. The government-wide rules are in 32 CFR Part 2002, and the Department of Defense adds its own in DoD Instruction 5200.48. The banner. A document containing CUI carries the marking CUI at the top of every page. Department of Defense practice is to put it at the top and the bottom. The designation indicator. The first page or cover carries a block that says who controls the information and how it may be shared. Defense marking guidance shows it in this form: Portion marks. Individual paragraphs may be marked (CUI) or (U) . If portion marking is used at all, it has to be used throughout the document. Things to remember: - Categories come from the CUI Registry. Do not invent one. - Older markings such as “For Official Use Only” are no longer applied to new documents. A document that still carries one is not automatically CUI, and not automatically free of it. - Do not mark something CUI to be safe. Marking information that does not qualify restricts it without authority. - CUI stays CUI until the government decontrols it. - Follow your contract and the marking guide from the agency you work for. Their instructions outrank a general description like this one.

title: What this does not cover
subtitle: Protecting government information
summary: - Classified information. Entirely separate rules. - Export controls. Technical data controlled under the ITAR or the EAR has its own rules about who may access...
content: What this does not cover Protecting government information - Classified information. Entirely separate rules. - Export controls. Technical data controlled under the ITAR or the EAR has its own rules about who may access it, on top of anything here. - Civilian agencies. A government-wide contract rule for CUI has been proposed but was not final when this guide was checked. Civilian agency contracts may carry their own security clauses. - Your particular contract. It can add requirements beyond any of these.

title: Is it current?
subtitle: Where the rules live
summary: A source can be official and still out of date on your screen. Four checks: 1. Look for the date. The eCFR shows the date its text is current as of, at the top ...
content: Is it current? Where the rules live A source can be official and still out of date on your screen. Four checks: 1. Look for the date. The eCFR shows the date its text is current as of, at the top of each page. FAR pages show the acquisition circular and its effective date. NIST publications carry a publication date and a revision number. 2. Check for something pending. A proposed rule in the Federal Register is not yet the rule, but it tells you a change is coming. 3. Check for a deviation. Agencies can direct their contracting officers to depart from the published regulation by issuing a class deviation. Defense deviations are published with the DFARS. 4. Check your contract. The version of a clause in your contract, identified by its date, is the version that binds you, even after the regulation changes. To see what a regulation said on an earlier date, the eCFR has a point-in-time view. That is how you check a tool’s figure against the rule as it stood when the tool was written.

title: Guidance is not regulation
subtitle: Where the rules live
summary: Agencies publish a great deal of helpful material that is not binding: frequently asked questions, guidebooks, training slides, memos. It is often the clearest ...
content: Guidance is not regulation Where the rules live Agencies publish a great deal of helpful material that is not binding: frequently asked questions, guidebooks, training slides, memos. It is often the clearest explanation available, and it can change without notice. When a tool or a guide relies on guidance instead of a regulation, it should say so. When guidance and the regulation conflict, the regulation governs.

title: What does not count as a source
subtitle: Where the rules live
summary: - A leaked document , or one marked for limited distribution that can be found online anyway. Public means officially released. - A document from behind a login...
content: What does not count as a source Where the rules live - A leaked document , or one marked for limited distribution that can be found online anyway. Public means officially released. - A document from behind a login that you can reach because of your job. - A consultant’s summary, a vendor’s white paper or a forum post , however accurate. They are useful for finding the rule. They are not the rule. - A generated answer from a chat assistant or a search summary. Ask it where the rule is, then go and read the rule. This project builds only from the first kind of material: officially released regulations, standards and guidance.

This guide explains how the document is organized so you can find the dozen facts that tell you whether to bid, and what a winning answer has to contain. The government is learning who can

content: The kinds of request Read a solicitation Not everything the government posts is a solicitation, and the different kinds are answered differently. | Name | What it is | What you send back | | --- | --- | --- | | Request for information (RFI) or sources sought | Market research. The government is learning who can do the work | A short description of your capability. It is not an offer and cannot win a contract | | Draft solicitation | An early version, posted for comment | Questions and comments | | Request for quotation (RFQ) | A request for prices, common for smaller and simpler buys | A quote | | Request for proposals (RFP) | The full process for negotiated contracts, with instructions and evaluation factors | A proposal, usually in several volumes | | Invitation for bids (IFB) | Sealed bidding. The award goes on price to a responsive, responsible bidder | A bid | Federal opportunities above a set dollar value are posted on SAM.gov under Contract Opportunities. Searching and reading there is free and needs no account. Downloading some attachments does need one. An RFI is worth answering. The answers help the government decide whether a purchase can be set aside for small businesses, and how to write the requirement.

summary: Many solicitations follow the uniform contract format, which divides the document into thirteen lettered sections. Even when a solicitation is laid out differen...
content: The lettered sections Read a solicitation Many solicitations follow the uniform contract format, which divides the document into thirteen lettered sections. Even when a solicitation is laid out differently, people in this field use the letters as shorthand, so they are worth learning once. | Section | Title | What you find there | | --- | --- | --- | | A | Solicitation/contract form | The cover form: solicitation number, issuing office, due date and time | | B | Supplies or services and prices/costs | The line items you will price | | C | Description/specifications/statement of work | The work | | D | Packaging and marking | How deliverables are packed and labeled | | E | Inspection and acceptance | How and where the government accepts the work | | F | Deliveries or performance | Dates, period of performance, place | | G | Contract administration data | Who administers the contract, and how to invoice | | H | Special contract requirements | Terms particular to this contract: security, key personnel, transitions | | I | Contract clauses | The standard clauses, mostly by reference | | J | List of attachments | Everything attached, by title | | K | Representations, certifications and other statements | Statements you make about your company | | L | Instructions, conditions and notices to offerors | How to prepare and submit the proposal | | M | Evaluation factors for award | How the proposal will be judged | Sections A through J become the contract. Section K is carried into it by reference. Sections L and M are about the competition, and are not part of the contract. The Federal Acquisition Regulation is being rewritten. For decades the uniform contract format has been at FAR 15.204-1, and it is still there in the codified text. The overhaul text that agencies have been working from since 2025 moves it to a different section and makes it optional. Expect to see both layouts for some time, and find the rule by its title on acquisition.gov instead of trusting a section number from memory, including the ones in this guide.

title: When the letters are missing
subtitle: Read a solicitation
summary: Purchases of commercial products and services often use a shorter layout, built around a standard form and a set of commercial clauses. There may be no Section ...
content: When the letters are missing Read a solicitation Purchases of commercial products and services often use a shorter layout, built around a standard form and a set of commercial clauses. There may be no Section L or M by name. The same content is still there under plainer headings: - Instructions to offerors is the equivalent of Section L. - Evaluation or basis for award is the equivalent of Section M. - Statement of work , performance work statement or statement of objectives is the equivalent of Section C. - Price schedule is the equivalent of Section B. Other transaction agreements, which some defense buyers use for prototypes, are not governed by the FAR at all. Their requests follow whatever format the issuing office chooses. Read them without assumptions.

title: What to read first
subtitle: Read a solicitation
summary: Reading from page one is the slow way. This order gets you to a bid decision fastest: 1. The cover page. Due date, time and time zone. How to submit. Who to ask...
content: What to read first Read a solicitation Reading from page one is the slow way. This order gets you to a bid decision fastest: 1. The cover page. Due date, time and time zone. How to submit. Who to ask. 2. Section L. What you must hand in: volumes, page limits, format, required forms. 3. Section M. What the government will score, and what matters most. 4. Section C. The work itself. Can you do it? 5. Section B. How the price is structured. 6. Section H. Anything unusual: clearances, key personnel, special security terms. 7. Sections I and K. The clauses and the statements you must make. 8. Section J attachments. Often the real detail lives here: the pricing workbook, the labor category descriptions, the data requirements.

title: The first-pass list
subtitle: Read a solicitation
summary: Before you spend a day on a solicitation, find these facts. Most are on the cover page or in Sections L and M. - Deadlines. When questions are due. When the pro...
content: The first-pass list Read a solicitation Before you spend a day on a solicitation, find these facts. Most are on the cover page or in Sections L and M. - Deadlines. When questions are due. When the proposal is due, to the minute, and in which time zone. - How to submit. A portal, email, or something else, and any size limit on files. - Who may bid. Whether the purchase is set aside for small businesses or a specific program, and under which NAICS code and size standard. See Codes, registration and small business status. - Contract type. Fixed price, time and materials, cost reimbursement, or an ordering contract with task orders. - Length. The base period and the option periods. - Place of performance. On a government site, at your own, or remote. - Security. Whether people or facilities need a clearance, and how government information must be protected. See Protecting government information. - Basis for award. Whether the government will trade price against quality, or take the lowest-priced proposal that is technically acceptable. - Past performance. How many references, how recent and how similar. - Mandatory qualifications. Certifications, registrations or experience that are pass or fail. If you fail a pass-or-fail item, nothing else in the proposal matters.

title: Clauses incorporated by reference
subtitle: Read a solicitation
summary: Section I can list a hundred clauses by number and title alone. Each one is a term of the contract, with the same force as if it were printed in full. The full ...
content: Clauses incorporated by reference Read a solicitation Section I can list a hundred clauses by number and title alone. Each one is a term of the contract, with the same force as if it were printed in full. The full text is on acquisition.gov. The numbers tell you where a clause comes from: | Pattern | Source | | --- | --- | | 52.2xx-xx | The Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) | | 252.2xx-7xxx | The Defense FAR Supplement (DFARS) | | Other prefixes | Another agency’s supplement | You do not need to read every clause on the first pass. These are worth finding early, because they change what the work costs: | Subject | Long-standing clause | Why it matters | | --- | --- | --- | | Safeguarding contractor systems | FAR 52.204-21 | Fifteen basic security requirements for any system holding federal contract information | | Safeguarding defense information | DFARS 252.204-7012 | NIST SP 800-171 and 72-hour incident reporting | | CMMC | DFARS 252.204-7021 | A required CMMC level | | Limitations on subcontracting | FAR 52.219-14 | How much of a set-aside contract you must perform yourself | | Service contract labor standards | FAR 52.222-41 | Minimum wages and benefits for covered service workers | | Prompt payment | FAR 52.232-25 | When you are paid, and interest if you are not | Some of these are being renumbered as part of the rewrite described above. Search by the clause title if a number does not match.

title: Amendments and questions
subtitle: Read a solicitation
summary: A solicitation changes after it is posted. Each change is an amendment, and each one is part of the solicitation. - Watch for amendments. On SAM.gov you can fol...
content: Amendments and questions Read a solicitation A solicitation changes after it is posted. Each change is an amendment, and each one is part of the solicitation. - Watch for amendments. On SAM.gov you can follow an opportunity. An amendment can move the due date, change the work or replace an attachment. - Acknowledge every amendment in the way the solicitation requires. A proposal that ignores an amendment can be rejected. - Ask questions in writing, by the deadline, to the person named. Answers are normally published to every bidder, so do not put anything proprietary in a question. - Do not rely on anything said informally. Only the written solicitation and its amendments count. A good question points to a page and paragraph, quotes the text and asks one thing.

title: Late is late
subtitle: Read a solicitation
summary: A proposal that arrives after the exact time stated is late, and with narrow exceptions a late proposal is not considered. Portals slow down in the last hour, a...
content: Late is late Read a solicitation A proposal that arrives after the exact time stated is late, and with narrow exceptions a late proposal is not considered. Portals slow down in the last hour, and email attachments are held up by size limits and scanners. Plan to submit a day early.

title: Decide whether to bid
subtitle: Read a solicitation
summary: A proposal costs real time. Before you commit, answer these honestly: - Are we eligible, and do we pass every pass-or-fail item? - Can we do the work in Section...
content: Decide whether to bid Read a solicitation A proposal costs real time. Before you commit, answer these honestly: - Are we eligible, and do we pass every pass-or-fail item? - Can we do the work in Section C with people we have or can hire? - Do we have past performance that matches what Section M asks for? - Can we meet the security requirements by the time they apply? - Does the price structure in Section B leave room to do the work properly? - Can we produce everything Section L asks for by the due date? Deciding not to bid is a legitimate result of reading a solicitation well. When the answer is yes, the next guide covers answering every requirement.

content: Request a tool Request a tool or add your own A useful request covers three things: - The job. What you need to produce, and what you do by hand today. “I rebuild a spreadsheet that turns our pools into rates for every proposal” is a job. “A pricing tool” is not. - Who needs it. For example, a solo developer pricing a first bid, or a small company preparing for a first assessment. - The public source. The regulation, standard or guide the tool would be based on, with a link if you have one. You can copy this outline into an issue or an email: The last line matters more than it looks. If a tool would be useless to you the moment it asked for a company name, say so. How a suggestion enters the 10-worker pipeline Community suggestions can be submitted directly on the Portal via ✎ Edit (no login required), via GitHub issue, or by email. Every suggestion enters cs-01-intake and moves through the 100% deterministic pipeline: Follow live progress in Pipeline and Decide, or read The 10-Worker Prior Art Engine.

title: Report a mistake

content: Report a mistake Request a tool or add your own A wrong result is the most useful thing you can report. Include: 1. what you entered, with made-up values in place of anything real 2. what the tool showed 3. what the correct answer is 4. the section of the regulation that shows it Check a tool’s answer explains how to find that section. The same goes for the guides. If one is unclear, out of date or wrong, say which sentence and what it should say.

title: Add a tool you built
subtitle: Request a tool or add your own
summary: Tools live in their own repositories, under your own name or organization. ClearedStack lists them. It does not take them over. To be listed, a tool has to be: ...
content: Add a tool you built Request a tool or add your own Tools live in their own repositories, under your own name or organization. ClearedStack lists them. It does not take them over. To be listed, a tool has to be: 1. Free and open source , under an OSI-approved license, with no paid tier and no ads. 2. Client-side. It runs in the browser or on the user’s own machine, and does not send what the user enters to any server. 3. Free of tracking : no analytics, no third-party scripts, no accounts. 4. Built from public sources , and clear about which ones. 5. Honest about its limits , including that its output is not professional advice. To list it: 1. Fork this site’s repository. 2. Add one entry to src/data/catalog.ts . 3. Open a pull request that links to your tool and its repository. The entry looks like this: The home page, the catalog and their counts are generated from that file, so the one entry is the whole change. Pull requests may include an optional provenance field documenting where the inspiration originated. Build a tool that can be listed goes through each condition in detail, with a checklist to run before you open the pull request.

title: How a listing is reviewed
subtitle: Request a tool or add your own
summary: A person reads the pull request and uses the tool. The review checks the five conditions and nothing else: - the license file is there - the Network tab stays q...
content: How a listing is reviewed Request a tool or add your own A person reads the pull request and uses the tool. The review checks the five conditions and nothing else: - the license file is there - the Network tab stays quiet while the tool is used, and the tool still works with the network disconnected - the page loads nothing from other companies’ servers - the README names the sources and says what the tool does not cover - the examples and test data are made up The review does not certify that every result is correct. That is why each tool has to name its sources: so that anyone can check. A tool that later breaks a condition is taken off the list until it is fixed.

title: What never goes in
subtitle: Request a tool or add your own
summary: Do not put any of these in a request, an issue, an email, a pull request, a tool or its test data: - classified information - controlled unclassified informatio...
content: What never goes in Request a tool or add your own Do not put any of these in a request, an issue, an email, a pull request, a tool or its test data: - classified information - controlled unclassified information (CUI) - export-controlled technical data - real contract data, real rates, or anything that identifies a real company’s bid - text copied from a solicitation that is not publicly posted “Public” means officially released. A document that leaked, or that is marked for limited distribution but can be found online anyway, is not public for this project. If you are unsure, leave it out and describe the problem in your own words with made-up numbers.

Contribute only on your own time and your own equipment, and only what you are free to share. If you are not sure whether something you know from work is public, treat it as not public.
