title: How Ideas Are Scored and Decided
subtitle: Guide · Section L.4
summary: How cs-03-evaluate runs deterministic knockout gates, the 100-point rubric, and tie-breakers, and how cs-04-decide powers the /guides/decide/ owner inbox for tool outcomes and anonymous public edits.
content: How Ideas Are Scored and Decided How cs-03-evaluate runs deterministic knockout gates, the 100-point rubric, and tie-breakers, and how cs-04-decide powers the /guides/decide/ owner inbox for tool outcomes and anonymous public edits. contribute L.4  In ClearedStack v3.1, evaluating candidate tools and approving changes is split between two focused Go services in the cs-workers namespace: cs-03-evaluate (which scores candidates with zero AI) and cs-04-decide (which powers the human owner's /guides/decide/ inbox). Every rule, weight, and decision outcome is visible to the public through read-only pub. database views on the Portal—no sign-in required. Deterministic evaluation with cs-03-evaluate cs-03-evaluate leases observed items from hub-queue-api and runs a 100% deterministic YAML/Go rule engine. Given the same observed facts, it produce

title: Deterministic evaluation with cs-03-evaluate
subtitle: How Ideas Are Scored and Decided
summary: cs-03-evaluate leases observed items from hub-queue-api and runs a 100% deterministic YAML/Go rule engine. Given the same observed facts, it produces the exact ...
content: Deterministic evaluation with cs-03-evaluate How Ideas Are Scored and Decided cs-03-evaluate leases observed items from hub-queue-api and runs a 100% deterministic YAML/Go rule engine. Given the same observed facts, it produces the exact same score on any cluster, with zero language-model calls or token costs. To handle differences across contracting domains without guesswork, cs-03-evaluate uses category-specific sub-tools under tools/rubric-profiles// (such as pricing , proposal , cyber , market , or devsecops ). Each profile defines domain-specific thresholds and golden test fixtures. If an item arrives with an unsupported category, the worker fails closed : it pauses the item in needs subtool and cs-10-notify opens a task in the cs-03-evaluate repository. Once a new profile is added and built by cs-runner , hub-queue-api automatically replays the paused item.

title: The five knockout gates
subtitle: How Ideas Are Scored and Decided
summary: Before any points are tallied, cs-03-evaluate checks five binary gates. Failing any single gate stops evaluation immediately and moves the item to screened-out ...
content: The five knockout gates How Ideas Are Scored and Decided Before any points are tallied, cs-03-evaluate checks five binary gates. Failing any single gate stops evaluation immediately and moves the item to screened-out with the failure reason logged publicly. 1. Public source. Rules, formulas, and thresholds must come from officially released public materials (statutes, FAR, DFARS, or NIST Special Publications)—never paywalled manuals or unwritten industry folklore. 2. Runs in the browser. The tool must execute entirely client-side using HTML, CSS, JavaScript, or WebAssembly, with no backend server or remote API. 3. Private by design. The tool must work offline, require no accounts, emit zero tracking telemetry, and enforce a strict Content Security Policy ( connect-src 'self' ). 4. One job. The tool must perform a single, focused task describable in one active sentence starting with a verb. Oversized suites fail this gate unless split into smaller proposals. 5. Arithmetic, not advice. The tool must compute numbers, structure data, or look up citations—never render legal advice or replace a contracting officer's discretion.

title: The 100-point rubric
subtitle: How Ideas Are Scored and Decided
summary: Candidates that pass all five gates are scored across seven weighted factors. Each factor receives an integer rating from 1 to 5 , multiplied by its weight for ...
content: The 100-point rubric How Ideas Are Scored and Decided Candidates that pass all five gates are scored across seven weighted factors. Each factor receives an integer rating from 1 to 5 , multiplied by its weight for a composite score between 20 and 100 . | Factor | Weight | Max points | What it measures | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Need for small businesses | ×4 | 20 | Severity of manual administrative burden or error risk for small contractors. | | Gap in existing free options | ×4 | 20 | Scarcity of free, private, tracking-free alternatives ( 5 means only paid or gated tools exist). | | Strength of the public source | ×3 | 15 | Grounding in enacted statute, Title 48 CFR, or published NIST standards. | | Fits in a browser | ×3 | 15 | Ability to run cleanly in browser memory without large remote datasets. | | Small enough to read | ×2 | 10 | Core logic is concise enough for a reviewer to audit in one sitting. | | Can be checked | ×2 | 10 | Availability of official worked examples or agency test vectors to verify outputs. | | Low upkeep of reference data | ×2 | 10 | Preference for stable statutory math over volatile tables requiring frequent updates. | Based on the composite score and deterministic override rules, cs-03-evaluate assigns a preliminary recommendation and moves the item to scored : - Build (Score ≥ 75 and Gap > 1): Recommended for clean-room implementation. - Link (Score ≥ 75 and Gap = 1): Override—an acceptable free, private tool already exists, so ClearedStack links to it rather than rebuilding. - Park (Score 55–74): Valid idea deferred due to missing public data, pending rulemaking, or capacity. - Reject (Score < 55): Below the inclusion threshold, logged publicly with its point breakdown. If a candidate scores 4 or 5 on Need but 1 or 2 on Small enough to read , the engine flags it for split/merge review so the owner can break it into atomic single-job tools.

title: Five deterministic tie-breakers
subtitle: How Ideas Are Scored and Decided
summary: When multiple scored candidates share the exact same composite score, cs-03-evaluate breaks ties in a fixed five-step order: 1. Roadmap phase fit — Direct align...
content: Five deterministic tie-breakers How Ideas Are Scored and Decided When multiple scored candidates share the exact same composite score, cs-03-evaluate breaks ties in a fixed five-step order: 1. Roadmap phase fit — Direct alignment with the active project phase wins. 2. Gap severity — Higher score on the Gap factor wins. 3. Low upkeep — Higher score on the Low upkeep factor wins. 4. Small code footprint — Higher score on the Small enough to read factor wins. 5. Community demand — Higher count of independent requests and issue upvotes wins.

title: Human decisions and /guides/decide/ (cs-04-decide)
subtitle: How Ideas Are Scored and Decided
summary: cs-04-decide has no tools// sub-tools because final judgment belongs strictly to the human project owner. It powers the /guides/decide/ inbox on clearedstack.co...
content: Human decisions and /guides/decide/ (cs-04-decide) How Ideas Are Scored and Decided cs-04-decide has no tools// sub-tools because final judgment belongs strictly to the human project owner. It powers the /guides/decide/ inbox on clearedstack.com , which handles two queues: - Tool determinations: The owner reviews scored (or overridden screened-out ) candidates and chooses Approve (Build) , Link , Merge , Park , Reject , or Override . Any override requires an explicit written reason, which is recorded in the public decision log. Approved items advance to cs-05-provenance ( approved state). - Anonymous public edit approvals: Any visitor can click ✎ anywhere on the Portal to propose a DATA , CONFIG , or ISSUE edit without signing in. After passing browser Proof-of-Work, a honeypot check, daily-salted IP hash rate limits, and ownership map.json schema validation, proposals wait in core.edit proposal ( pending approval ). Nothing touches cs-git or the cluster until the owner clicks Approve in /guides/decide/ , which dispatches cs-10-notify on the urgent lane ( Proposed -> Approved -> Building -> Live ).

title: How the Self-Building Factory Loop Works
subtitle: Guide · Section L.6
summary: How the 11 pipeline repositories (clearedstack.com plus cs-01 through cs-10) and 4 clean-room control-plane services close the loop from public signal or edit proposal to live software.
content: How the Self-Building Factory Loop Works How the 11 pipeline repositories (clearedstack.com plus cs-01 through cs-10) and 4 clean-room control-plane services close the loop from public signal or edit proposal to live software. project L.6 draft intent ClearedStack is organized as a self-building software factory rather than a monolith. Every component has one bounded responsibility, runs 100% deterministic code at runtime, and connects to the rest of the factory through explicit schemas, Git commits, and signed OCI image digests. Why 11 pipeline repositories stay separate The factory is intentionally split into eleven core pipeline repositories —the hub ( clearedstack.com ) plus ten single-stage deterministic workers ( cs-01-intake through cs-10-notify )—supported by four tiny MIT Go control-plane repositories ( cs-git , cs-registry , cs-ru

title: Why 11 pipeline repositories stay separate
subtitle: How the Self-Building Factory Loop Works
summary: The factory is intentionally split into eleven core pipeline repositories —the hub ( clearedstack.com ) plus ten single-stage deterministic workers ( cs-01-inta...
content: Why 11 pipeline repositories stay separate How the Self-Building Factory Loop Works The factory is intentionally split into eleven core pipeline repositories —the hub ( clearedstack.com ) plus ten single-stage deterministic workers ( cs-01-intake through cs-10-notify )—supported by four tiny MIT Go control-plane repositories ( cs-git , cs-registry , cs-runner , and cs-store ). | Repository group | Repositories | Primary role in the factory | | --- | --- | --- | | Hub & contracts (1 repo) | clearedstack.com | Public static/SSR Portal, ownership map.json , canonical JSON Schemas, hub-queue-api deployment config, and the catalog index under /tools/ . | | Deterministic pipeline (10 repos) | cs-01-intake .. cs-10-notify | Ten isolated Go worker pods in cs-workers (~30 MiB each). Each owns one stage, its own tools// deterministic sub-tools, and its own golden test fixtures. | | Clean-room control plane (4 repos) | cs-git , cs-registry , cs-runner , cs-store | Internal bare Git + GitHub code mirror, internal 5-digest OCI store, Dockerless ko /BuildKit builder, and Server-Side Apply reconciler in clearedstack . | | Shipped browser tools (1 repo per tool) | Individual tool repos | Standalone, zero-backend, offline-capable MIT web utilities listed on /tools/ once verified by cs-07-verify . | Keeping the eleven pipeline repositories separate guarantees three operational properties: 1. Blast-radius isolation: Updating an extractor in cs-02-observe or a rubric profile in cs-03-evaluate rebuilds and rolls out only that 30 MiB worker pod—never touching clearedstack.com or the other nine workers. 2. Clean-room enforcement by repository boundary: Raw public observation snapshots stay sealed inside cs-02-observe . cs-06-build lives in a separate repository with zero access to observation artifacts; it reads only sanitized JSON specifications stamped by cs-05-provenance and primary federal regulations. 3. Independent rollback: cs-registry retains the last five signed OCI digests per repository, allowing cs-store to roll back a single worker in seconds if a new sub-tool regresses.

title: Three closed loops that make the factory self-improving
subtitle: How the Self-Building Factory Loop Works
summary: A static catalog decays as regulations change, third-party pages shift layout, and users spot edge cases. ClearedStack turns all three failure modes into closed...
content: Three closed loops that make the factory self-improving How the Self-Building Factory Loop Works A static catalog decays as regulations change, third-party pages shift layout, and users spot edge cases. ClearedStack turns all three failure modes into closed, deterministic loops gated by human accountability. cs-git)", detail: "cs-10-notify writes the approved DATA/CONFIG change or opens a fingerprinted sub-tool task in the owning repo inside cs-git.", }, { tag: "4 · Build & Verify", label: "Dockerless build & golden fixtures (cs-runner)", detail: "cs-runner runs golden fixture tests, builds via ko or rootless BuildKit, signs with cosign, and pushes to cs-registry.", }, { tag: "5 · Reconcile & Replay", label: "Server-Side Apply & queue replay (cs-store + hub-queue-api)", detail: "cs-store rolls out the new digest, cs-git mirrors code to GitHub, and paused needs subtool records replay automatically.", }, ]} /> Loop A: Unknown layouts grow tools// sub-tools Workers never call an LLM at runtime to guess how to parse an unfamiliar page or edge case. When cs-02-observe , cs-03-evaluate , or cs-09-monitor encounters an unrecognized structure, it transitions the item to needs subtool ( E NEEDS SUBTOOL ). cs-10-notify deduplicates the fingerprint and opens a structured task in the owning worker repository in cs-git . Once a deterministic Go sub-tool and golden fixture are committed (authored by a human or with authoring-time AI review), cs-runner verifies the fixture, cs-store deploys the worker, and hub-queue-api automatically replays every record waiting on that case. Loop B: Anonymous ✎ Edit proposals route directly to owning repos Every editable element across /guides/command/ , /guides/apps/ , /guides/pipeline/ , /guides/decide/ , and /tools/ carries an elementId registered in src/data/ownership map.json . Visitors propose corrections without an account. After clearing the 5-layer anti-spam shield in hub-queue-api and receiving human approval in /guides/decide/ , cs-10-notify routes the change straight to the target repository in cs-git , which triggers cs-runner and pushes a code-only mirror to GitHub. Loop C: Regulatory drift triggers verification and rebuilds cs-09-monitor watches official public feeds (Federal Register, eCFR, NIST CSRC) alongside live and linked tools. When a cited clause in FAR, DFARS, or NIST SP 800-171 changes, cs-09-monitor queues a drift event back into the pipeline so formulas, citations, and worked examples are re-verified by cs-07-verify and republished by cs-08-catalog .

title: Shared Contracts Without an 11th Repo

content: How Software Decides What Appears on Screen How deterministic priority rules, six fixed UI primitives, anti-flicker guardrails, and six screen states control what appears on ClearedStack without AI. start L.1  Most dashboards force humans to hunt through dozens of charts to figure out if something is broken. ClearedStack flips that around: deterministic software rules—with zero AI at runtime—decide what floats to the top of your screen, what stays collapsed, and when a number is too old to trust. Every color, alert, and card position on the Portal follows the exact same public rules. Whether you are a visitor checking pipeline health or the owner reviewing pending decisions, the interface stays calm when things are quiet and loud only when something genuinely needs attention. content: Deterministic P0–P4 attention rules (no AI) How Software Decides What Appears on Screen Instead of letting a language model guess what looks important, the Portal sorts every worker, app, and queued item into one of five fixed priority tiers ( P0 through P4 ). title: Anti-flicker rules
subtitle: How Software Decides What Appears on Screen
summary: Live systems change state constantly. Without guardrails, pushing every raw queue tick straight to the browser makes numbers jitter and causes status badges to ...
content: Anti-flicker rules How Software Decides What Appears on Screen Live systems change state constantly. Without guardrails, pushing every raw queue tick straight to the browser makes numbers jitter and causes status badges to flap back and forth between green and amber. - Hysteresis (~2-minute hold): A status color cannot flip immediately on a single brief spike. A state change must hold steady for roughly two minutes before the UI promotes or clears a color, preventing noisy flapping. - Batched updates: Instead of streaming every individual database write to every visitor, updates are grouped into short batches every few seconds (or served as cached snapshots for anonymous visitors), keeping numbers readable. - Freshness timestamps: Every status and MetricCell carries a generation timestamp. If the server stream goes silent for more than 15 seconds, the UI refuses to show frozen green numbers and automatically switches to the stale state.

summary: Every component on screen is always in one of six explicit visual states. Idle components are never painted red, and missing data is never disguised as healthy....
content: The 6 screen states How Software Decides What Appears on Screen Every component on screen is always in one of six explicit visual states. Idle components are never painted red, and missing data is never disguised as healthy. | Screen State | Visual Treatment | When It Appears | | --- | --- | --- | | healthy | Green indicator | The app or worker is running normally, health checks pass, and updates are arriving on time. | | idle | Muted grey (never red) | The worker is healthy and ready, with zero queued items and zero errors; collapsed into a quiet summary row. | | erroring | Crimson ( --danger ) + icon + code | An active failure, crash, or dead-lettered item exists; shows a sanitized code such as E TIMEOUT or E PARSE (never raw stack traces or internal IPs). | | recovering | Amber ( --warn ) | A component is retrying after an error, waiting on a needs subtool fix, or inside its hysteresis cooldown window. | | stale | Dashed grey border | The live stream has been silent for more than 15 seconds, warning that the view is paused rather than live. | | empty | Muted placeholder | Initial clean state ( "Nothing has been collected yet" ) before any items have entered the pipeline. |

title: Inside the Worker Namespace (cs-workers)
subtitle: Two-Namespace Kubernetes Topology
summary: All ten workers ( cs-01-intake through cs-10-notify ) live in cs-workers and are 100% deterministic—there is zero AI at runtime. Each worker reads and writes ta...
content: Inside the Worker Namespace (cs-workers) Two-Namespace Kubernetes Topology All ten workers ( cs-01-intake through cs-10-notify ) live in cs-workers and are 100% deterministic—there is zero AI at runtime. Each worker reads and writes tasks through hub-queue-api rather than touching the database directly. To keep baseline memory tiny, cs-02-observe runs as a lightweight Go HTTP pod (~30 MiB) and spawns on-demand headless browser Jobs only when it encounters a JavaScript-heavy website.

title: Default-Deny Network Policies
subtitle: Two-Namespace Kubernetes Topology
summary: Both namespaces enforce a default-deny network posture. In Kubernetes, a default-deny network policy means every pod is blocked from sending or receiving networ...
content: Default-Deny Network Policies Two-Namespace Kubernetes Topology Both namespaces enforce a default-deny network posture. In Kubernetes, a default-deny network policy means every pod is blocked from sending or receiving network traffic unless an explicit allow rule exists. - One public door: Only clearedstack-web accepts traffic from the cluster Ingress. Every other pod in both namespaces is cluster-private. - No direct database access from workers: Pods in cs-workers can only call hub-queue-api over authenticated ServiceAccount HTTP (plus approved outbound public fetches for observation and monitoring). They cannot reach postgres , cs-git , or cs-registry directly. - Hidden internals: Because cs-store strips node names, pod hostnames, and internal IPs before forwarding status to hub-queue-api , the public Portal never leaks cluster topology.

subtitle: Two-Namespace Kubernetes Topology
summary: When a single node gets busy—for example, when cs-runner compiles a new image or cs-02-observe launches a headless browser Job—Kubernetes priority class rules d...
content: Priority Classes Two-Namespace Kubernetes Topology When a single node gets busy—for example, when cs-runner compiles a new image or cs-02-observe launches a headless browser Job—Kubernetes priority class rules decide which pods keep their resources first. | Priority Tier | Assigned Workloads | Behavior Under Pressure | | --- | --- | --- | | High (Control Plane) | postgres , hub-queue-api , clearedstack-web , cs-git , cs-registry , cs-store | Protected from eviction so the Portal, queues, and storage stay responsive | | Standard (Workers) | cs-01-intake through cs-10-notify | Run steadily with predictable small footprints; yield before control-plane pods | | Low (Ephemeral Jobs) | cs-runner build Jobs and on-demand headless browser Jobs | Scheduled when capacity is available and preempted first if memory tightens |

title: Non-Root Security Without Docker
subtitle: Two-Namespace Kubernetes Topology
summary: Every pod in both clearedstack and cs-workers runs as an unprivileged non-root user with dropped Linux capabilities, no privilege escalation, and read-only root...
content: Non-Root Security Without Docker Two-Namespace Kubernetes Topology Every pod in both clearedstack and cs-workers runs as an unprivileged non-root user with dropped Linux capabilities, no privilege escalation, and read-only root filesystems wherever state does not need to be written. There is no Docker daemon anywhere in the cluster. k3s runs containers directly through containerd , cs-runner builds Go binaries with ko and web assets with rootless BuildKit, and cs-store applies manifests natively without custom CRDs.

title: Why It Fits on a Single 4 GiB k3s Node
subtitle: Two-Namespace Kubernetes Topology
summary: Traditional self-hosted Git, registry, CI, and GitOps stacks easily consume several gigabytes of RAM before a single application runs. By replacing them with cl...
content: Why It Fits on a Single 4 GiB k3s Node Two-Namespace Kubernetes Topology Traditional self-hosted Git, registry, CI, and GitOps stacks easily consume several gigabytes of RAM before a single application runs. By replacing them with clean-room Go microservices, ClearedStack keeps its entire 7-pod control plane around ~640 MiB of requested RAM (~1.25 GiB limit). Adding all 10 deterministic Go workers (~300 MiB) brings the whole 17-pod platform under 1 GiB of baseline memory—leaving plenty of headroom on a single 4 GiB k3s node ($10–$20/month) for ephemeral builds, browser Jobs, and Kubernetes itself.

title: When a Worker Turns Red: Troubleshooting Big Picture
subtitle: Guide · Section L.3
summary: How live error reporting, sanitized error codes, local worker spools, 1-click Pause and Rollback in /guides/apps/, and automatic issue deduplication in cs-10-notify work together when a worker fails.
content: When a Worker Turns Red: Troubleshooting Big Picture How live error reporting, sanitized error codes, local worker spools, 1-click Pause and Rollback in /guides/apps/, and automatic issue deduplication in cs-10-notify work together when a worker fails. host L.3  Because ClearedStack runs 100% deterministic workers with zero AI at runtime, a worker never guesses when it hits something unexpected. Instead, it stops cleanly, reports what happened in plain terms, and protects both your data and your cluster internals. Understanding how the pieces fit together turns a red status card from a guessing game into a predictable five-step loop. 1. Live Error Reporting Without Exposing Cluster Internals When a worker pod in the cs-workers namespace stalls, crashes, or fails a job, cs-store notices immediately. It watches pod, deployment, and Kubernetes event heal

title: 1. Live Error Reporting Without Exposing Cluster Internals
subtitle: When a Worker Turns Red: Troubleshooting Big Picture
summary: When a worker pod in the cs-workers namespace stalls, crashes, or fails a job, cs-store notices immediately. It watches pod, deployment, and Kubernetes event he...
content: 1. Live Error Reporting Without Exposing Cluster Internals When a Worker Turns Red: Troubleshooting Big Picture When a worker pod in the cs-workers namespace stalls, crashes, or fails a job, cs-store notices immediately. It watches pod, deployment, and Kubernetes event health across the cluster and strips out all private infrastructure details—such as internal IP addresses, node names, pod hostnames, and cluster DNS names—before forwarding a sanitized status update to hub-queue-api . From there, hub-queue-api updates the read-only pub. database views and pushes live updates over Server-Sent Events (SSE) to the Portal. On Command ( /guides/command/ ), urgent P0 errors and P1 stalled queues float straight to the top while healthy, idle workers stay collapsed. On Apps ( /guides/apps/ and /tools/ apps ), the affected worker card turns red and displays its active error code. Because the Portal is an open public sandbox with no login wall, anyone can inspect live worker health and sanitized errors without ever seeing credentials or private network topology.

title: 2. Sanitized Error Codes
subtitle: When a Worker Turns Red: Troubleshooting Big Picture
summary: Every public error is mapped to a short, sanitized code so you know why a worker stopped without reading raw stack traces or leaking internal paths. | Error Cod...
content: 2. Sanitized Error Codes When a Worker Turns Red: Troubleshooting Big Picture Every public error is mapped to a short, sanitized code so you know why a worker stopped without reading raw stack traces or leaking internal paths. | Error Code | What It Means in Plain Language | What Happens Next | | --- | --- | --- | | E TIMEOUT | A worker waited too long for an external website, PDF download, or internal step to respond. | The item stays safe in the queue and can be retried without losing earlier progress. | | E PARSE | A worker received data that broke its expected format, such as malformed JSON or a corrupted file. | The worker refuses to guess, logs the sanitized failure, and halts that item cleanly. | | E NEEDS SUBTOOL | A worker saw a valid but unfamiliar layout, such as a new government table structure it has no rule for yet. | The worker fails closed, pauses the item in needs subtool , and requests a new deterministic sub-tool. | When an item lands in needs subtool , nothing is lost. Once a developer or owner adds a new deterministic sub-tool and golden test fixture to that worker's repository, cs-runner tests and builds the updated image, cs-store deploys it, and hub-queue-api automatically replays all paused items matching that pattern.

title: 3. Worker Local Spools
subtitle: When a Worker Turns Red: Troubleshooting Big Picture
summary: Sometimes the problem is not the data—it is a brief hiccup between a worker and hub-queue-api , such as a control-plane restart or a momentary network blip. Eac...
content: 3. Worker Local Spools When a Worker Turns Red: Troubleshooting Big Picture Sometimes the problem is not the data—it is a brief hiccup between a worker and hub-queue-api , such as a control-plane restart or a momentary network blip. Each worker keeps a local spool, which is a small on-disk holding queue inside the worker pod. If hub-queue-api is temporarily unreachable when a worker finishes a job or needs to report an error, the worker writes the result to its local spool instead of dropping it on the floor. As soon as the connection recovers, the worker flushes its spooled updates in order. Because every worker is deterministic, replaying or flushing spooled work produces the exact same outcome.

title: 4. 1-Click Pause and Rollback in /guides/apps/
subtitle: When a Worker Turns Red: Troubleshooting Big Picture
summary: If a worker turns red right after an update—or keeps hammering a broken external site—you do not need to edit cluster manifests by hand. In Owner Mode on /guide...
content: 4. 1-Click Pause and Rollback in /guides/apps/ When a Worker Turns Red: Troubleshooting Big Picture If a worker turns red right after an update—or keeps hammering a broken external site—you do not need to edit cluster manifests by hand. In Owner Mode on /guides/apps/ (or /tools/ apps ), cs-store gives you two immediate safety switches on every worker card: | Action | What It Does | When to Use It | | --- | --- | --- | | Pause | Uses built-in Kubernetes Server-Side Apply to halt the worker cleanly without deleting its queues or configuration. | Use when an external target is down or you want to stop retries while investigating. | | Rollback | Switches the worker back to a previous signed image digest stored locally in cs-registry (which keeps the last 5 digests per app). | Use when a newly built worker version introduced a regression and you want a known-good build back in seconds. | Because cs-registry holds recent signed digests inside the cluster, Rollback works without pulling anything from GitHub or running Docker.

title: 5. Automatic Issue Deduplication in cs-10-notify
subtitle: When a Worker Turns Red: Troubleshooting Big Picture
summary: If 200 queued items hit the exact same unfamiliar table layout or timed-out endpoint, you do not want 200 identical bug reports flooding your inbox. Before any ...
content: 5. Automatic Issue Deduplication in cs-10-notify When a Worker Turns Red: Troubleshooting Big Picture If 200 queued items hit the exact same unfamiliar table layout or timed-out endpoint, you do not want 200 identical bug reports flooding your inbox. Before any alert or repository task is created, cs-10-notify computes a deterministic fingerprint from the worker name, sanitized error code, and failure pattern. If an open issue with that fingerprint already exists in cs-git (which mirrors code and tasks to GitHub on change), cs-10-notify updates the existing issue count instead of opening a duplicate. Only genuinely new failure patterns create new issues or trigger fresh owner alerts, keeping troubleshooting focused on root causes rather than noise.

title: Adding deterministic sub-tools and golden fixtures
subtitle: Work on this site & its 10 worker repos
summary: Every worker runs with 100% deterministic logic —there are no language models, no guesswork, and no hidden network calls at runtime. When a worker encounters an...
content: Adding deterministic sub-tools and golden fixtures Work on this site & its 10 worker repos Every worker runs with 100% deterministic logic —there are no language models, no guesswork, and no hidden network calls at runtime. When a worker encounters an unfamiliar page layout, document format, or edge case, it fails closed : it pauses the item in a needs subtool state, and cs-10-notify opens a fingerprinted task in the owning worker repository. Contributors solve these edge cases permanently by adding a deterministic sub-tool inside the worker repository: 1. Create a new folder under tools// and register it in tools/registry.yaml . 2. Add the matching rules and deterministic Go extraction or evaluation logic for that specific case. 3. Add golden fixtures in fixtures/ —saved sample inputs paired with the exact expected JSON output—so the behavior is locked in and repeatable on every run. When a sub-tool and its golden fixtures are merged into cs-git , cs-runner runs the golden test suite, builds the updated worker image, and cs-store deploys it. The queue service ( hub-queue-api ) then automatically replays all paused needs subtool items that match the new pattern.

content: Rules for every contribution Work on this site & its 10 worker repos - MIT and clean-room only: Write original code and documentation; never copy code from upstream projects or other licenses. - Zero AI at runtime: Workers and shipped tools must produce the exact same output every time for the same input. - Zero tracking or external assets: The Portal loads nothing from third-party servers and sets no tracking cookies. - Public data only: Never include classified information, CUI, export-controlled data, or real contract figures in code, fixtures, guides, or commit messages.

content: Workers 09 & 10: Continuous Monitoring & Notifications How cs-09-monitor watches federal feeds, live tools, and parked items with deterministic diffs, and how cs-10-notify deduplicates issues, commits approved Portal edits to cs-git, and drives alerts and live SSE updates. project L.6  Publishing a tool in clearedstack.com is not the end of its lifecycle. Federal rules change, external websites break, and visitors propose improvements on the open Portal. Workers cs-09-monitor and cs-10-notify close those loops. Like every service in the cs-workers namespace, both are lightweight, 100% deterministic Go programs with zero AI at runtime, pulling leased work from hub-queue-api and producing identical results on any cluster. cs-09-monitor: Scheduled Diffs and Reopening Items cs-09-monitor keeps the catalog accurate over time by running scheduled checks against external government

title: cs-09-monitor: Scheduled Diffs and Reopening Items
subtitle: Workers 09 & 10: Continuous Monitoring & Notifications
summary: cs-09-monitor keeps the catalog accurate over time by running scheduled checks against external government sources and already-published entries. Instead of scr...
content: cs-09-monitor: Scheduled Diffs and Reopening Items Workers 09 & 10: Continuous Monitoring & Notifications cs-09-monitor keeps the catalog accurate over time by running scheduled checks against external government sources and already-published entries. Instead of scraping pages blindly, it uses lightweight HTTP ETags (headers that ask a server whether a file has changed since the last check), structured XML feeds, and deterministic DOM (page structure) diffs. Each source type is handled by a dedicated sub-tool under tools// inside the cs-09-monitor repository: | Sub-tool | What it checks | How it detects change | |---|---|---| | federal-register | Federal Register notices and rulemakings | Scheduled XML and API diffs for FAR, DFARS, and small-business rule updates. | | ecfr | Electronic Code of Federal Regulations | ETag and XML diffs tracking modified clauses, thresholds, and effective dates. | | nist-csrc | NIST Computer Security Resource Center | Scheduled feed and DOM diffs for cybersecurity standards such as SP 800-171. | | linked-tool-watch | External tools marked linked in the catalog | Periodic HTTP and DOM checks for dead links, new paywalls, or added tracking scripts. | | live-catalog | Tools built and published as live | Scheduled health and rule-version checks against active ClearedStack tools. | When a diff confirms a meaningful change, cs-09-monitor does not patch tools itself—it reopens the affected PA-XXXX item in hub-queue-api so the main pipeline handles it deterministically: - Reopening live items: If a regulation shifts or a live tool drifts out of date, cs-09-monitor places the item in the urgent priority lane and routes it back toward building for an updated release—or toward retired if the underlying rule was repealed. - Reopening parked items: Items previously deferred in parked because of a pending rule or missing public data are re-checked on schedule. Once the blocker clears, cs-09-monitor returns the item to observed for a fresh evaluation. - Reopening linked items: If an external free tool goes offline or starts tracking users, cs-09-monitor moves it back to observed so the owner can decide whether to build a clean-room replacement.

title: cs-10-notify: Deduplication, Git Routing, and Alerts
subtitle: Workers 09 & 10: Continuous Monitoring & Notifications
summary: cs-10-notify is the cross-cutting router that turns worker failures, needs subtool pauses, and owner-approved Portal proposals into clean repository commits, al...
content: cs-10-notify: Deduplication, Git Routing, and Alerts Workers 09 & 10: Continuous Monitoring & Notifications cs-10-notify is the cross-cutting router that turns worker failures, needs subtool pauses, and owner-approved Portal proposals into clean repository commits, alerts, and live browser updates. A key job of cs-10-notify is issue deduplication by deterministic fingerprint . If two hundred queued items hit the exact same unfamiliar HTML table or timed-out endpoint, creating two hundred identical tickets would drown out real problems. Before opening an issue or firing an alert, cs-10-notify computes a repeatable fingerprint from the worker name, sanitized error code (such as E TIMEOUT or E NEEDS SUBTOOL ), and failure pattern. If an open issue with that fingerprint already exists in cs-git , cs-10-notify increments the occurrence count on that existing issue instead of creating noise. To keep responsibilities cleanly separated, cs-10-notify relies on four deterministic sub-tools: | Sub-tool | Responsibility | Where it writes | |---|---|---| | internal-git | Commits owner-approved anonymous Portal edits ( DATA , CONFIG , ISSUE from cs-04-decide ), needs subtool tasks, and fingerprinted error issues. | Cluster-private cs-git repositories. | | github-mirror | Coordinates outbound code mirroring on change so public contributors can inspect every commit and issue. | Public GitHub mirror (source code only; zero container images). | | webhook-alert | Dispatches concise owner notifications when a genuinely new fingerprinted error, P0 failure, or urgent regulatory shift occurs. | Configured external webhook endpoint. | | portal-sse | Pushes sanitized real-time Server-Sent Events (SSE) through hub-queue-api to clearedstack-web . | Public Portal UI ( /guides/command/ , /guides/apps/ , /guides/pipeline/ , /tools/ apps , and live ✎ edit status pills). | Through portal-sse , a visitor who submits an anonymous ✎ edit watches their proposal move live from Proposed to Approved (in cs-04-decide ), then Building (as internal-git commits to cs-git and cs-runner builds), and finally Live —all without signing in or refreshing the page.

content: The Redesigned 10-Worker Workflow & Lifecycle How the ten deterministic worker repositories replace the original ten website stages, how items move through fourteen states including non-linear loops, and how priority lanes keep the pipeline responsive. project L.6  ClearedStack v3.1 turns the original ten-stage prior-art workflow from a static set of essays into a live, 100% deterministic pipeline. Ten small Go services ( cs-01-intake through cs-10-notify ) run in the cs-workers Kubernetes namespace and pull leased work from hub-queue-api . There is zero AI at runtime: every step uses repeatable rules, templates, and sub-tools so the same inputs always produce the same outputs. title: The 14 item states and non-linear moves
subtitle: The Redesigned 10-Worker Workflow & Lifecycle
summary: An item ( PA-XXXX ) does not always march straight from intake to live. The state machine supports 14 explicit states, including early exits, side-branches, rev...
content: The 14 item states and non-linear moves The Redesigned 10-Worker Workflow & Lifecycle An item ( PA-XXXX ) does not always march straight from intake to live. The state machine supports 14 explicit states, including early exits, side-branches, revisit loops, and a fail-closed pause state when a worker encounters an unfamiliar format. | State | Meaning | Normal next step | Non-linear moves & loops | |---|---|---|---| | discovered | Candidate URL detected by cs-01-intake . | recorded | Moves to rejected if dead, unreachable, or duplicate. | | recorded | Assigned a PA-XXXX ID and deduplicated. | observed | Pauses in needs subtool if intake source format is unknown. | | observed | Public pages extracted and raw snapshot sealed. | scored or screened-out | Pauses in needs subtool if cs-02-observe hits an unknown layout. | | screened-out | Failed one of the 5 knockout gates. | Terminal (archived) | Owner override in cs-04-decide can return it to observed . | | scored | Graded on the 100-point rubric by cs-03-evaluate . | approved | Owner in cs-04-decide can choose parked , linked , merged , or rejected . | | approved | Owner chose Build ; provenance & spec compiled. | building | Pauses in needs subtool if cs-05-provenance lacks a spec profile. | | building | Static repo generated ( cs-06-build ) and verified ( cs-07-verify ). | live | Moves to parked if blocked by regulatory ambiguity. | | live | Published in the catalog ( cs-08-catalog ). | Monitored by cs-09-monitor | Revisit loop: regulatory drift sends it back to building ; repeal moves it to retired . | | parked | Valid idea deferred for missing data, pending rules, or capacity. | Held in backlog | Revisit loop: cs-09-monitor returns it to observed when the blocker clears. | | linked | Acceptable free, private tool already exists; linked in catalog. | Monitored by cs-09-monitor | Revisit loop: if the external tool breaks or adds tracking, returns to observed . | | merged | Scope folded into an existing or planned tool repository. | Catalog note published | Re-opens to observed only if the parent tool is retired. | | rejected | Declined with a public rationale in the decision log. | Terminal (archived) | None unless re-submitted as a new candidate after major changes. | | retired | Decommissioned from live with historical note retained. | Terminal (archived) | None. | | needs subtool | Fail-closed pause when a worker hits an unknown layout or rule. | Resumes previous worker | cs-10-notify opens a task in the owning repo; once cs-runner builds the new sub-tool and cs-store deploys it, hub-queue-api automatically replays the item. |

title: How priority lanes flow end-to-end
subtitle: The Redesigned 10-Worker Workflow & Lifecycle
summary: Every queue lease served by hub-queue-api belongs to one of three priority lanes. Workers always drain urgent before normal , and normal before backfill , so a ...
content: How priority lanes flow end-to-end The Redesigned 10-Worker Workflow & Lifecycle Every queue lease served by hub-queue-api belongs to one of three priority lanes. Workers always drain urgent before normal , and normal before backfill , so a single 4 GiB node stays responsive even during large discovery sweeps. | Priority lane | What enters this lane | End-to-end flow behavior | |---|---|---| | urgent | Regulatory changes from cs-09-monitor affecting live tools, owner-approved public edits, and replayed needs subtool items after a sub-tool fix ships. | Preempts all other work at every worker ( cs-01 through cs-10 ) so live catalog fixes and unblocked items finish first. | | normal | Standard single candidates from community submissions or owner research, plus routine scheduled revisit checks. | Processed in FIFO order once the urgent lane is empty. | | backfill | Bulk automated web-sweep discoveries and low-urgency historical records. | Runs only when both urgent and normal queues are clear, preventing bulk sweeps from stalling user-facing updates. |

title: What happens to what you type
subtitle: Guide · Section L.1
summary: Where your information goes when you use a shipped tool or the ClearedStack v3.1 Portal, how public views and anonymous edits protect privacy, and what never to enter.
content: What happens to what you type Where your information goes when you use a shipped tool or the ClearedStack v3.1 Portal, how public views and anonymous edits protect privacy, and what never to enter. start L.1  The short answer is that everything you type into a shipped tool stays on your computer, and everything on the public Portal is sanitized before it ever leaves the cluster. This guide explains how both halves work in ClearedStack v3.1, where the limits are, and how to check them yourself. Shipped tools run locally in your browser Most web applications collect what you type, send it to a server, and return an answer. Your information leaves your machine before you see a result. Every shipped ClearedStack tool has only the local half. When you open a tool, your browser downloads the static page

title: Shipped tools run locally in your browser
subtitle: What happens to what you type
summary: Most web applications collect what you type, send it to a server, and return an answer. Your information leaves your machine before you see a result. Every ship...
content: Shipped tools run locally in your browser What happens to what you type Most web applications collect what you type, send it to a server, and return an answer. Your information leaves your machine before you see a result. Every shipped ClearedStack tool has only the local half. When you open a tool, your browser downloads the static page and its compiled JavaScript once. After that, all arithmetic, text parsing, and file reading happen on your workstation. There is no backend server waiting for your input, no login, no analytics, and zero network calls. Every page and shipped tool enforces a Content Security Policy with connect-src 'self' . That instruction tells your browser to block any outbound network request, third-party API call, or form submission to another server. If a line of code tried to send your numbers elsewhere, your browser would refuse.

title: Zero AI at runtime
subtitle: What happens to what you type
summary: Neither the shipped tools nor the 10 platform workers ( cs-01 through cs-10 ) run artificial intelligence models at runtime. Calculations, parsers, and pipeline...
content: Zero AI at runtime What happens to what you type Neither the shipped tools nor the 10 platform workers ( cs-01 through cs-10 ) run artificial intelligence models at runtime. Calculations, parsers, and pipeline rules are 100% deterministic code that you can inspect in each MIT-licensed repository. AI tools (Claude Code and Antigravity) are used only during development to help the human maintainer draft code, documentation, and tests. Every formula and rule is verified by a person against official regulations before release. See How AI is used to build this project.

title: What the public Portal exposes (pub. views)
subtitle: What happens to what you type
summary: ClearedStack v3.1 has a single public door: the clearedstack-web Portal at clearedstack.com . Everything running in the cluster is visible there without signing...
content: What the public Portal exposes (pub. views) What happens to what you type ClearedStack v3.1 has a single public door: the clearedstack-web Portal at clearedstack.com . Everything running in the cluster is visible there without signing in—live app and worker health, queue depths, item trails, and sanitized error codes such as E TIMEOUT , E PARSE , or E NEEDS SUBTOOL . Internal infrastructure stays strictly cluster-private. The Portal queries Postgres only through read-only pub. views under the pub ro database role, and cs-store strips node, pod, and network metadata before reporting status. The following never appear in pub. views or on the Portal: - internal cluster IPs, node names, pod hostnames, and .svc.cluster.local addresses - NetworkPolicy rules and Ingress internals - database passwords, ServiceAccount tokens, GitHub push tokens, signing keys, and the daily IP salt

title: Anonymous edits use daily-salted IP hashes
subtitle: What happens to what you type
summary: Anyone can propose an edit anywhere on the Portal using the ✎ button without creating an account. To stop spam and automated abuse without storing personal data...
content: Anonymous edits use daily-salted IP hashes What happens to what you type Anyone can propose an edit anywhere on the Portal using the ✎ button without creating an account. To stop spam and automated abuse without storing personal data or requiring a login, submissions pass through a five-layer shield: 1. Browser Proof-of-Work: your browser solves a ~1-second SHA-256 puzzle on submit. 2. Honeypot field: a hidden input silently discards automated scraper submissions. 3. Daily-salted IP hash rate limit: the Portal hashes your IP address with a secret salt that rotates daily to enforce rate limits. Raw IP addresses are never stored in the database. 4. Strict schema validation: ownership map.json checks the target element, edit class ( DATA , CONFIG , or ISSUE ), and 4 KB maximum size, stripping all HTML and scripts. 5. Human approval gate: accepted proposals sit in core.edit proposal as pending approval and never touch cs-git or the cluster until the owner approves them in cs-04-decide .

title: Check it yourself
subtitle: What happens to what you type
summary: You can confirm that a shipped tool makes zero network calls in about a minute using made-up numbers: 1. Open the tool and open your browser’s developer tools (...
content: Check it yourself What happens to what you type You can confirm that a shipped tool makes zero network calls in about a minute using made-up numbers: 1. Open the tool and open your browser’s developer tools ( F12 on Windows or Linux, Command-Option-I on Mac). 2. Select the Network tab and click the clear button. 3. Type numbers, paste text, or load a file, then watch the list. A compliant tool adds nothing to the Network tab while you work. You can also right-click any page, choose View Page Source , and search for Content-Security-Policy to confirm connect-src 'self' is present. Load any shipped tool, then disconnect from the network by turning off Wi-Fi or unplugging the cable. Keep using the tool. If it still computes answers, all work is happening locally on your computer.

title: What a web server and your screen can still see
subtitle: What happens to what you type
summary: To send you a webpage, the host serving clearedstack.com sees standard HTTP request metadata: your IP address, the page requested, the timestamp, and your brows...
content: What a web server and your screen can still see What happens to what you type To send you a webpage, the host serving clearedstack.com sees standard HTTP request metadata: your IP address, the page requested, the timestamp, and your browser user agent. Nothing you type into a local tool is part of that request. Keeping data off a server also does not protect your screen locally. Browser extensions, employer endpoint monitoring, clipboard managers, screen sharing, and built-in browser translation or AI assistant features can all read what is on your screen. Use a clean browser profile or private window for sensitive work, and clear browser storage when using a shared computer.

title: What never to enter
subtitle: What happens to what you type
summary: - Classified information: never enter it into any tool, browser, or form. - Controlled Unclassified Information (CUI) and real contract rates: never enter CUI, ...
content: What never to enter What happens to what you type - Classified information: never enter it into any tool, browser, or form. - Controlled Unclassified Information (CUI) and real contract rates: never enter CUI, export-controlled technical data, or real contract rates into public Portal forms (such as ✎ edit proposals, which are public by design) or into AI prompts. For local shipped tools, remember that running in a browser does not change the rules for the workstation you sit at—handle CUI and proprietary rates only on systems your contract and company policy allow, or host a copy inside your own network. - Unsure how a tool behaves? Test it with made-up numbers first.

title: If you find a tool that breaks the rule
subtitle: What happens to what you type
summary: Stop using it and report it. Email contact@clearedstack.com or open an issue in the tool’s repository with the request address you saw in the Network tab. Any t...
content: If you find a tool that breaks the rule What happens to what you type Stop using it and report it. Email contact@clearedstack.com or open an issue in the tool’s repository with the request address you saw in the Network tab. Any tool that sends user input over the network is removed from the catalog until it is fixed.
